## §1 Conventions

### 1.1 Requirements Language

> **Requirement keywords**
> The key words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT** and **MAY** in this protocol are
> to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 when, and only when, they appear in
> capitals.

| Keyword | Meaning | A violation is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **MUST** / **MUST NOT** | An absolute requirement of the protocol. | an error: the output does not conform |
| **SHOULD** / **SHOULD NOT** | A strong recommendation. Deviation is allowed only for a reason that holds for this document. | a warning |
| **MAY** | A truly optional behaviour. A consumer MUST accept output with or without it. | never reported |

The same words in lower case carry their ordinary English meaning and state no requirement.

Examples, sketches and captions are **informative**: they illustrate a requirement and never add
one. Where an example and a requirement disagree, the requirement governs and the example is a
defect.

#### Related

- Conformance (§1.2) — what an output has to satisfy to conform
- Rule Status and Scope (§1.3) — how settled each requirement is

### 1.2 Conformance

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `conventions-conformance` · Tags: conventions

> **✅ Normative**
> A **conforming output** is a Markdown rendering of a document that satisfies every MUST of this
> protocol, optionally accompanied by a sidecar that satisfies The Sidecar (§3.4). A **producer**
> conforms when every output it emits conforms.

#### What is judged

An output is judged against the **document as rendered** — the pages a reader sees — and never
against the file's text layer, OCR, or another output. See The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1).

| Part | Required | Governed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Markdown | always | Markdown Rendering (§3.2) and chapters 4–13 |
| Sidecar | when boxes are requested | The Sidecar (§3.4), Boxes and Granularity (§3.3) |

#### Verdicts

A check of an output against the protocol yields findings, each tied to one requirement:

- a violated **MUST** is an **error**; any error makes the output **non-conforming**;
- a violated **SHOULD** is a **warning**; warnings do not affect conformance;
- a requirement marked ❓ open yields warnings only, whatever its keyword, until it is settled.

#### Equivalent forms

Where the protocol accepts more than one rendering (⚖️), every accepted rendering conforms, and a
consumer MUST treat them as equal. A document MUST NOT mix accepted renderings of the same
situation — see Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2) and Accepted Alternatives (§A.1).

#### Output options

A few requirements depend on what the producer was asked to produce, such as whether table
fragments are joined across pages. They are listed in Output Options (§3.5); an output is judged under
the options it was produced with.





#### Related

- Requirements Language (§1.1) — the meaning of MUST, SHOULD and MAY
- Output Options (§3.5) — requirements that depend on the producer's settings
- Accepted Alternatives (§A.1) — renderings that are equal for conformance

### 1.3 Rule Status and Scope

Every rule carries two badges: its **status**, which says how settled it is, and its **scope**,
which says what evidence applying it needs.

#### Status

| Badge | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ✅ **Normative** | Settled. The requirement holds as written. |
| ⚖️ **Equivalent forms** | Two renderings conform. A document uses one of them throughout. |
| ❓ **Open point** | Not yet settled. The rule states a working default, which conforming output follows, and a proposed resolution. Violations are reported as warnings only. Every open point is closed before the protocol is published — see Ambiguity List. |

#### Scope

| Badge | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 📄 **Page rule** | Can be applied from the page alone. |
| 📚 **Document rule** | Needs other pages of the same document; decided once and applied on every page. See Document Rules (§4.1). |

#### How a rule is laid out

1. **The requirement** — in the status callout, in the language of Requirements Language (§1.1).
2. **The situation** — how the element is recognised on the page, often with a sketch.
3. **Sub-cases** — each with its own requirement and its examples beneath it.
4. **Examples** — ✅ *Sample* (the rule applies) or ❌ *Counter-sample* (it looks like it applies and
   does not, or a rendering got it wrong), each with its **Expected Markdown**.
5. **Related** — neighbouring rules, with why each resolves differently.

#### Conventions in the examples

- Fenced `text` blocks sketch **printed layout**, not output.
- `Expected Markdown` blocks are conforming output for the region shown. A line holding only
  `<!-- … -->` marks elided content.
- `Non-conforming output` blocks show a rendering that violates the rule, for contrast.
- `ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE` in a sketch marks a cell covered by a rowspan from the row above.

#### Related

- Requirements Language (§1.1) · Conformance (§1.2) · Document Rules (§4.1)

## §2 Principles

### 2.1 The Page Is the Ground Truth

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `principles-the-page-is-the-ground-truth` · Tags: principles

> **✅ Normative**
> The output MUST represent the document **as rendered**: what a careful reader extracts from the
> pages, semantic structure over visual appearance, with text transcribed verbatim — typos
> included.

The PDF text layer, OCR and any other output are **supporting evidence, never authority**. Where
they disagree with the rendered page, the page governs.

- Text MUST be transcribed exactly as printed. Spelling, punctuation, capitalisation and numbers
  MUST NOT be corrected, normalised or completed.
- Content that is not visible on the rendered page — hidden text-layer strings, text clipped by the
  page edge, white-on-white text — MUST NOT appear in the output. See Clipped Text (§7.3.1).
- Structure MUST be read from what the page prints and how it is laid out, not from what the
  content "should" be: a table is a table because the page lays it out as one.
- A disputed character SHOULD be settled from a zoomed view of the page or the word geometry,
  never from what looks plausible.

#### Which text counts as page content

Text is in scope only when it has a **visually perceptible presence in the rendered page**.
A string existing in the source file, being selectable, or being returned by OCR does not make it
visible content. Visibility is judged on the supplied rendition with its original colours,
opacity, clipping and overlays intact. Ordinary zoom or a higher-resolution rendering MAY be
used to inspect real fine print; changing contrast, recolouring text, removing an overlay, or
magnifying a microscopic source object until it becomes readable MUST NOT bring hidden content
into scope.

| Situation | Required treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Hidden OCR/text layer, transparent text, invisible rendering mode, text behind an opaque object, or text wholly outside the crop | Omit the hidden string. It MUST NOT be transcribed or given an output element or box. |
| White text on white, black on black, or effectively imperceptible contrast such as `#010101` on `#000000` | Omit text whose presence cannot be perceived with the original appearance. Contrast enhancement or the source colour values MUST NOT be used to recover it into the output. |
| Microscopic text such as `0.01 pt` at its final rendered scale | Omit it when it has no perceptible textual presence. Arbitrarily large zoom or a source-text dump does not make it page content. |
| Small but visible fine print, a faint watermark, or low-contrast text still perceptible as text | Keep it. Inspect at ordinary zoom or higher rendering resolution; size or low contrast alone is not an exclusion. |
| A visible text region whose characters remain unreadable | Preserve legible fragments and use `[illegible]` for the unreadable span. Do not guess from OCR or context, and do not treat a visibly present region as invisible. |
| Partly clipped, covered or redacted text | Keep only visible characters and apply Clipped Text (§7.3.1), Overlapping Text (§7.3.6) or Redacted Text (§7.3.8); never recover concealed characters from the source layer. |

A font-size or colour threshold alone MUST NOT decide visibility: source transforms can enlarge a
small font, and contrast depends on the actual rendered background. `0.01 pt` refers to final
appearance, not an untransformed font-size field. The distinction is **no perceptible text**
(omit) versus **perceptible text with unreadable characters** (retain the evidence without guessing).
The hidden string MUST NOT leak into labels, descriptions, alternate text or sidecar metadata.
An optional review note MAY describe the exclusion without copying the hidden content.

These exclusions define the scope of Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2). They do not permit dropping
readable footnotes, margin text, rotated text, dense tables or deliberately faint but visible marks.
For damaged regions or unusable pages, apply Ignoring and Rejecting (§5.6).





#### Related

- Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2) — the two failures every rule guards against
- Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) — verbatim transcription inside tables
- Clipped Text (§7.3.1) — what is visible is what is transcribed

### 2.2 Never Drop, Never Invent

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `principles-never-drop-never-invent` · Tags: principles

> **✅ Normative**
> Every piece of printed content MUST survive into the output (**never drop**), and the output
> MUST NOT contain a label, value, span, header, structure or relationship that the page does not
> print (**never invent**).

Almost every rule in this protocol exists to prevent one of these two failures.

#### Never drop

Printed content means visually perceptible content under The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1). Hidden,
microscopic or imperceptibly low-contrast source strings are outside that scope; visible but
unreadable text is retained as evidence with `[illegible]`, not silently discarded.

A visible row, column, cell, marker, header, caption, footnote, stamp or repeated table MUST appear
in the output. The most-dropped items are the last row of a table, trailing summary lines, detached
cells beside a grid, sparse columns proven only by their header, and text in the margins.

Where the protocol is unsure how to represent something, the rendering that loses no content is
the conforming one.

#### Never invent

The output MUST NOT add what the page does not print. A `rowspan` is a claim that the page merged
those cells; if the page printed them separately, the claim is false. A heading level, a header
tier, a list nesting or a table boundary is likewise a claim about the page and MUST be supported
by it.

Placeholders that stand for content — `[image]`, `[The image shows…]`, `...` — are invented and
MUST NOT appear, except the explicit markers this protocol defines (such as `[blank]` for an empty
form field and `[signature]`).





#### Related

- The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1) — what the output is judged against
- Traceability (§2.3) — every output element points back at printed content
- Accepted Alternatives (§A.1) — where two renderings are equally faithful

### 2.3 Traceability

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `principles-traceability` · Tags: principles, boxes

> **✅ Normative**
> Every element of the output MUST be attributable to the place on the page it was read from. When
> boxes are requested, every Markdown element MUST have a box, and every box MUST cover exactly the
> printed content of its element.

Traceability is what lets a reader of the Markdown — a person or a model — go back to the page to
check, cite or highlight a statement. It is also what makes the two principles checkable: a
Markdown element with no printed source is invented; printed content with no Markdown element is
dropped.

- An element is traced by its **box**: the region of the page its content occupies. What a box
  covers and how fine boxes go are defined in Boxes and Granularity (§3.3); how boxes are carried is
  defined in The Sidecar (§3.4).
- Content the protocol moves out of its printed position — a watermark placed first, a sidenote
  placed after its paragraph, a folio recorded on its own — still traces to where it was printed.
- A Markdown element that was synthesised rather than transcribed (for example a chart table built
  from marks) traces to the region of the page it was read from.





#### Related

- Boxes and Granularity (§3.3) — what a box covers, and how fine boxes go
- The Sidecar (§3.4) — where boxes are carried
- Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2) — traceability makes both failures visible

## §3 Output model

### 3.1 Elements

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `output-elements` · Tags: output, output-model, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A document is represented as a sequence of pages, each a sequence of **elements** in reading
> order. Every element MUST have exactly one class from the table below and MUST be rendered in
> Markdown as that class prescribes.

An element is the smallest unit the protocol reasons about: it has one class, one rendering, one
position in reading order and — when boxes are requested — one box. The classes are the layout
classes of Block Classes (§5.3); the rendering column says how each appears in the Markdown.
An element's class MUST be identical in its layout annotation and its Markdown representation.
Its Markdown syntax MAY be shared by several classes; the element's role determines the class.

| Class | Rendering in Markdown | Defined in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Title** | ATX heading at the document's top level | Document Type (§4.4), Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5) |
| **Section-header** | ATX heading (`#`…`######`) at its document depth | Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5), Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7) |
| **Text** | Paragraph; inline marks per Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) | chapter 7 |
| **List-item** | Markdown list item, nesting by printed indentation | Bullets and Sub-Bullets (§8.1) |
| **Table** | HTML `<table>` | chapter 9 |
| **Caption** | For a table or chart, `<caption>` first or last inside its table HTML according to reading order; otherwise a paragraph adjacent to its object | Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) |
| **Footnote** | Paragraph at its printed position | Footnotes Inside the Frame (§9.7.2) |
| **Formula** | `$$ … $$` LaTeX, with its printed equation number | Displayed Equations (§7.2.2) |
| **Picture** | Its content as text: a chart table (`<table data-source="chart">`), a `diagram/<language>` block, a `description` fallback block, or a prose description | Images and Figures (§12.1.2) |
| **Code** | Fenced code block | Block Classes (§5.3) |
| **Page-header** / **Page-footer** | Its own block, never a heading | Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6), Markdown Rendering (§3.2) |
| **Form** / **Key-Value Region** | Key-value lines with `[blank]` for empty fields | chapter 10 |
| **Checkbox-Selected** / **-Unselected** | `[x]` / `[ ]` before its label | Checkboxes (§10.4.2) |
| **Document Index** | Nested list, label then page number | Table of Contents (§6.10) |

#### Elements inside elements

A table contains **cells**; a list contains **items**; a form contains **fields**. These inner
elements are rendered inside their parent's Markdown and receive boxes only at the granularity that
was requested — see Boxes and Granularity (§3.3).

A table or chart caption is rendered inside its object's `<table>` but retains the Caption class
and its own layout box. HTML nesting does not merge the caption into the Table or Picture class.

#### Content outside the reading flow

Watermarks, margin banners, stamps, seals, handwriting and sidenotes are elements too. Each has a
defined place in the Markdown even though it sits outside the body flow on the page — see
Watermarks (§7.3.13), Margin Banners (§7.3.5), Seals and Round Stamps (§7.3.9), Handwritten Annotations (§7.3.3) and
Marginal Notes (§6.4).





#### Related

- Block Classes (§5.3) — how to tell the classes apart on the page
- Markdown Rendering (§3.2) — the rules that hold across every class
- Boxes and Granularity (§3.3) — which elements get boxes

### 3.2 Markdown Rendering

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `output-markdown-rendering` · Tags: output, output-model, markdown

> **✅ Normative**
> The output MUST be one Markdown document for the whole document, with pages in order separated
> by a line holding only `---`, and each page's elements in reading order. Where Markdown has no
> syntax for a construct, the output MUST use the HTML element this protocol names, and MUST NOT
> invent a notation of its own.

#### Page boundaries

- Pages MUST appear in document order, each separated from the next by a line containing only
  `---`, preceded and followed by a blank line.
- `---` MUST NOT be used for anything else. A printed separator rule is `<hr/>` — see
  Line Separators and Breaks (§6.3) — and printed text that begins with `---` is escaped — see
  Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4).
- A page with no ink at all is represented by the single line `<!-- blank page -->` — see
  Ignoring and Rejecting (§5.6).
- Content MUST stay on the page it is printed on: a table, paragraph or cell that runs onto the
  next page is split at the boundary — see Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) and Output Options (§3.5).

#### Markdown first, HTML where Markdown cannot

| Construct | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| Headings | ATX `#` headings |
| Bold / italic | Markdown `**` / `*`; inside HTML tables, see Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) |
| Underline, superscript, subscript, highlight | `<u>`, `<sup>`, `<sub>`, `<mark>` |
| Meaningful text colour | `<font color="NAME">` |
| Tables | HTML `<table>` with `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>`, `rowspan`, `colspan` |
| Tables representing charts | HTML `<table data-source="chart">` — see Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1) |
| Table and chart captions | `<caption>…</caption>` first or last inside `<table>` according to reading order — see Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) |
| Printed separator rule | `<hr/>` |
| Line break inside one block | a plain newline — see Line Breaks Inside a Block (§6.2) |
| Maths | `$$ … $$`, inline and displayed |
| Diagrams and blueprints | fenced `diagram/<language>` block; fenced `description` only when no suitable language can faithfully represent the content |

Tables MUST be HTML because spanning cells, multi-tier headers and multi-line cells cannot be
expressed in pipe tables; pipe tables MUST NOT be used. See Nested Tables (§9.5.2).

#### Markers

The protocol defines a small set of bracketed markers for printed things that are not text. They
are the only placeholders allowed: `[blank]` an empty field, `[x]` / `[ ]` a checkbox,
`[signature]` / `[signature:{name}]`, `[seal: …]`, `[logo: …]` / `[logo]`, `[watermark: …]`, `[stamp: …]` / `[stamp]`, `[handwritten: …]`, `[REDACTED]`. Each is
defined in its own rule.

#### Page header and footer bands

A header band MUST be rendered as its own paragraph(s) at the start of its page's content and a
footer band at the end, never as a heading. A producer MAY wrap each band in `<header>…</header>` /
`<footer>…</footer>`, so a consumer can drop or keep furniture without guessing where it ends; the
wrapper is optional, and output with or without it conforms.





#### Related

- Elements (§3.1) — the rendering of each element class
- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the inline markup table
- Line Separators and Breaks (§6.3) — why `---` is reserved for page boundaries

### 3.3 Boxes and Granularity

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `output-boxes-and-granularity` · Tags: output, output-model, boxes, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A box is the region of the page that an element's printed content occupies. Boxes MUST be given at
> exactly the granularity that was requested, and at that granularity every element MUST have one
> box. A producer MUST NOT return several granularities in place of one.

#### What a box covers

A box MUST enclose all of its element's printed content and SHOULD enclose nothing else. What
belongs to an element — whether a caption is inside a table's box, whether a list item's box
includes its bullet, where a picture ends — is decided by the layout rules: Block Boundaries (§5.2),
Block Annotation (§5.1) and Block Classes (§5.3). A box never covers content moved out of its position
in the Markdown: a watermark's box is where the watermark is printed.

#### The four levels

| Level | A box is given for… | Suited to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **none** | each element (region level) | the default: region-level grounding |
| **cell** | each element, and each table cell | per-value verification and highlighting |
| **line** | each element, and each printed line | line-level citation, reading-order checks |
| **word** | each element, and each word | per-token grounding |

#### The levels are a ladder

The levels subsume one another, and the resolution rule is strict precedence:

```text
word  >  line  >  cell  >  none
```

A request naming several levels MUST be served at the finest one named; naming coarser levels
alongside it changes nothing.

#### Choosing a level

Finer is not better. Each step down multiplies the number of boxes, and every box can be wrong,
mis-attributed or drift out of alignment with its text. A consumer SHOULD request the coarsest
level that answers its question.

Where a rule turns on geometry — *is this value printed once or three times? does this ruling
line stop before that column?* — the evidence lives at **cell** level or finer. A coarser output
can neither settle nor dispute those questions.





#### Related

- Traceability (§2.3) — why every element has a box
- Block Boundaries (§5.2) — what a Picture or Table box contains
- The Sidecar (§3.4) — how boxes are carried

### 3.4 The Sidecar

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `output-the-sidecar` · Tags: output, output-model, boxes, sidecar

> **✅ Normative**
> When boxes are requested, the output MUST include a sidecar: a structured file that lists, page by
> page, every element with its class, its Markdown and its box. The sidecar is the source the
> Markdown is rendered from; the Markdown MUST be exactly the concatenation of the sidecar's element
> Markdown in reading order, each element preceded by its inline box anchor, with pages joined as Markdown Rendering (§3.2) requires.

The sidecar is secondary to the rest of this protocol: the rules that matter are how the document
is interpreted and rendered, and what a box covers. This note fixes only what a sidecar must carry.
Its encoding is the page-and-items structure LlamaParse already returns, normalised.

#### Contents

| Level | Carries |
| --- | --- |
| Document | its pages, in order |
| Page | 1-based page number; page width and height; printed page number when requested — see Printed Page Numbers (§6.6); `line_numbers` when requested — see Pleading Line Numbers (§5.8) |
| Element | class — see Elements (§3.1); its Markdown; its box; finer boxes at the requested granularity |
| Box | `x`, `y`, `w`, `h` in the page's coordinate space, origin top-left |
| Table element | additionally `continuesFromPreviousPage` and `continuesOnNextPage`, booleans — see Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) |
| Finer box | as a box, plus the character range of the element's Markdown it covers (`startIndex`, `endIndex`, end exclusive, counted in the element's Markdown including its syntax) |

```json
{"page": 3, "width": 612, "height": 792, "printedPageNumber": "iv",
 "items": [{"type": "Section-header", "md": "## 9.2 Pressure",
            "bBox": {"x": 72, "y": 80, "w": 200, "h": 18},
            "layoutAwareBbox": [{"x": 72, "y": 80, "w": 200, "h": 18, "startIndex": 3, "endIndex": 15}]}]}
```

- Every element of the Markdown MUST correspond to one sidecar item, and every item to one element.
- Character ranges MUST point into the element's own Markdown, so any span of the Markdown resolves
  to a box.

#### Boxes in the Markdown itself

When boxes are requested, the Markdown MUST also carry each element's box inline, so that a single
Markdown file is traceable on its own: each element is preceded by an HTML comment anchor holding
the same box as the sidecar.

```markdown
<!-- el p=3 x=72 y=80 w=200 h=18 -->
## 9.2 Pressure
```

The anchors are invisible when rendered and are stripped when the Markdown is given to a model that
does not need them. When boxes are not requested, the Markdown carries no anchors.





#### Related

- Boxes and Granularity (§3.3) — what the boxes cover and how fine they go
- Traceability (§2.3) — why every element is traced
- Printed Page Numbers (§6.6) — the page-level printed number

### 3.5 Output Options

*❓ Open point · document rule*
Rule ID: `output-output-options` · Tags: output, output-model, options

> **❓ Open point**
> Four situations have more than one conforming output, depending on what the producer was asked
> to produce. **Working default:** the narrower reading — fragments separate, graphics described,
> everything printed recorded — which conforms under either setting. **Proposed resolution:** make
> each an explicit, named option of the request, and judge the output under the options it was
> produced with.

Every other requirement holds whatever the producer was configured to do. These four do not: an
output that assumes a setting the producer did not use is not held to a stricter standard; it is
held to an unreachable one.

#### The four options

| The page shows | With the option | Without it (working default) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A printed folio | The number is also recorded on its own, per page | It survives only inside the band text |
| A logo, seal or icon | The mark MAY be referenced as a saved image | Its content MUST be put into the text stream — see Images (§12.1.1) |
| A table continuing overleaf | The fragments MAY be joined into one table | Each fragment MUST stand alone — see Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) |
| A table titled `(continued)` | As above | The marker is kept and the fragment stands alone — see Continued in the Title (§9.2.3) |

#### Why the narrower reading is the default

Nothing in the narrower reading is wrong under the wider setting; it is only less than the wider
setting allows. The reverse is not true: an output that fuses two fragments cannot be split into two
again if the setting turns out to be off.





#### Related

- Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) — fragments and their continuation flags, which a join would build on
- Printed Page Numbers (§6.6) — the folio option
- Images (§12.1.1) — what a mark becomes when it is not referenced

## §4 Document level

### 4.1 Document Rules

Almost every rule in this protocol is a **page rule**: it can be applied with only the page in
view. A handful are **document rules**: applying them needs other pages of the same document. Every
rule carries a 📄 or 📚 badge saying which it is — see Rule Status and Scope (§1.3).

| | 📄 Page rule | 📚 Document rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evidence** | this page alone | this page and others in the document |
| **When it is decided** | on each page | once, at or before the first page that forces it |
| **What a later page does** | decides again from its own print | follows the earlier decision |

#### The document rules

- Document Type (§4.4) — slide deck or paged document, and which sheet is the cover
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — a band that is furniture anywhere is furniture everywhere
- Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5) — a new page does not restart the hierarchy
- Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2) — every ⚖️ rendering is held for the whole document
- Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) — fragments stay on their pages, with continuation flags set across each break

#### Precedence

The document decisions come first: the document type and the cover gate the Title class and the
heading depth on every page, and the furniture decision gates which margin bands are headers and
footers. Page rules are then applied within those decisions, and each ⚖️ choice, once made, holds
for the rest of the document.

#### A single page

A document rule cannot be settled from a single page. Each document rule states the conforming
behaviour for that case, and the pattern is always the same: the output applies what the page
itself supports and never assumes what other pages print.

#### Related

- The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1) — the requirement every rule, page or document, serves
- Document Representation Protocol — the full index

### 4.2 Choices Made Once Per Document

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `document-choices-made-once-per-document` · Tags: rule, document, either

> **✅ Normative**
> Where the protocol accepts two renderings of a situation, the rendering chosen at the first page
> that forces the choice MUST be used on every later page of the same document. A document MUST NOT
> mix the accepted renderings of one situation.

An ⚖️ rule accepts either of two renderings. Accepting either does not mean switching between them:
a document whose units rows are header rows on page 3 and folded into labels on page 7 is
non-conforming, even though each page on its own conforms.

#### The choices

| Choice | The two renderings | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Units line under a header | second header row · folded into the label above | Units Row (§9.3.5) |
| Printed blank row | kept · left out | Blank and Spacer Rows (§9.5.1) |
| Full-width band inside a grid | spanning header cell · spanning body cell | Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1) |
| Section-divider row | bold `<td>` · `<th>` | Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) |
| Totals block with no frame either way | footer rows · its own key-value table | Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1) |
| Gantt bar edge on a period tick | last period filled · tick reached | Gantt and Sankey Charts (§11.2.3) |

- Where a rule names a default rendering, the output SHOULD use the default, unless an earlier page
  of the same document already used the other rendering; in that case the output MUST keep the
  earlier one.
- The choice holds for the situation, not for the page: two pages that both print a units line
  MUST render it the same way, however far apart they are.

#### A single page

Where only one page of a document is available, the output SHOULD use the rule's default, and MUST
be consistent within that page. Consistency with the rest of the document cannot be judged until
the other pages are available.





#### Related

- Accepted Alternatives (§A.1) — the full list of renderings that are equal for conformance
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — the other decision made once and applied to every page
- Conformance (§1.2) — why mixing two accepted renderings is non-conforming

### 4.3 Cross-Page Tables

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `tables-cross-page-tables` · Tags: continuation, tables

> **✅ Normative**
> A table that runs across a page break MUST be rendered as one fragment per page, each on its own
> page, complete and exactly as that page prints it. Fragments MUST NOT be joined. In the sidecar,
> each fragment MUST carry two continuation flags — *continues from the previous page* and
> *continues onto the next page* — decided at document level, from the pages on both sides of the
> break.

A table runs off the bottom of one page and picks up on the next, sometimes with the headers
repeated, sometimes not, sometimes with "(continued)" in the title.

```text
── page 12 ──                    ── page 13 ──
| State | Rate |                 | State | Rate |   ← header repeated
| AL    | 1.10 |                 | MT    | 0.95 |     (sometimes it isn't)
| …     | …    |                 | …     | …    |
```

#### Fragments stay on their pages

- Rows from two pages MUST NOT be merged into one table, unless a join is requested under
  Output Options (§3.5).
- A header from one page MUST NOT be copied onto another page's fragment. What is printed on a page
  is what that page's fragment holds (**never invent**).
- A cell cut by the page break MUST end at the page boundary; the next page's fragment holds only
  the text visible there. Missing labels or values MUST NOT be repeated to complete either half.
- A printed continuation marker such as `(continued)` is text and MUST be transcribed — see
  Continued in the Title (§9.2.3).

Reading a table's true extent needs a page that is not in view, so a join made from one page is a
guess. A fragment with its continuation flags loses nothing and claims nothing false; a wrong join
loses both fragments, and a fused table cannot be split again.

#### Continuation flags — a document-level decision

Each table fragment in the sidecar carries two boolean flags, `continuesFromPreviousPage` and
`continuesOnNextPage` (see The Sidecar (§3.4)). They are decided with both sides of the break in view,
not from one page alone:

- A fragment that ends a page and the fragment that opens the next page are **one table** when the
  second has the same columns and either prints no header, repeats the first one's header, or is
  marked as continued. Then the first MUST have `continuesOnNextPage: true` and the second
  `continuesFromPreviousPage: true`.
- The two flags MUST agree across the break: a fragment flagged as continuing onto the next page
  requires the first table of the next page to be flagged as continuing from the previous one, and
  the reverse.
- A fragment that does not continue across a break MUST have both flags `false`.

```text
page 12  last table     continuesFromPreviousPage: false   continuesOnNextPage: true
page 13  first table    continuesFromPreviousPage: true    continuesOnNextPage: false
```

#### Signals worth reading

- A repeated header at the top of the second fragment does **not** mean it is a new table — a
  continued table routinely re-declares its columns after a page break. This is the one place
  where header repetition is not a boundary; see Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7).
- A second fragment that starts straight into data rows, with no header, is the strongest ordinary
  continuation signal.
- An explicit "(continued)" in the title or at the foot of the page is stronger still.
- A first fragment whose rows run to the foot of the page with no total row supports the reading;
  a closing total row argues against it.

### 4.4 Document Type

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `document-document-type` · Tags: rule, document, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> Whether a document is a slide deck or a paged document, and which sheet is its cover, MUST be
> decided once from the whole document and applied to every page. Only the cover MAY carry a
> **Title** element.

Two decisions change how single pages are read, and neither can be made from one page:

| Decision | How it is recognised | What it changes on every page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Slide deck or paged document** | A deck is landscape sheets with one title per sheet, each sheet a self-contained slide. | In a deck every slide title is a top-level heading; in a paged document depth carries over page breaks. See Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5). |
| **Which sheet is the cover** | The title or front page: the document's own name set large, often with authors, a date or a logo, and no body text. | Only the cover carries the **Title** class and the document title. The same words on a later page are page furniture or Text. |

```text
sheet 1  QUARTERLY RESERVING REVIEW       ← cover: Title
sheet 2  Quarterly Reserving Review · 2   ← running header: furniture, not Title
```

#### Requirements

- The decisions MUST be made from the document, not from one sheet. A landscape page on its own
  does not make a deck — reports insert landscape tables — and the largest line on sheet 1 is not a
  title if sheet 1 is a transmittal letter.
- A document with **no cover** MUST NOT have a Title element anywhere. The first heading MUST NOT be
  promoted to fill the gap — that is the **never invent** failure.
- The same words printed on a later sheet MUST NOT be a Title element; they are page furniture or
  Text.

#### Mixed documents

A report with a slide deck appended, or a deck with printed appendix pages, MUST be decided per
part. The boundary between the parts is where the decision changes, and each decision MUST be
applied to its whole part rather than sheet by sheet.

#### A single page

Where only one page is available, neither decision can be made. The page MUST be treated as a paged
document with no cover: no Title element, and any title-sized line rendered as a heading at the
depth the page itself supports.





#### Related

- Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5) — the deck exception is decided here and applied there
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — a cover may repeat the running title; the cover occurrence is the title
- Block Classes (§5.3) — the Title class that this decision gates
- Slide Furniture (§5.10) — what a slide carries besides its title

### 4.5 Heading Depth Across Pages

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `headings-heading-depth-across-pages` · Tags: headings, rule, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A new page MUST NOT restart the heading hierarchy. A heading MUST be given the depth its place in
> the document implies, and a top-level heading MUST appear only where the page prints one.

A page break is a printing accident, not a structural boundary. The section that was open at the
foot of one page is still open at the head of the next, and a heading that continues it keeps its
depth.

```text
page 4 …    ## 9.2 Pressure
                9.2.1 Pascal's Law          ← depth 3: inside 9.2
─── page break ───
page 5 …    9.2.2 Variation with Depth      ← still depth 3, not a fresh top level
```

#### Depth comes from the document, not the page

Two signals settle almost every case, in this order:

1. **Printed numbering.** `9.2.1` sits under `9.2` sits under `9`. Where the document numbers its
   sections, the numbering MUST decide the depth, even where the typography disagrees.
2. **Typography, compared across pages.** Where nothing is numbered, a heading's depth MUST be
   judged against the other headings of the same document, not against the rest of its own page.
   The largest line on page 5 is not automatically a top-level heading.

A subsection MUST NOT come out at the same depth as its parent, or shallower. If `9.2` is depth 2
then `9.2.1` is depth 3, on whatever page it lands.

#### Decks are the exception

In a slide deck the slides are peers and each slide title is legitimately top level. Whether the
document is a deck is decided once for the whole document — see Document Type (§4.4) — never slide by
slide.

#### A single page

Where only one page is available, the hierarchy the page itself shows MUST be consistent — a
subsection always deeper than its parent — and the depth MUST be taken from printed numbering where
there is any. Where the absolute depth depends on pages that are not available, the output takes the
depth the page supports and asserts nothing more.

#### Whether it is a heading at all

Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7) separates standalone section titles from run-in labels, repeated
item labels and captions. Principal statement and numbered schedule titles are structural; a
company line directly above one stays a separate paragraph (see Stacked Headings (§6.9)), as do units
lines. A title
inside a grid is transcribed once, in its table position.

The following MUST NOT be rendered as headings:

- a running header — see Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6);
- a label naming the kind of document, such as `ORIGINAL ARTICLE` or `EXHIBIT 2` — it is text; the
  title beneath it is the heading;
- a value typed into a form field, however prominent;
- a table or figure caption — see Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3).





#### Related

- Document Type (§4.4) — decides whether the deck exception applies
- Block Classes (§5.3) — Title vs Section-header
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — a running header never earns a depth at all
- Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) — a caption never becomes a heading

### 4.6 Recurring Page Furniture

*✅ Normative · document rule*
Rule ID: `layout-recurring-page-furniture` · Tags: rule, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> Whether a margin band is page furniture MUST be decided once for the document. A band that is
> page furniture on one page MUST be page furniture — a Page-header or Page-footer, never body text
> and never a heading — on every page it appears on.

The repeated strip at the top or bottom margin: an agency name, a running title, a brand mark, a
document or exhibit stamp, a revision date, a folio. It carries no argument; it tells the reader
which document the sheet belongs to.

```text
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES        PRINTED: 03/18/2021   ← header band
CENTERS FOR MEDICARE & MEDICAID SERVICES       OMB NO. 0938-0391

… the page's actual content …

FORM CMS-2567  Previous Versions Obsolete            Page 3 of 12    ← footer band
```

#### Decided from the document

The same string is easy to read as a title on the page where it is largest or first, and as
furniture everywhere else. The decision MUST be made from several pages: a string that recurs in the
same margin with the same wording is furniture on **all** of them, including the first.

A cover page is the one place a repeated string MAY also be the document title. The cover
occurrence is then the Title and every later occurrence is furniture; the cover MUST NOT decide the
rest of the document. Which sheet is the cover is decided in Document Type (§4.4).

#### A single page

Where only one page is available, a band in the top or bottom margin that carries no argument of its
own — a running title, an agency name, a folio — is furniture. Where the only reason to call it
furniture would be that it repeats on pages that are not available, it MUST be kept where the page
prints it, in its printed position.

#### Never a heading

A running header MUST NOT be rendered as a heading. Promoted, it corrupts the outline twice over: it
invents a section that does not exist, and it repeats that invented section on every page. A
document whose outline is its own masthead repeated forty times has no usable structure left. This
is the **never invent** failure — the page prints a margin band, not a section.

A heading that repeats on more than half the pages of a document is almost always furniture filed as
structure.

#### Bands that contain a graphic

A band MUST be kept together, graphic included; the mark MUST NOT escape into the body flow. What
the graphic itself becomes is decided by Images (§12.1.1) and Logos (§12.1.3).

#### Bands that change partway through

Long documents revise their furniture — a new date, a new form number, a different layout after a
section break. A change of wording does not make the band content. The same disposition MUST apply
before and after the change, and each variant MUST be transcribed as it is printed.





#### Related

- Document Type (§4.4) — which sheet is the cover, where a repeated string may be the title
- Block Classes (§5.3) — the Page-header and Page-footer classes, and Title vs Section-header
- Printed Page Numbers (§6.6) — the folio inside the band
- Images (§12.1.1) — what a logo inside the band becomes

## §5 Layout

### 5.1 Block Annotation

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-block-annotation` · Tags: rule, layout, blocks

> **✅ Normative**
> Every meaningful visible region of a page MUST be one element with one class, one position in the
> page's reading order and — when boxes are requested — one box. Printed content covered by no
> element is dropped content, and makes the output non-conforming.

An element at region level is one coherent visual region — a paragraph, a heading, a list item, a
picture, a table, a caption, a form area. This note fixes what gets an element and how its box is
drawn; the class is chosen by Block Classes (§5.3) and the order by Reading Order (§5.9).

#### What an element is not

Printed lines, table cells, rows, columns and words MUST NOT be region-level elements. A table is
**one** Table element around the whole table; a picture or chart is **one** Picture element around
the unified graphic. Finer boxes exist only at the granularity that was requested — see
Boxes and Granularity (§3.3). Going finer at region level is not more thorough; it is the wrong layer.

#### Completeness

- Every region carrying printed content MUST be covered by an element, except the narrow exclusions
  of Ignoring and Rejecting (§5.6).
- Duplicate elements for one region, and elements for regions that print nothing, MUST NOT appear.

#### The box

- A box MUST be the smallest rectangle that contains the complete element.
- A box MUST include all of the element's visible ink: borders, diacritics, superscripts, meaningful
  shadows. Slight extra whitespace is better than clipped content: where the two conflict, the box
  SHOULD err towards whitespace.
- A box MUST NOT extend beyond the page, and boxes SHOULD NOT substantially overlap one another.

#### Splitting

- Each paragraph MUST be its own Text element. Separate paragraphs, columns, list items, captions or
  unrelated labels MUST NOT be merged into one element.
- An element MUST be split at a page boundary and at a column boundary.
- A displayed Formula, Picture or Table that interrupts prose MUST split the surrounding prose into
  separate Text elements above and below it.
- Where prose **wraps around a picture**, the prose MUST be split into the fewest elements whose
  non-overlapping boxes each keep complete lines.

##### A paragraph continued in the next column

The layout boxes stay split: one box per column piece, as above. A Markdown-attribution
ground truth (the `markdown_attribution` rule) records the paragraph as the **one** element it is
in the Markdown, with a box budget:

- The reference's `regions` MUST be the pieces, one per column (or page), with
  `exception: "multi_column"` (or `"cross_page"`).
- `expected_bbox_count` MUST equal the number of pieces. It is an integer of at least 1, and 1 is
  the default: an engine that claims more boxes than the count scores 0 for that element.
- Each piece SHOULD also be a `spans` entry with its own text and box, so an output that keeps the
  pieces as two paragraphs is still matched.
- Set it only when the text really runs on (no paragraph break at the column foot). Separate
  paragraphs, list items, table rows and formulas keep one box each and the default count.





#### Related

- Block Classes (§5.3) — which class each element takes
- Block Boundaries (§5.2) — where a Picture or Table box stops
- Reading Order (§5.9) — the position each element takes
- Ignoring and Rejecting (§5.6) — the only regions allowed no element
- Boxes and Granularity (§3.3) — finer boxes, when requested

### 5.2 Block Boundaries

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-block-boundaries` · Tags: rule, layout, blocks

> **✅ Normative**
> A Picture or Table element MUST contain the **complete object and nothing else**. Its caption, its
> title, its source note and nearby prose MUST NOT be absorbed into it; each is an element of its own.

In the diagrams below the overlays show boxes by class colour; a red ✗ or green ✓ marks an incorrect
or a correct boundary and is not a class colour.

#### Picture boundaries

A Picture MUST include the **full unified graphic** — plots, axes, tick labels, legends, arrows,
symbols, and any text drawn inside the graphic. Clipping the axis labels or the legend off a chart
is the common error, and it removes exactly the parts that make the chart readable. A caption
printed outside the graphic stays a separate Caption element.

#### One caption or several

- **One caption shared across several panels → one Picture element.**
- **Separate captions → separate Picture elements.**

The caption says what the author considered one figure. Multi-panel figures labelled `a)`, `b)`,
`c)` under a single caption MUST be one Picture; the same panels each with their own caption MUST
be several.

The Table element MUST include the complete grid, its headers, aligned totals and all column
content. It MUST exclude the table's title, its caption, its source note, and any prose beside it.

These are layout boundaries. A table or chart caption is rendered as `<caption>` inside its
object's HTML table, first or last according to reading order, while retaining its own Caption
class and box. See Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3).

#### Table boundaries: the structure, not the ink

The Table element MUST follow the **actual row-column structure**, not every visible rule around
it. Decorative borders, section rules and frame lines drawn around a table are not part of it.
There MUST be **exactly one** Table element around the full table, and no region-level element for
its rows, columns, cells or internal text.

### 5.3 Block Classes

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-block-classes` · Tags: rule, layout, blocks

> **✅ Normative**
> Every element MUST have exactly one of the seventeen classes below. Its layout class MUST match
> the class of the corresponding Markdown element defined in Elements (§3.1). A class MUST NOT be chosen
> merely to complete a page: where the class is genuinely unclear, the output MUST NOT assert a
> class the page does not support.

#### The seventeen classes

| Class | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| **Text** | One coherent paragraph or prose block |
| **Title** | The overall document title, on its title or front page |
| **Section-header** | A separate heading introducing a section or subsection |
| **List-item** | One marked or hanging list item, **including its continuation lines** |
| **Caption** | Text outside normal flow that names or explains a table, picture or formula |
| **Footnote** | A footnote, source note, method note, or small explanatory note tied to the body |
| **Page-header** | Repeated or page-specific content in the top margin |
| **Page-footer** | Bottom-margin content — **a page number alone qualifies** |
| **Picture** | A unified photo, diagram, chart, logo, map or molecular structure |
| **Table** | A ruled *or borderless* row-and-column structure whose alignment matters |
| **Formula** | A standalone displayed expression, **including its displayed equation number** |
| **Checkbox-Selected** | A selected checkbox mark **only** — not its label |
| **Checkbox-Unselected** | An unselected checkbox mark **only** — not its label |
| **Code** | Preformatted source, commands, logs, or fixed-width output |
| **Document Index** | A table of contents, index, or directory-like navigation block |
| **Form** | Irregular controls or fields arranged for data entry |
| **Key-Value Region** | A compact label/value group **without** a regular table grid |

How each class is rendered in Markdown is set out in Elements (§3.1).

#### One class across layout and Markdown

The layout box and the corresponding Markdown represent the same element and MUST use the same
class. A producer MUST resolve a disagreement using the printed content and update both
representations to agree. A detected label is only a suggestion — see Layout Regions (§5.7).

The class describes the element's role; Markdown syntax alone does not determine it. Text and
Footnote both render as paragraphs while keeping their distinct classes. A table or chart Caption
uses `<caption>` inside its object's table HTML and keeps its own Caption class and layout box. A Picture
rendered as `<table data-source="chart">` keeps the Picture class; a printed Table has the Table class. The
renderings prescribed in Elements (§3.1) govern these cases.

#### The distinctions that decide most cases

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Table vs Form** | A Table has a **regular** row-column structure. A Form has irregular fields or controls for data entry. |
| **Table vs Key-Value Region** | A Table **repeats** rows and columns. A Key-Value Region is a compact label/value group with no regular grid. |
| **Title vs Section-header** | Title is **only** the document's overall title on its cover — which sheet that is, is decided once in Document Type (§4.4). A repeated title on a later page is Text or page furniture. |
| **Caption vs Text** | **Proximity is not enough.** A Caption names or explains an object and sits outside normal flow. Ordinary nearby prose is Text. |
| **Caption vs Footnote** | A Caption *identifies* an object. A Footnote adds a source, method, qualification or note. |
| **Picture vs Formula** | A complex chemical structure is a **Picture**. An ordinary standalone mathematical expression is a **Formula**. |
| **Checkbox** | The box covers only the square, circle or check mark — **never its label**. |

The diagrams below are synthetic pages shown with their element overlays, one colour per class.
There is no diagram yet for Checkbox-Selected, Checkbox-Unselected, Code, Document Index, Form or
Key-Value Region; the definitions above govern those.

#### Title and Text

**Title** MUST be used only for the document's overall title. Authors, dates, addresses and other
front-matter prose MUST stay separate **Text** elements.

#### Footnote and Formula

Each distinct Footnote MUST be its own element. A Formula MUST contain the complete displayed

### 5.4 Court Caption Blocks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-court-caption-blocks` · Tags: layout, legal, forms

> **✅ Normative**
> Every printed string of a court caption MUST be transcribed, the left column as one block of lines
> and then the right column, each printed line on its own line. Blank party and case-number lines
> MUST be `[blank]`. The `§` divider and the rules MUST NOT be transcribed, and the caption MUST NOT be
> rendered as a table.

The head of a court filing: the parties stacked on the left (`Plaintiff`, `v.`, `Defendant`), a
divider — a vertical rule, a column of `§` signs, or a box edge — and the court, case number and
document title on the right.

```text
______________________,        §    IN THE JUSTICE COURT
PLAINTIFF                      §
v.                             §    PRECINCT NO. __________
______________________,        §
DEFENDANT                      §    GREGG COUNTY, TEXAS
```

The `§` column is the one thing that is not content; everything else is.

#### Requirements

- Every printed string of the caption MUST appear in the output, including labels such as
  `PLAINTIFF` and `v.`.
- The left column MUST come first and the right column after it, each as one block, each printed
  line on its own line within its block. Where the caption has more than two cells, they are taken
  left to right, one block each.
- A blank party line or case-number line MUST be `[blank]`, with its printed label beside it — see
  Blanks Inside Sentences (§10.4.1).
- The caption MUST NOT be rendered as a two-column table, a key-value list, or row by row
  alternating left and right. The `§` divider and the rules MUST NOT be transcribed.

`DEPOSITION` in the centre; an empty `File Stamp Here` box on the right. The cells are taken left
to right, each as one block of lines. On this page `SUBPOENA FOR DEPOSITION` is the document's own

### 5.5 Embedded Pages

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-embedded-pages` · Tags: rule, layout, legal

> **✅ Normative**
> A page reproduced inside another page MUST be rendered as the wrapper's furniture followed by the
> embedded page in its own reading order. Both page numbers MUST be kept, each with its own region,
> and titles inside an embedded form screenshot MUST NOT be promoted into the wrapper's outline.

A page reproduced inside another page: a statute page shrunk into the middle of an exhibit sheet, a
slide placed on a letter-size page. Each carries its own header and page number, so the sheet has
two of everything.

```text
      Case 1:23-cv-06750   Document 1-4   Filed 08/02/23   Page 4 of 4     ← wrapper header
                              EXHIBIT D
                          ┌────────────────────┐
                          │   H. R. 2617—507   │  ← embedded header
                          │   (1) The term …   │
                          └────────────────────┘
                              Page 3 of 3                                  ← wrapper footer
```

#### Requirements

- The wrapper's label and filing stamp MUST be kept: they identify the particular copy.
- The embedded content MUST appear between the wrapper header and the wrapper footer, in the
  embedded page's own reading order.
- The wrapper's page number and the embedded page's number MUST both be kept, each where its own
  band prints it.
- A title printed inside an embedded form screenshot MUST NOT become a heading of the wrapping
  document.

### 5.6 Ignoring and Rejecting

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-ignoring-and-rejecting` · Tags: rule, layout, blocks

> **✅ Normative**
> A visible region MAY be left out of the output only on the narrow grounds listed below, and a
> page MAY be declared unrepresentable only when the problem is the page itself. Content that is
> merely difficult to read MUST NOT be left out on either ground.

Two exclusions, for two different situations. Both are narrow. Visibility is determined by
The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1), including hidden text, microscopic text and imperceptible
contrast. A visibly present but unreadable text span is represented as `[illegible]`; it is not
an invisible source object.

#### Excluding one region

A bounded region of an otherwise sound page MAY be left out of the output — no element, no box —
only when it is:

- a scan artifact;
- an invisible source object;
- damaged content;
- an irreconcilable source error;
- an element explicitly out of scope;
- a genuinely unresolved ambiguity.

Ordinary logos, page numbers, and content that is difficult but readable MUST NOT be excluded.
That is the requirement that matters. Exclusion is not a way past a hard page: a dense figure, an
awkward multi-column spread and a badly kerned table are all representable, just slower. Excluding
them turns a slow page into missing data, silently — the **never drop** failure.

#### An unrepresentable page

A page MAY be declared unrepresentable, and left out of evaluation rather than represented in part,
only when it is corrupt, badly cropped, mismatched to its document, unusable, or cannot be
represented unambiguously. An unrepresentable page MUST NOT be given a partial or guessed
rendering.

#### Choosing between them

The test is **scope**. One bad region on an otherwise sound page: that region is excluded and the
rest of the page represented. A page where the problem is the page: the page is declared
unrepresentable. Excluding twenty regions to rescue a broken page MUST NOT be done — it is a
rejection in disguise, and it produces an output that looks complete and is not.

#### A page that is genuinely blank

A page with **no ink at all** MUST keep its position in the page sequence with **zero elements**.
Its Markdown MUST consist of the single line `<!-- blank page -->` between the two `---` separators
that bound it, and its sidecar entry MUST list no items.

```text
…end of page 1

---

<!-- blank page -->

---

Start of page 3…
```

Blank pages are ordinary in real documents — section breaks, duplex backs, deliberate spacers. A
three-page file whose second page carries no ink and no text is not corrupt, and declaring it
unrepresentable would misreport the document's length.

Neither exclusion fits:

- **Excluding a region** is for a bounded exception *within* a page. Here there is nothing to
  bound.
- **Unrepresentable** is for a page that cannot be represented. A blank page represents perfectly —
  as nothing.

The page MUST NOT be dropped — a missing page is far harder to notice than an empty one, and every
later page number would shift. It MUST NOT be given an element either: an "empty" element with a
box around nothing is invented. The comment says, inline and invisibly, that the page is blank on
purpose, so a reader of the Markdown can tell a blank page from a lost one.

A page that prints only a notice such as *"This page intentionally left blank"*, or only a folio or
running header, has ink: it is an ordinary page whose content is that text.

CALDRIVANE ENERGY CORP.
INTEROFFICE MEMORANDUM

TO: Finance Committee
FROM: R. Donovan, Treasury
DATE: November 4, 2001
RE: Off-Balance-Sheet Treatment — Borvika Partners

This memorandum summarizes the accounting treatment applied to Borvika Partners, L.P., a related-party investment vehicle organized to acquire certain merchant assets that the Company did not wish to consolidate. Under the structuring in place, an outside investor holds a three-percent equity interest, which under the applicable accounting guidance is treated as sufficient independent equity at risk to keep the vehicle's assets and liabilities off the Company's consolidated balance sheet.

The Company has, however, guaranteed certain of Borvika's obligations through a series of put and forward arrangements tied to the Company's own stock. Should the Company's share price fall below the thresholds specified in those arrangements, the Company would be required to issue additional shares or make cash payments to Borvika's outside investors, which could require the vehicle's assets to be consolidated retroactively.

Management believes the three-percent threshold continues to satisfy the applicable accounting literature, and that the exposure described above, while real, is not probable of being triggered under current pricing. We recommend the Committee note this exposure for quarterly review rather than for immediate balance-sheet recognition, and that Treasury continue to monitor the share-price thresholds monthly.

### 5.7 Layout Regions

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-layout-regions` · Tags: rule, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A region's class MUST be settled before its content is rendered, because the class decides which
> rule governs the rendering. A region rendered under the wrong class is non-conforming however
> faithfully its text is transcribed.

A producer segments each page into **regions**, each carrying a label. The label decides which rule
applies — so getting the region right is upstream of every other decision in this protocol.

This note maps the vocabulary that region detectors commonly emit onto the protocol. The protocol's
own classes, and what box each gets, are defined in Block Classes (§5.3) and Block Annotation (§5.1).
Detector labels MUST be resolved to those classes before they become layout annotations. The
resulting layout class MUST match the corresponding Markdown element's class in Elements (§3.1).

#### The vocabulary

**Structure**
`title` · `doc_title` · `section-header` · `paragraph_title` · `text` · `content` · `abstract` ·
`list-item` · `document-index`

**Data**
`table` · `chart` · `formula` · `formula_number` · `code` · `algorithm` · `number`

**Figures**
`picture` · `image` · `figure_title` · `caption`

**Forms**
`form` · `key-value-region` · `checkbox-selected` · `checkbox-unselected`

**Page furniture**
`header` · `page-header` · `footer` · `page-footer` · `footnote` · `aside_text` · `reference` ·
`reference_content` · `seal`

#### The label decides the rule

| Label | Governing rule |
| --- | --- |
| `table` | Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) and the whole Tables chapter |
| `chart` | Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1) |
| `picture` / `image` | Images and Figures (§12.1.2) |
| `form` / `key-value-region` | The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) |
| `list-item` | Bullets and Sub-Bullets (§8.1) |
| `caption` / `figure_title` | Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) |
| `formula` | Displayed Equations (§7.2.2) — LaTeX in `$$ … $$` |
| `checkbox-*` | Checkboxes (§10.4.2) |

#### A detected label is evidence, not a verdict

A region labelled `table` is **not automatically a table.** Address blocks, two-column prose and
ungridded specification stacks are routinely labelled `table` by layout detection, and
Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) exists to overrule that. A detected label MUST NOT be accepted on its own:
the region MUST be classed by what is actually printed.

The same holds in reverse: a genuine grid that detection missed MUST still be rendered as a table.





#### Related

- Block Classes (§5.3) — the protocol's own classes
- Block Annotation (§5.1) — what gets an element and a box
- Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) — the test that overrules a `table` label
- Images and Figures (§12.1.2) — what a `picture` region becomes

### 5.8 Pleading Line Numbers

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-pleading-line-numbers` · Tags: layout, legal, furniture, line-numbers

> **✅ Normative**
> Printed gutter line numbers MUST NOT appear in the Markdown: the body is rendered as continuous
> paragraphs, as if the margin were blank. When line numbers are requested, each page MUST carry a
> `line_numbers` list that links every printed number to the body line it stands beside.

US court filings are printed on pleading paper: the numbers 1–28 run down the left margin, one per
ruled line, with a double vertical rule between the numbers and the text. The numbers are cited in
practice ("page 9, line 14") but they belong to the paper, not to the prose.

```text
 1 ║ school year, the District set the average ratio
 2 ║
 3 ║ based.
 4 ║      29.  Additional race-based benefits provided
```

#### In the Markdown

- A line number MUST NOT appear in the body text — not between two words, not at the start of a
  line, and not as a column of its own. The page MUST NOT be rendered as a `number | text` table:
  numbers pair with printed *lines*, not with sentences or paragraphs.
- The body MUST be rendered as paragraphs, wrapped lines joined, exactly as if the margin were blank.
- The double rule beside the numbers is layout and MUST NOT be transcribed.

#### The line-number map

When line numbers are requested (the `annotate_line_numbers` option of the parse request), the
numbers are carried in the page's structured output instead of the text. Each page with line
numbers MUST carry a `line_numbers` list of entries:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `line_number` | the printed label, as a string, exactly as printed (`14`, `1196`) |
| `start_index` | zero-based, inclusive offset of the body line's text in the page's final Markdown, in UTF-16 code units |
| `end_index` | exclusive end of that span, same convention |

- An entry MUST point at the text of the body line printed level with the number, so a citation
  such as "page 9, line 14" resolves to text.
- A number beside a line with no text — a blank line between paragraphs, the numbers running on
  below the last line — MUST NOT get an entry.
- Entries MUST be in page order and MUST NOT overlap; every span MUST lie within the page's
  Markdown and cover non-blank text.
- A page without printed line numbers carries no `line_numbers` list.

```text
Markdown, page 3:   …the District set the average ratio based.  29. Additional race-based benefits…
line_numbers:       [{"line_number": "1", "start_index": …, "end_index": …},
                     {"line_number": "3", …}, {"line_number": "4", …}, …]
```

The same holds for any page with a printed gutter of line numbers, such as a line-numbered
manuscript, and for court transcripts, whose speaker turns are rendered as described in
Transcript Pages (§6.11).

### 5.9 Reading Order

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-reading-order` · Tags: rule, layout, blocks

> **✅ Normative**
> The elements of a page MUST form one reading-order sequence that includes **every** element of the
> page exactly once — no element left out, none placed twice. The sequence MUST follow the order in
> which a reader reads the page, not the elements' geometric position.

The reading order is the order of the page's elements in the Markdown and in the sidecar. Where
positions are numbered, the numbering MUST start at 0 and be contiguous — no gaps and no duplicates.

#### The reader, not the geometry

Elements MUST be ordered the way a person reads the page — **not** by simple top-to-bottom,
left-to-right position. On a two-column page, top-to-bottom order interleaves the columns and
produces text that is unreadable in sequence.

The usual shape:

1. the page header;
2. the intended column or section flow;
3. the page footer.

Sidebars, callouts, captions and notes MUST be placed **where a reader would encounter them** — a
caption belongs beside the figure it names, not collected at the end.

#### Panels

Where a page prints its own section bands or panel headers, they define the order, and position only
breaks ties **inside** a panel.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a conference poster

*(Source image corpus-poster-panels.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A poster laid out as titled panels — *Motivation* and *Dataset* side by side, *Methods* below
Motivation, then *Results* spanning the full width, then *Conclusion*. The order is **panel by
panel**, not column by column and certainly not top-to-bottom across the sheet: read by geometry,
the first bullet of *Motivation* would be followed by the first bullet of *Dataset*, because they sit
at the same height. The two round marks in the top corners print no text and yield no Markdown; the
Results strip of labelled colour swatches is a Picture, rendered as a `description` block.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown</summary>

````markdown
# A Distribution-Shift Benchmark for Highland Cacao Smallholders

Do Foundation Models Improve Geographic Generalization?

R. Okonkwo<sup>1</sup>, T. Vasilenko<sup>1</sup>, M. Aday<sup>2</sup>, F. Renwick<sup>1</sup>

Bramwell University<sup>1</sup>, Highland Agroforestry Centre<sup>2</sup>

**ICLR 2025 ML4RS Workshop**

## Motivation

* Recent work has reported high accuracy in applying deep learning to individual tree-canopy detection
* Performance drops under distribution shifts are common for these approaches

**We introduce the first distribution-shift benchmark for highland cacao smallholders and ask:**

(1) How does performance drop under geographic distribution shift?
(2) Do foundation models improve robustness?

## Dataset

* stratify Kelanoa province into 8 agro-climatic zones
* sample train & test images for each zone
* annotate individual tree masks for each image
* split In-Distribution (ID) & Out-of-Distribution (OOD) zones for distribution shift evaluation
* do QA using inter-annotator agreement & field inventories

## Methods

* We perform three types of evaluations:
  - (1) Conventional
  - (2) Distribution shift
  - (3) Few-shot domain adaptation
* Compare performance of a baseline (Faster-RCNN) with computer-vision foundation models (SAM, Grounding DINO)
* Report per-zone accuracy metrics and calibration curves

## Results

```description
- In-Distribution: Ridge Zone, Basin Zone, Terrace Zone, Valley Zone
- Out-of-Distribution: Highland Rim, Plateau Rim, Foothill Rim, Delta Rim
```

## Conclusion

Foundation models close part of the distribution-shift gap seen with the Faster-RCNN baseline, but a sizeable generalization gap remains between in-distribution and out-of-distribution zones; few-shot adaptation on a handful of OOD tiles recovers most of the remaining gap.
````

</details>

### 5.10 Slide Furniture

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-slide-furniture` · Tags: rule, layout, slides

> **✅ Normative**
> Every printed navigation tab of a slide MUST be transcribed, in printed order, as furniture, and a
> highlight that identifies the active section MUST be kept with the highlight convention. Labels
> printed on a photograph MUST be kept with the photograph's description; purely decorative
> background art MUST NOT be described.

Presentation decks print things around their content that a document does not: a row of section
tabs along the top edge with the current one highlighted, name labels overlaid on photographs, a
running footer with the deck name and slide number.

#### Requirements

| The slide prints | The output |
| --- | --- |
| A row of navigation tabs | Every tab, in printed order, as furniture; the active tab's highlight as `<mark style="background-color: …">` with the nearest HTML colour name — see Highlighted Text (§7.2.5) |
| A label printed on a photograph | The label, kept with the photograph's description |
| Background art with no labels, values or meaningful relationships | Nothing |
| Background art whose geography or shape conveys content | A description of what it conveys |

### 5.11 Stat Tiles

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-stat-tiles` · Tags: rule, layout, slides

> **✅ Normative**
> Each stat tile MUST be rendered as one printed label–value pair, in tile reading order, under the
> panel's heading where the panel prints one. Units and qualifiers MUST stay attached to their value.

A slide panel that prints a big number with a short label — `Out-of-home +26.5%`, `Total -19.8%` —
usually two or three of them side by side under a heading.

```text
┌─ 2025 volume growth¹ ──────────┐
│  Out-of-home        Total       │
│  ┌────────┐       ┌────────┐    │
│  │ +26.5% │       │ -19.8% │    │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
```

Read top to bottom, the labels come first and the values after, so a geometric reading separates
each figure from its label — the failure to avoid.

#### Requirements

- Each tile MUST be one key-value line, `- label: value`, with the label and the value as printed;
  bold only where the glyphs are heavier.
- The tiles MUST follow tile reading order, each label next to its own value.
- A printed panel heading MUST come before its tiles. A heading MUST NOT be invented where the panel
  prints none.
- A unit, sign, footnote marker or qualifier (`LFL`, `(+1.9%)`) MUST stay with the value it
  qualifies; an icon that carries the direction MUST be kept — see Iconography and Symbols (§7.3.4).

## §6 Headings and page structure

### 6.1 Dot Leader Lines

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-dot-leader-lines` · Tags: text, rule, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> Dot leaders MUST NOT appear in the output. The label and the value on either side of a leader
> MUST be kept exactly as printed; the dots themselves produce nothing.

> **A deliberate exception to verbatim transcription**
> Everywhere else printed ink survives — see Values Are Verbatim (§10.3.3) and Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3).
> Dot leaders are the one carve-out: they exist only to guide the eye across a gutter and carry no
> information.

A dot leader is a run of dots filling horizontal space between a label and a value, most often in a
table of contents, a directory or a price list.

```text
Chapter 3 — Reserving  . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  47
```

#### Requirements

- A run of leader dots MUST be removed wherever it is printed: in running text, in a directory
  line and in a table's stub cell.
- The label and every value the leader connects MUST be kept, verbatim. **The dots go; everything
  they connect stays.**
- Removing a leader MUST NOT split a label or a value, and a leader MUST NOT be absorbed into
  either side (no trailing dots on a label, no leading dots on a number).
- Where a leader separates two values on one line, the values remain on that line, separated by a
  space.

A dot leader is typesetting, not content: it exists because a label and a number are far apart on
the line, and it disappears the moment the text is reflowed. Transcribing it damages what is around
it — a run of dots inside a label breaks any string match on that label.
