### 6.2 Line Breaks Inside a Block

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-line-breaks-inside-a-block` · Tags: text, layout, line-breaks

> **✅ Normative**
> One printed block set on several lines MUST stay one element, with a plain newline between its
> printed lines — no trailing spaces, no `<br>`. The same spelling MUST be used for every multi-line
> block in the document. Inside a table cell, where a newline cannot be written, the break is `<br>`.

One printed block that runs to more than one line because the page sets it that way: a stacked
masthead, a postal address, a two-line banner, a title broken across a rule. The lines belong
together; only the typesetting separates them.

```text
MEREVALD                     ← one block, two printed lines
Merevald Retail Ltd
```

#### Settled: the block stays whole

- One printed block MUST be one element, whatever break is written between its lines. Two stacked
  lines of a masthead MUST NOT become two headings, two paragraphs, or a heading with a subtitle.
  Splitting it is the **never invent** failure: the page printed one block, and a split claims it
  printed two.
- Whether lines form one block is judged by the printing, not the wording: a single set, a single
  alignment and a single leading mean one block, even when the two lines read as separable phrases.

#### The break is a plain newline

The Markdown source keeps every printed line on its own source line. A renderer shows a single
newline inside a paragraph as a space, so a rendered view runs the lines together; that is a
display artefact, not a change to the output, which is judged on its source (see
Numbered Section Headings (§6.5) for the same principle). Two trailing spaces are invisible and are
stripped by most whitespace normalisation; `<br>` puts markup on every line. Neither is used outside
table cells.

- The break MUST be a plain newline, and the same spelling MUST be used for **every** multi-line
  block in the document — paragraphs, addresses, headers and footers alike.
- Inside a table cell a newline cannot be written, so a printed break there is `<br>` — see
  Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3).
- A line that Markdown would parse as a list item or heading (`- `, `1. `, `# ` at its start) is
  escaped — see Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4).

#### Not this rule's case

- A rule printed *between* blocks is a separator, not a break inside one — see
  Line Separators and Breaks (§6.3).
- A line that wraps because it ran out of column width is not a printed break at all: its lines
  MUST be joined with a space.
- Text whose line breaks carry meaning, such as verse, is governed by Verse and Hard Line Breaks (§7.2.13).





#### Related

- Line Separators and Breaks (§6.3) — a rule between blocks, which resolves differently
- Verse and Hard Line Breaks (§7.2.13) — text whose breaks are content
- Stacked Headings (§6.9) — a title wrapped over several lines, joined with spaces
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — header and footer bands, which take the same break

### 6.3 Line Separators and Breaks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-line-separators-and-breaks` · Tags: rule, layout, model-divergence

> **✅ Normative**
> A printed section separator MUST be rendered as `<hr/>`, at its place in reading order. `---`
> MUST NOT be used for it: `---` is reserved for page boundaries. A rule MUST NOT be inserted where
> the page prints only whitespace.

A horizontal rule or separator printed between sections of a page. It is printed content: it tells
a reader that one block has ended and another begun, so it survives into the output.

```text
… end of the first section.
────────────────────────────        ← printed rule between sections  →  <hr/>
Start of the next section …
```

#### Requirements

- Each printed separator between sections MUST produce one `<hr/>` line, placed between the
  elements it separates in reading order.
- The separator MUST NOT be written as `---`, `***`, `___` or any other Markdown thematic break.
- Vertical whitespace between sections, with no printed line, MUST NOT produce `<hr/>`.

#### Why never `---`

`---` is already load-bearing twice. It is the page-break marker of Markdown Rendering (§3.2), and at
the top of a file it opens frontmatter. A separator that renders identically to a page break makes
page attribution ambiguous for anything splitting on it, and can silently truncate a document at
the top of a file. `<hr/>` avoids both collisions and follows the general posture of falling back
to HTML wherever a Markdown spelling is ambiguous — see Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1).





#### Related

- Markdown Rendering (§3.2) — `---` as the page boundary
- Line Breaks Inside a Block (§6.2) — a break *within* one block, which resolves differently
- Dot Leader Lines (§6.1) — the other printed line-filler, which is removed rather than kept
- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — HTML where a Markdown spelling is ambiguous

### 6.4 Marginal Notes

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-marginal-notes` · Tags: layout, rule, structure, legal

> **✅ Normative**
> Each printed marginal note MUST be rendered as a separate block placed immediately after the
> element it annotates. Where the element it belongs to cannot be established, the note MUST still
> be kept as a separate block and MUST NOT be merged into body text.

Statutes and some textbooks print short notes in the outer margin — a citation, a one-word
gloss — aligned with the line they annotate. They are printed text, not handwriting, and they
belong to a particular line.

```text
SEC. 105. INVESTIGATIONS AND DISCIPLINARY PROCEEDINGS.        15 USC 7215.
   (a) IN GENERAL.—The Board shall establish, by rule, …      Establishment.
```

#### Requirements

- A marginal note MUST be its own element, never part of the heading or paragraph it sits beside.
- It MUST follow the element it annotates — the heading or paragraph level with it — in reading
  order, before the next element of the body.
- A geometric reading that inserts `15 USC 7215.` into the middle of the section heading, or
  splices a gloss into a line of the paragraph, does not conform.

### 6.5 Numbered Section Headings

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `headings-numbered-section-headings` · Tags: structure, headings, lists

> **✅ Normative**
> A numbered line that stands alone as a title with body text beneath it MUST be rendered as a
> heading, one level deeper per level of numbering. A numbered line that is itself the content —
> including a bare number printed above its paragraph — MUST be rendered as a list item carrying
> that content. The printed number MUST be kept exactly as printed, on the same line as its text.

Legal and technical documents number their sections — `1.`, `1.1.`, `2.3.` — and set each on its
own line, often underlined or bold, with a paragraph beneath. On the page this is a heading; in the
text layer it is indistinguishable from an ordered list.

```text
1.    AFFIDAVIT

1.1.  COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE
      The Commissioner of Oaths must print his full name …
1.2.  SECURITY
      If security is claimed, then the amount …
```

#### Heading or list item

| The page prints | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| A numbered title on its own line, with body text beneath (`1. AFFIDAVIT`) | heading, depth from the numbering: `## 1. AFFIDAVIT`, `### 1.1. COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE` |
| A numbered line that is itself the content | list item: `3. The Registrar will set the matter down …` |
| A bare number on a line of its own, above its paragraph (`29.`) | list item: the number joins its paragraph's line, `29. As a direct and proximate result …` |

The test is the one Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7) applies: a title organises the block
beneath it; a numbered paragraph is an item of an enumeration. Heading depth follows the printed
numbering, as Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5) requires.

A bare number is moved onto its paragraph's line because it labels that paragraph ("paragraph
29"). Left on a line of its own it would read as an empty list item followed by an unrelated
paragraph. Only the centring is lost, and centring is layout.

#### Numbers are written verbatim

The printed number MUST be written as printed — `29.`, `1.1.`, `(a)`, `IV.` — and MUST NOT be
renumbered, normalised or escaped to prevent list parsing. A number that is a valid Markdown list
marker (`29.`) then renders as a list item; one that is not (`1.1.`, `(a)`) renders as a paragraph
beginning with the number. Both carry the printed numbering exactly in the source, which is what
the output is judged on; a renderer that shows skipped numbers (29, 31) as consecutive is a display
artefact, not a change to the output.

The one exception is a line that Markdown would turn into a list although the page prints no list,
such as a sentence that begins `1995. was a record year`. Its marker MUST be escaped (`1995\.`) —
see Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4).

##### ✅ **Sample** — two-level numbered notes

*(Source image bag-numbered-headings.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

"1. AFFIDAVIT" over "1.1. COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE", "1.2. SECURITY", each sub-heading underlined
with a paragraph beneath it. Four top-level numbers on the page, sub-numbered under two of them.
Each numbered line is a heading, one level deeper per level of
numbering; the depths shown assume this page opens the document, under its title.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown</summary>

```markdown
# NOTES ON WINDING-UP PROCEDURE

## 1. AFFIDAVIT

### 1.1. COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE

The Liquidator must print his full name, capacity and date of appointment on the affidavit before signing it in the presence of a Commissioner of Oaths. An unsigned or undated affidavit will be returned without further consideration.

### 1.2. SECURITY

If security is claimed on any asset listed in the affidavit, the amount claimed and the name of the secured party must be stated in full. Where no security is claimed, the affidavit must say so expressly rather than leaving the field blank.

## 2. FILING

The completed affidavit, together with the annexed schedule of assets, must be filed with the Registrar within fourteen days of the Liquidator's appointment. A copy is retained on the estate file for the duration of the winding-up.

## 3. OBJECTIONS

### 3.1. NOTICE PERIOD

Any creditor wishing to object to an item in the schedule must lodge a written objection with the Registrar within twenty-one days of the affidavit being filed, stating the item objected to and the grounds.

### 3.2. HEARING

Where an objection is lodged in time, the Registrar will set the matter down for hearing and notify the Liquidator and the objecting creditor of the date.

## 4. COSTS

The costs of preparing and filing the affidavit are a first charge on the estate and are payable before any distribution to creditors.
```

</details>

```markdown
29. As a direct and proximate result of Defendant Harlan Office Supply Co.'s breach of the Purchase Agreement described above, Plaintiff Midvale Clinic LLC was unable to furnish its new waiting room in time for its scheduled opening and was forced to delay the opening by six weeks.

30. Plaintiff was required to source substitute seating from a third-party vendor on an emergency basis, at a cost substantially higher than the price agreed with Defendant for the same quantity and specification of chairs.

32. Plaintiff lost revenue from patients who could not be scheduled during the delay described in Paragraph 29, in an amount to be proven at trial.

33. Plaintiff's reputation in the community was harmed by the delayed opening, which was reported in a local business newsletter and required Plaintiff to issue a public clarification to patients and referring physicians.

34. As a further direct and proximate result of Defendant's breach, Plaintiff has suffered damages in an amount to be determined at trial, but believed to exceed $75,000, together with interest, costs, and such other relief as the Court deems just and proper.
```

#### Repeated item labels

“Question N”, “Interrogatory No. N” and “Request for Production N” are item labels, even when bold
and alone on a line, and MUST NOT be rendered as headings. A standalone section title organises a
block; a recurring label merely identifies the next item. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7)
for the distinction in context.

- Bullets and Sub-Bullets (§8.1) — ordered lists keep their printed numbering

### 6.6 Printed Page Numbers

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-printed-page-numbers` · Tags: rule, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A printed page number (the folio) MUST be kept in the header or footer band it is printed in,
> verbatim, and MUST NOT appear as a loose element in the body. When the printed page number is
> requested, it MUST also be recorded on its own for the page, as printed, and MUST NOT be inferred
> for a page that prints none.

The folio is the number a document prints on itself: `26`, `Page 6`, `Page 3 of 12`, `iv`, `A-3`.
It sits in the top or bottom margin, often beside a date, a form number or a URL.

```text
FORM CMS-2567  Previous Versions Obsolete       If continuation sheet Page 3 of 12
                                                                      ↑ the folio
```

#### Two records

| Record | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **In the band** | The folio is part of the header or footer it is printed in. The band MUST be kept together and verbatim — see Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6). |
| **On its own** | When the printed page number is requested (Output Options (§3.5)), the number MUST also be recorded alone for the page — the sidecar's `printedPageNumber`, see The Sidecar (§3.4). The label MUST be stripped and the numbering kept as printed: `6`, not `Page 6`; roman numerals stay roman; `A-3` stays `A-3`. |

#### The offset is the point

Front matter, covers and inserts mean printed page 1 is often not sheet 1. A magazine feature can
open on sheet 1 and print `26`; a report can run twelve sheets of front matter before printing `1`.
That mapping is a fact about the **document**, not the page, and it is the reason the number is
worth recording separately — a reader citing "page 26" cannot otherwise be sent to the right sheet.

- The recorded number MUST be the number the page prints. It MUST NOT be renumbered to match the
  sheet position.
- A folio MUST NOT be inferred for a page that prints none.

#### Pages that print nothing

Covers, plates and continuation sheets frequently carry no folio; their printed page number is
empty, which is not an error. A pre-printed blank, `Page ___ of ___`, is also no folio: the blank
MUST be transcribed in the band (as `[blank]`) and no number recorded.

#### A folio never sits in the body

A number that ends up as a loose line among the page's content means the band was read wrongly. The
folio MUST belong to its margin band whether or not the rest of that band was recognised — the same
**never invent** failure as promoting furniture to a heading.





#### Related

- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — the band the folio belongs to
- Output Options (§3.5) — the option that asks for the number on its own
- The Sidecar (§3.4) — where the number is recorded
- Block Classes (§5.3) — a page number alone qualifies as Page-footer

### 6.7 Recognising Ambiguous Headings

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `headings-recognising-ambiguous-headings` · Tags: rule, headings, structure

> **✅ Normative**
> A standalone structural title that organises what follows MUST be rendered as a heading. Run-in
> labels, repeated item labels, captions and page furniture MUST keep their own roles and MUST NOT
> be rendered as headings. Font size alone MUST NOT decide whether a line is a heading.

What a line does decides its role; its depth is chosen afterwards. A short bold line can organise a
section; a large banner can belong entirely to a form or a table.

```text
Company name over a title    ← its own line, above the heading
Company name alone           ← furniture
Document title               ← heading
Standalone section title     ← heading
Bold label: value or sentence ← inline label
Table 1: ...                 ← caption
```

Heading depths in the samples below are relative wherever the crop does not show the outline above
the heading: the rendering keeps the hierarchy the crop shows, and the absolute level comes from
Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5).

#### Run-in labels

A label followed on the same line by a sentence, value or URL MUST stay inline, with its printed
emphasis preserved. A line that wraps onto another line remains the same paragraph. See
Run-In Headings (§6.8).

body-text size. Weight, colour and underlining support the reading; none decides it alone.

#### Principal statement and schedule titles

The principal title of a financial statement or numbered schedule is structural and MUST be a
heading. The company line and the units or audit-status line MUST stay separate. This is a
specific exception to the caption rule below: a statement or schedule can itself be a document
section.

A numbered schedule title remains structural when printed inside a grid. Its text MUST appear once,
in its printed table position; it keeps its heading role in the element classes and boxes (see
Boxes and Granularity (§3.3)) and MUST NOT be duplicated as a Markdown heading outside the table.
Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) governs its cell placement.

#### Running headers and decorative marks

Whether a page-top label is a running header is a document decision, made in
Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6): the same words may have been a section heading where the section
began, and repetition at a page boundary does not open it again. From one page alone, a margin
label that carries no argument of its own is furniture. A purely decorative arrow before a heading
MUST be omitted from the heading text; a printed section number MUST be kept.

#### Depth comes after role

Heading levels MUST be the document-absolute levels of Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5). When only
one page is available, the relative hierarchy the page shows MUST be kept consistent. The first
heading on a page MUST NOT be assumed to be the top level, and a level that is common elsewhere
MUST NOT be assumed for this page. Whether the deck convention applies is decided once for the file
in Document Type (§4.4); a level MUST NOT be copied from another document.





#### Related

- Heading Depth Across Pages (§4.5) — choose the level after deciding that a line is a heading
- Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6) — the document-wide call on repeated page-top labels
- Run-In Headings (§6.8) — a label kept within its paragraph
- Numbered Section Headings (§6.5) — numbered titles versus numbered content
- Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) — table titles kept once, in their printed position

### 6.8 Run-In Headings

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `headings-run-in-headings` · Tags: rule, structure, headings

> **✅ Normative**
> A run-in label and the sentence, value or URL that follows it on the same line MUST be rendered
> as one paragraph, with the label's printed emphasis preserved. The label MUST NOT be rendered as a
> Markdown heading.

A run-in heading is set at the start of its own paragraph, in bold or colour, with the body text
continuing on the same line. Contracts number their clauses this way; glossaries print the term
this way.

```text
Section 11.1.1 The Department requires that business enterprises so certified by …
AMBIGUOUS  Confusing question in that it is capable of being understood in more than one sense.
  ↑ bold label, text continues on the same line
```

#### Requirements

- The label and its text MUST stay in one paragraph; a label that wraps onto a further line remains
  part of the same paragraph.
- The label's printed bold, italic, underline or small capitals MUST be kept as inline marks (see
  Bold and Italics (§7.2.1), Underlined Text (§7.2.12), Small Capitals (§7.2.10)).
- The label MUST NOT be split onto a line of its own or promoted to a heading: a lead-in rendered as
  a heading creates a false outline entry.
- A numbered title set **on its own line**, with its text beneath, is not run-in; it is a heading —
  see Numbered Section Headings (§6.5).

##### ✅ **Sample** — numbered contract clauses

*(Source image bag-run-in-sections.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

`Section 11.1.1` through `11.1.4` open their paragraphs in bold; `Section 11.1` and `11.2` are set
on their own lines, underlined, and behave as ordinary headings. Both shapes on one page. The
two-line `ARTICLE 11` title is one heading (see Stacked Headings (§6.9)). Heading depths are relative:
the page, sheet 41 of 96, does not show the outline above the article.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown</summary>

```markdown
## ARTICLE 11 ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS

### Section 11.1 Definitions

For purposes of this Article, the following terms have the meanings set out below, and apply to every Contract issued under this Agreement regardless of funding source.

**Section 11.1.1** The Department requires that business enterprises so certified by the Office of Contract Compliance as a Locally Owned Small Business (an "LSB") be given a good faith opportunity to participate in the performance of Contracts financed in whole or in part with Department funds.

**Section 11.1.2** "Utilization" means the dollar value of Work self-performed or subcontracted to a certified LSB, expressed as a percentage of the total base Contract value, exclusive of Owner-furnished materials and allowances.

**Section 11.1.3** "Good Faith Effort" means the documented steps a Contractor takes to solicit, evaluate, and, where practicable, engage certified LSB firms, including the record-keeping described in Section 11.3.

**Section 11.1.4** "Commercially Useful Function" means that the LSB firm is responsible for the execution of a distinct element of the Work and carries out its responsibilities by actually performing, managing, and supervising that element.

### Section 11.2 Utilization Requirements

Each Contractor shall achieve a minimum LSB Utilization of eighteen percent (18%) of the total base Contract value, unless a lower or higher goal is stated in the Special Conditions for this Contract. Utilization credit is available only for Commercially Useful Function performed by a currently certified LSB firm, and is measured at Contract closeout as well as at the time of award.

Failure to meet the goal stated above, without a Good Faith Effort accepted in writing by the Office of Contract Compliance under Section 11.1.3, is a material breach of this Agreement and may result in the remedies described in Article 14.

Standard Construction Agreement — Article 11 — Page 41 of 96
```

##### ✅ **Sample** — a glossary of objections

*(Source image bag-objections-glossary.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Thirty-odd entries, each a red bold term followed on the same line by its definition and a rule
citation. Two entries carry a bold `Note:` inside the definition. The red is decoration and is not
carried; the italic citations are. The left column is read before the right.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt</summary>

```markdown
# Evidentiary Trial Objections

A quick-reference glossary for use at counsel table

**Ambiguous.** The question is capable of more than one reasonable meaning and calls for the witness to guess which one is intended. *(R. Evid. 611)*

**Argumentative.** The question states a conclusion and asks the witness to agree rather than seeking testimony. *(R. Evid. 611)*

<!-- … -->

**Badgering the Witness.** Counsel is harassing or intimidating the witness rather than eliciting testimony. *(R. Evid. 611)* **Note:** distinct from Argumentative, which attacks the answer rather than the witness.

<!-- … -->

**Invades the Province of the Jury.** The question asks the witness to decide an ultimate issue reserved for the jury. *(R. Evid. 704)* **Note:** most jurisdictions permit ultimate-issue opinions from experts; this objection is strongest against lay witnesses.

<!-- … -->
```

#### Labels followed by values

A label followed on the same line by a value or URL MUST be kept as a label–value pair in one
paragraph. Small caps, colour or underlining do not make it a heading. See
Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7).

### 6.9 Stacked Headings

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `headings-stacked-headings` · Tags: rule, structure, headings

> **✅ Normative**
> The wrapped lines of one title MUST be joined with spaces into one heading. An article number
> MUST stay with its title. A company name printed above a statement or document title, exhibit
> labels, units lines and other furniture MUST be kept separate from the title; a title and subtitle MAY be split only where the document establishes
> distinct roles for them.

A stacked heading is printed over two or three centred lines: an article number over its title, a
note number over a title that wraps. A company name printed over a statement name looks the same
but is not part of the title.

```text
                ARTICLE 11
     ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS

21 Total equity
   reconciliation
```

The question is whether the break is a wrap or a hierarchy. `21 Total equity / reconciliation` is a
wrap. `ARTICLE 11 / ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS` reads as a number and a title — and the number
stays with the title.

#### Requirements

- The lines of one title MUST be joined with a single space, in printed order, into one heading.
- Its lines MUST NOT become two headings at the same level, nor a parent heading with a child.
- An article or note number printed above its title MUST be the start of that title's heading.
- A subtitle MAY be a separate element only where the document gives title and subtitle distinct
  roles; otherwise the lines are one heading.

`ARTICLE 11` and `ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS` are centred on two lines, both bold and
underlined, at the same size. They form one heading. Its depth is relative: the page does not show
the outline above the article.

<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt</summary>

```markdown
## ARTICLE 11 ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS

### Section 11.1 Definitions

<!-- … -->
```

#### Company name over a statement title

A company or entity name set directly above a statement, report or agreement title is **not** part
of the title. It MUST be rendered as its own paragraph above the heading, keeping its printed
emphasis, and the heading is the title alone:

```markdown
**CORVANE MEDIA CORPORATION**

# CONDENSED CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS

(unaudited; $ in millions)
```

The heading then names the document, so an outline reads "Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheets"
rather than repeating the company in every statement title. The same holds for financial
statements, agreements and reports alike. The units or date line beneath MUST also stay a separate
paragraph. A company name with no title beneath
it — only a grid, or a running stack repeated on every page — is furniture; the repetition is
judged across the document, see Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6).

#### Furniture is separated before a title is joined

Exhibit labels, units lines and other furniture MUST be separated from the title before its lines
are joined; only the lines of the title itself are joined. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7)
for the distinction between titles and furniture.

### 6.10 Table of Contents

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `lists-table-of-contents` · Tags: layout, lists, navigation

> **✅ Normative**
> A table of contents, table of authorities or index MUST be rendered as a list: one item per
> entry, nested as the page indents it, each item the label then its page number(s) exactly as
> printed, separated by a space. It MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

A contents page pairs each label with a page number, usually across a dot leader.

```text
Chapter 3 — Reserving  . . . . . . . . . . . .  47
Chapter 4 — Pricing    . . . . . . . . . . . .  63
```

#### Rendering

```text
Printed:   1  Introduction ....................  3
              1.1  Scope ......................  4
           2  Reserving .......................  47
```

```markdown
- 1 Introduction 3
  - 1.1 Scope 4
- 2 Reserving 47
```

- Every printed entry MUST survive, with its page number(s) attached to the right label.
- The label and the number are separated by a single space. The dot leaders produce nothing — see
  Dot Leader Lines (§6.1).
- Nesting shown by indentation MUST be carried as list nesting, not flattened.
- An entry with several page references keeps them all, as printed: `HCR 2.603(A) 4-50, 4-57`.
- A contents page is navigation, not data: rendering it as a table would make it read as facts to
  anything that consumes the page. A list also holds a run of page references that a two-column
  table could only cram into one cell.

The exception is a contents page printed as a **real ruled grid with column headers** (`Section |
Title | Page`). That is a table by the ordinary rules of Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5), not a contents
exception.

no leaders, one to twelve references per line. A label paired with a *list* of numbers. The

### 6.11 Transcript Pages

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `layout-transcript-pages` · Tags: layout, structure, legal, line-numbers

> **✅ Normative**
> On a transcript page, each speaker turn MUST be rendered as one paragraph that begins with its
> printed marker (`Q`, `A`, `THE COURT:`), with its wrapped lines joined. Printed line numbers MUST
> NOT appear in the Markdown; when line numbers are requested they are carried in the page's
> `line_numbers` map, exactly as for Pleading Line Numbers (§5.8).

A deposition or hearing transcript: numbered lines 1–25, a `Q` / `A` column, and text that wraps
to the left margin on its continuation lines. The line numbers are cited ("page 47, line 12"), so
the line structure is part of the content in a way ordinary prose is not.

```text
 4    Q    Was ████████ paying that before?
 5    A    Yes, he was.
 6    Q    At the time of the temporary hearing, he was
 7  paying the car insurance?
```

#### Rendering

- Each speaker turn — a `Q`, an `A`, or a colloquy line such as `MR. HALE:` or `THE COURT:` — MUST
  be its own paragraph, separated from the next by a blank line.
- The turn MUST begin with its speaker marker exactly as printed (`Q`, not `Q:`), followed by its
  text.
- A turn that wraps onto further printed lines MUST be joined into one paragraph: the continuation
  lines carry no marker on the page, and they carry none in the output.
- The printed line numbers MUST NOT appear in the Markdown, and the page MUST NOT be rendered as a
  `line | speaker | text` table.

#### Citing a line

Transcripts are cited by page and line ("page 83, line 13"). The citation is carried by the
`line_numbers` map defined in Pleading Line Numbers (§5.8): when line numbers are requested, each
printed number beside text gets an entry whose span covers that line's text inside its turn's
paragraph. A wrapped turn therefore keeps both of its line numbers even though it is one
paragraph.

*(Source image bag-deposition-transcript.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

to the left margin (lines 6–7, 12–13 and 24–25), each joined into one paragraph, a black redaction bar inside line 4, the folio `83`
above the frame and the reporting firm's name and telephone number as a footer.

```markdown
A No. We pay $60.

Q Are you telling me I'm getting the wrong number?

A We have a loyalty discount.

Q And the third route, that's something you're discussing, but it hasn't started yet?

HALVERSTON REPORTING (415) 555-0148
```

</details>

## §7 Text

### 7.1 Text Formatting Conventions

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-text-formatting-conventions` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> Inline marks MUST be written with exactly the markup in the table below. Where Markdown has no
> syntax for a mark, the output MUST use the HTML element named here and MUST NOT use a notation of
> its own.

This is the inline-markup table for the whole protocol. Each row states its requirement; the linked
rule holds the detail, the sub-cases and the examples.

| Printed mark | Requirement | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maths, inline or displayed | MUST be LaTeX inside `$$ … $$`; single `$` delimiters MUST NOT be used | Inline Equations (§7.2.6), Displayed Equations (§7.2.2) |
| Hyperlink or email address | MUST be raw text by default; link syntax MAY be used only when link extraction was requested | Links (§7.2.8) |
| Bold / italic | MUST be Markdown `**bold**` / `*italic*`, and only where the glyphs are heavier or slanted | Bold and Italics (§7.2.1) |
| Underline | MUST be `<u>…</u>` | Underlined Text (§7.2.12) |
| Strikeout | MUST be `~~…~~` over exactly the struck glyphs | Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) |
| Superscript / subscript | MUST be `<sup>…</sup>` / `<sub>…</sub>`, never a Unicode raised or lowered glyph | Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11) |
| Highlight | MUST be `<mark>…</mark>` over exactly the highlighted run | Highlighted Text (§7.2.5) |
| Highlight colour | MUST be carried as `style="background-color: HTML_COLOR_NAME"` on the `<mark>`, using the nearest HTML colour name | Highlighted Text (§7.2.5), Text Colors (§7.3.12) |
| Text colour, when it is the only distinguisher | MUST be `<font color="HTML_COLOR_NAME">…</font>` | Text Colors (§7.3.12) |
| Signature | MUST be `[signature:{name}]`, or bare `[signature]` when the name is not legible | Signatures (§7.3.10) |
| Logo | MUST be `[logo: printed words]`, or bare `[logo]` when it prints no text | Logos (§12.1.3) |
| Watermark | MUST be `[watermark: printed words]`, first in its page's content | Watermarks (§7.3.13) |
| Stamp | MUST be `[stamp: printed words]`, or bare `[stamp]` when illegible | Stamps (§7.3.11) |
| A printed character that is also Markdown syntax | MUST be escaped — `\*\*`, `\_`, `\|`, `` \` `` — and MUST NOT be dropped to avoid the collision | Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4) |

#### Why HTML elements at all

Markdown has no syntax for underline, superscript, subscript or highlight. The HTML element passes
through every downstream Markdown renderer unchanged, and it survives a round-trip: a reader can
strip it, render it or read the base characters underneath. A Unicode substitute (`²`, `₂`) does
not, which is why Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11) forbids it.





#### Related

- Markdown Rendering (§3.2) — the block-level constructs, of which this table is the inline half
- Elements (§3.1) — the Text class takes its inline marks from this table
- Quick Reference (§D.1) — every rule's requirement on one page

### 7.2 Inline formatting

#### 7.2.1 Bold and Italics

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-bold-and-italics` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> Bold MUST be written `**bold**` and italic `*italic*`, in Markdown, except where the Markdown
> delimiter cannot close, where `<strong>` / `<em>` MUST be used. They MUST be applied only where the
> printed glyphs are heavier or slanted than their neighbours.

HTML elements are reserved for marks Markdown cannot express at all — see Underlined Text (§7.2.12),
Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11) and Highlighted Text (§7.2.5). `<b>`, `<i>`, `<strong>` and `<em>` MUST NOT
be used for ordinary emphasis in the Markdown text.

#### Where `**` cannot close

CommonMark cannot close `**` or `*` between a punctuation mark and a letter: `**---**To be` is not
bold when rendered. In exactly that case — the emphasised run ends in punctuation and a letter or
digit follows with no space — the run MUST be written with `<strong>` (bold) or `<em>` (italic)
instead: `<strong>---</strong>To be`. Everywhere else the Markdown delimiters are used. (Inside HTML
table cells, emphasis is always `<strong>` / `<em>` — see Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2).)

#### Styling comes from the glyphs, not from the role

The syntax is the easy half. The failure that costs fidelity is styling text because of what it
*is* rather than what it *looks like*: bolding a heading because headings are usually bold, or
bolding a whole column because one cell in it is heavy.

- Styling MUST be decided from the glyphs on the page, one run of text at a time.
- A run MUST NOT be styled because of its role (heading, label, total) when its glyphs are not
  heavier or slanted.
- Where it cannot be established whether a run is heavier than its neighbours, the run SHOULD be
  left unstyled. An unmarked run loses a nuance; a wrongly marked one asserts something the page
  does not print — the **never invent** failure.

Tables are where this goes wrong most often, and they are judged cell by cell — see
Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2).





#### Related

- Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) — the same rule applied cell by cell, where over-application is most common
- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- Drop Caps (§7.2.3) — size is typography, not a style the output records

#### 7.2.2 Displayed Equations

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-displayed-equations` · Tags: text, formatting, math

> **✅ Normative**
> Displayed mathematics MUST be written as LaTeX inside `$$ … $$`. Its printed equation number
> MUST follow the closing delimiter as plain text in the same formula block: `$$ … $$ (1)`.

A displayed equation is set on its own line, usually centred, often with a number at the right
margin — `(1)`, `(2)` — that the prose cites.

```text
                 ΔE = ΔE⁰ − (RT / m·F) [ ln(θ / 1−θ) + fθ + gθ^(3/2) ]          (1)
```

#### Requirements

- The delimiters are those of Inline Equations (§7.2.6): `$$ … $$`, never single `$`.
- The equation number MUST be kept. It is content — "as shown in (1)" appears in the prose — and
  dropping it is the one option that loses something (**never drop**).
- The number MUST be written after the closing `$$`, as plain text, in the same block — not inside
  the LaTeX, and not as a separate paragraph. The Formula block includes its number; see
  Block Classes (§5.3).
- An unnumbered display MUST NOT be given a number.

##### ✅ **Sample** — numbered equations in a two-column article

*(Source image bag-journal-drop-cap-equations.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Two display equations, numbered (1) and (2) at the right margin, each cited in the surrounding
text. Equation (2) spans the full column width and wraps after `⇒`; the wrap is typesetting, so the
LaTeX is one line. The symbol cited in the prose after (1) is itself maths and takes the inline
form.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, right column</summary>

```markdown
UPD represents a potential dependent adsorption with great sensitivity and selectivity towards the nature of the metal surface and its termination. The complexity of the voltammetry features arises from the existence of one or more UPD ML superstructures<sup>22,23</sup> and/or one or more UPD MLs formed.<sup>24,25</sup>

$$\Delta E = \Delta E^{0}_{\theta \to 0} - (RT / mF) \cdot [\ln(\theta/(1-\theta)) + f\theta + g\theta^{3/2}]$$ (1)

Here the $$\Delta E^{0}_{\theta \to 0}$$ term represents the underpotential of the most positive stripping peak of the UPD adlayer where its coverage approaches zero. The term f is the Temkin parameter describing the attractive UPD ML–substrate interactions, as given in Eq. (1).

<!-- … -->

The UPD ML coverage can be controlled effectively down to a fraction of a monolayer by proper choice of an underpotential. The amount of deposited P is controlled by the reaction stoichiometry and the coverage of the UPD ML of metal M. The most general formulation of the SLRR reaction is given by the following equation:<sup>16</sup>

$$(\theta_{M} \cdot \rho_{M}^{\mathrm{UPD}}) \cdot M^{0}_{\mathrm{UPD}}/S(h,k,l) + (\theta_{M} \cdot \rho_{M}^{\mathrm{UPD}}) \cdot (m/p)P^{p+}_{\mathrm{solv}} \Rightarrow (\theta_{M} \cdot \rho_{M}^{\mathrm{UPD}}) \cdot M^{m+}_{\mathrm{solv}} + (\theta_{M} \cdot \rho_{M}^{\mathrm{UPD}}) \cdot (m/p)P^{0}_{s}/S(h,k,l)$$ (2)

*(continued on next page)*
```

</details>

##### ✅ **Sample** — a typewritten paper

*(Source image bag-typewritten-equations.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Equation `V = pu_y` numbered `(2)` at the right margin, then an unnumbered display `½ mV²`, in a
scanned typewritten proceedings page. Run-in underlined headings, also set in italic, open two
paragraphs.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt</summary>

```markdown
<!-- … -->

*<u>Velocity Spectra.</u>* Another method of presenting the same data is of interest here. This method involves the concept of a spectral velocity for the elasto-plastic system. The definition which is most convenient is to define the spectral velocity V by the relationship

$$V = pu_{y}$$ (2)

where p denotes the undamped circular natural frequency of the system. Then the quantity

$$\frac{1}{2} mV^{2}$$

represents the maximum recoverable strain energy of the system. It should be noted that this definition of the spectral velocity for the elasto-plastic system is consistent with that used for elastic systems, since in an elastic system the yield deformation may be taken equal to the maximum elastic deformation.

*<u>Relation Between Input Motion and Response Values.</u>* It is convenient to plot velocity spectra on a four-way logarithmic grid, so that displacement, velocity, acceleration and period may all be read from a single chart.
```

</details>

#### Formulas drawn as boxes

A formula laid out as boxes joined by operators is still an equation.

- A boxed arithmetic formula MUST be written in `$$ … $$`, keeping every printed operand, operator
  and label; the box labels become the operands.
- Where the boxes express a process rather than an equation, the region is a diagram and MUST be
  rendered as a diagram block instead — see Images and Figures (§12.1.2).

#### 7.2.3 Drop Caps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-drop-caps` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> A drop cap MUST be joined directly to the rest of its word, with no space, line break or styling
> added. The output MUST NOT mark the letter as bold, enlarged or otherwise distinct.

A drop cap is an enlarged first letter, sunk two or more lines into the opening paragraph. The
letter belongs to the first word; the text layer often separates it, and a line-by-line reading
puts the rest of the word on a different line from its initial.

```text
T  he modern Recreational Boating Safety (RBS)
   Program traces its inception to the Federal Boat
   Safety Act (FBSA) of 1971.
```

#### Requirements

- The initial MUST be joined to its word. The page prints one word in two sizes, not two words.
- The letter MUST NOT be bolded, enlarged or otherwise marked. Size here is typography, not
  emphasis — the same reasoning as Bold and Italics (§7.2.1).
- A decorated or ornamental initial is treated the same way: it is still the letter.
- The letter MUST be read from the image, not the text layer — see Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3). A
  legible initial MUST NOT be dropped or replaced by the text layer's reading.

*(Source image bag-uscg-drop-cap.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

The article opens with a three-line "T"; the first word is "The". The text layer of the file splits
it as `T` then `he`.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, first paragraph</summary>

```markdown
The modern Recreational Boating Safety (RBS) Program traces its inception to the Federal Boat Safety Act (FBSA) of 1971. The Act’s purpose was to improve boating safety by encouraging and assisting participation by the states, industry, and public. It also established national construction and performance standards and created flexible regulatory authority concerning boats. Since then, the many elements of the National RBS Program have successfully reduced incidents, injuries, and deaths. Led by the State RBS and National Nonprofit Organization grant programs, the combined effects of many program elements, and safer boats and boaters, the RBS Program achieved the fewest number of boating deaths in its history—a key measure of success.
```

#### 7.2.4 Escaping Printed Marks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-escaping-printed-marks` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> A character the page prints is content, even when Markdown would read it as syntax. It MUST be
> escaped so that it cannot open a span — `\*\*`, `\_`, `\|` — and it MUST NOT be deleted to avoid
> the collision.

Some marks a document prints are also Markdown's own punctuation: a menu that flags allergens with
`**`, a form that labels a field `_____`, a legal citation using `|`. The mark is transcribed, and
kept from being read as markup.

```text
Melt-in-the-Middle Fish Pie Fishcake**      ← ** is a printed allergen marker
Beer-Battered Haddock & Chips§**               pointing at a legend elsewhere
```

Written unescaped, that `**` opens a bold span that never closes and swallows the rest of the
block.

#### What to escape

| Printed | Output | Would otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `*` `**` | `\*` `\*\*` | Open emphasis or bold |
| `_` `__` | `\_` `\__` | Open emphasis, or vanish inside a word |
| `#` at line start | `\#` | Become a heading |
| `|` inside a table cell | `\|` | Split the cell |
| `` ` `` | `` \` `` | Open a code span |
| `~~` | `\~\~` | Strike the text through |
| `---` at line start | `\-\-\-` | Become a horizontal rule, or collide with the page separator |
| A literal bracketed number or word — `[1]`, `[date]` | `\[1\]`, `\[date\]` | Read as a marker (`[x]`, `[blank]`) or a form id |
| A literal angle-bracket placeholder — `<NAME>` | `&lt;NAME&gt;` | Be read as an HTML tag and vanish |

- Escaping SHOULD be applied only where the collision is real. A `*` in the middle of a word, or a
  `#` mid-sentence, needs nothing.
- A printed character MUST NOT be replaced by a different mark to avoid the collision: rewriting
  `**` as `<sup>2</sup>` or as a word is the **never invent** failure, and dropping it is the
  **never drop** one. The marker is the only thing tying an item to its legend; a legend entry
  with nothing pointing at it is unusable.

#### A raised marker is still a superscript

Escaping decides how the character survives; it does not decide its position. A marker printed
above the baseline MUST be written `<sup>\*\*</sup>` — both rules apply, and neither substitutes
for the other. See Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11).

#### Dashes, literal brackets and angle brackets

#### 7.2.5 Highlighted Text

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-highlighted-text` · Tags: text, formatting, color

> **✅ Normative**
> Highlighted text MUST be wrapped in `<mark>` carrying the highlighter colour as an attribute:
> `<mark style="background-color: yellow">the highlighted phrase</mark>`.

Text printed on a highlighter background is content, not decoration. The highlight MUST NOT be
dropped, and MUST NOT be reduced to bold or italic.

```text
<mark style="background-color: yellow">the highlighted phrase</mark>
```

#### Requirements

- The colour MUST be named with the nearest HTML colour name — `yellow`, `green`, `cyan`,
  `magenta`, `lightgray` — not a hex value or an invented label. That keeps the vocabulary finite
  and matches the treatment of colour in Text Colors (§7.3.12) and Color as the Value (§9.6.4).
- The `<mark>` MUST cover exactly the run of text that carries the background. If the highlight
  stops mid-sentence, so does the `<mark>`.
- Inside a table, only the cells whose background is actually coloured are marked; a whole row or
  column MUST NOT be marked because part of it is highlighted — the same over-application problem
  as Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2).

#### Why keep the colour

In a reviewed document, different highlight colours usually mean different things — one reviewer
per colour, or one category per colour. A bare `<mark>` collapses that distinction and there is no
way to recover it afterwards.





#### Related

- Text Colors (§7.3.12) — the same colour vocabulary for coloured text
- Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) — highlighting inside tables inherits the over-application problem
- Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4) — highlighted template placeholders, marked and escaped

#### 7.2.6 Inline Equations

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-inline-equations` · Tags: text, formatting, math

> **✅ Normative**
> Every equation MUST be written as LaTeX inside `$$ … $$`, inline ones included. Single-`$`
> delimiters MUST NOT be used.

```text
the coefficient $$\alpha$$ is fixed
```

The same delimiters apply whether the equation sits in the middle of a sentence or on a line of
its own; there is no separate inline form. Displayed equations and their numbers are covered in
Displayed Equations (§7.2.2).

#### Why double delimiters

A lone `$` is ambiguous. Notebook and Markdown renderers treat an unrelated currency sign further
down the page as the closing delimiter, open an unterminated maths span and swallow everything
after it. Doubling the delimiter removes the ambiguity. It is non-standard for inline maths, and
that cost is accepted.





#### Related

- Displayed Equations (§7.2.2) — equations on their own line, with their printed number
- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- Chemical Molecules (§13.1) — LaTeX packages for chemistry

#### 7.2.7 Line-End Hyphenation

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-line-end-hyphenation` · Tags: text, formatting, fidelity

> **✅ Normative**
> A word broken across a line end MUST be joined, and a hyphen that exists only for the break MUST
> be removed. A hyphen that belongs to the word MUST be kept. Where the two cannot be told apart,
> the visible hyphen MUST be kept.

Justified prose breaks words at line ends with a hyphen. The break is typesetting; the word is one
word. But a compound that happens to break at its own hyphen looks identical.

```text
… judges on the Court of Appeals for the District of Co-
lumbia Circuit concluded …                              ← join: Columbia

… And sales of air-
conditioning, industrial and other equipment …          ← keep: air-conditioning
```

| The line ends with | Output |
| --- | --- |
| A fragment of a word that has no hyphen of its own — `Co-` / `lumbia` | **Joined, hyphen removed** — `Columbia` |
| A compound broken at its own hyphen — `air-` / `conditioning` | **Joined, hyphen kept** — `air-conditioning` |
| A break that could be either | **Joined, hyphen kept** — the visible glyph is not removed on a guess |

Keeping the hyphen when unsure is the **never drop** side of the choice: a printed glyph survives,
and nothing the page does not show is asserted.

*(Source image bag-scotus-hyphenation.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

`[c]on-trol`, `Shaugh-nessy`, `en-trusted` and `Ho-tel` at line ends, plus a footnote with
`Im-migration`. None of these are compounds. A hyphenated compound elsewhere on the page,
`separation-of-powers`, sits mid-line and keeps its hyphens.

#### 7.2.8 Links

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-links` · Tags: text, formatting

> **✅ Normative**
> Hyperlinks and email addresses MUST be transcribed as raw text. Link syntax — `<email>`,
> `[url](url)` — MAY be used only when link extraction was explicitly requested.

#### Default

```text
Contact support@example.com or see https://example.com/pricing
```

#### When link extraction is requested

```text
Contact <support@example.com> or see [https://example.com/pricing](https://example.com/pricing)
```

#### Why raw text

The output is read mostly by a model or an extraction step. Link punctuation adds noise to every
chunk for a payload most readers never use. Raw text keeps the default output clean and still
leaves the address recoverable.

#### Anchor text that differs from its target

When the printed words differ from the target — `click here` pointing at a long URL — the output
MUST keep the printed words as they appear. Under the raw-text default the target is not
represented, and it MUST NOT be added in place of, or beside, the printed words: the page does not
print it (**never invent**).





#### Related

- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- QR Codes and Bar Codes (§7.3.7) — a URL carried by a code rather than printed text
- Output Options (§3.5) — other outputs that depend on what the producer was asked for

#### 7.2.9 Quote Blocks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-quote-blocks` · Tags: text, formatting

> **✅ Normative**
> A quoted or inset region MUST be flattened: its content is rendered as ordinary text, headings
> and tables included. The output MUST NOT add `>` block-quote markers.

A boxed or inset region on the page renders as:

```text
## here we go
Yeah
```

not:

```text
>
> ## here we go
> Yeah
```

#### Why flatten

Block-quote markers interact badly with headings and tables that sit inside the quoted region. Most
inset regions in real documents are not quotations at all — they are callouts, pull quotes or
sidebars that happen to be visually offset. Flattening keeps the content addressable. The cost is
losing the "this was inset" signal, and that cost is accepted.

#### A real quotation

In prose documents an inset block sometimes does mean *someone else said this*. It is flattened
all the same: the words survive, and every printed character of them — quotation marks, attribution
line — MUST be kept.





#### Related

- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- Reading Order (§5.9) — where an inset region's content falls in the page's sequence
- Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4) — printed characters that are also Markdown syntax

#### 7.2.10 Small Capitals

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-small-capitals` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> Text set in small capitals MUST be transcribed as uppercase letters. The output MUST NOT add
> small-caps styling, and MUST NOT substitute the text layer's mixed case for the capitals the page
> shows.

Running heads, bylines and firm names are often set in small capitals: capital letterforms at
lowercase height, usually with a full-size initial. The text layer may hold `Jackson` while the page
shows `JACKSON`; Markdown has no small-caps mark.

```text
JACKSON, J., dissenting          ← small caps on the page
WASSON & ASSOCIATES, CHARTERED   ← the same face, full name
```

#### Requirements

- Every letter printed as a capital letterform — full-size or small — MUST be an uppercase letter
  in the output.
- The rendered letterforms take precedence over the text layer's casing — see
  Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3).
- Small caps are not emphasis: they MUST NOT be turned into bold, italic or an HTML style. Bold or
  italic set in small caps is still marked, from the glyph weight and slant — see
  Bold and Italics (§7.2.1).
- Letter-spacing is typography, not content: the letters of a spaced word MUST be written as one
  word.

```markdown
(2) NO PARTICULAR OR UNIFORM ELECTRONIC VISIT VERIFICATION SYSTEM REQUIRED.—Nothing in the amendment made by this section shall be construed to require the use of a particular or uniform electronic visit verification system (as defined in subsection (l)(5) of section 1903 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396b), as inserted by subsection (a)) by all agencies or entities that provide personal care services or home health care under a State plan under title XIX of the Social Security Act (or under a waiver of the plan) (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.).

(3) NO LIMITS ON PROVISION OF CARE.—Nothing in the amendment made by this section may be construed to limit, with respect to personal care services or home health care services provided under a State plan under title XIX of the Social Security Act (or under a waiver of the plan) (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.), provider selection, constrain beneficiaries’ selection of a caregiver, or impede the manner in which care is delivered.

(4) NO PROHIBITION ON STATE QUALITY MEASURES REQUIREMENTS.—Nothing in the amendment made by this section shall be construed as prohibiting a State, in implementing an electronic visit verification system (as defined in subsection (l)(5) of section 1903 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396b), as inserted by subsection (a)), from establishing requirements related to quality measures for such system.

<!-- … -->
```

#### 7.2.11 Superscript and Subscript

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-superscript-and-subscript` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> Raised and lowered text outside maths MUST be written with `<sup>` and `<sub>`. A Unicode
> superscript or subscript character MUST NOT be substituted for the tag.

```text
H<sub>2</sub>O        ← conforming
H₂O                   ← non-conforming
```

The same applies to superscripts: `x<sup>2</sup>`, not `x²`. Inside an equation, raised and
lowered terms are LaTeX `^{…}` and `_{…}` within `$$ … $$` — see Inline Equations (§7.2.6).

#### Why the tag

A tag round-trips: a reader can strip it, render it, or read the base character underneath. A
Unicode glyph is lossy in the other direction — `₂` does not compare equal to `2`, so a downstream
numeric parse or string match silently fails. Unicode also has no raised or lowered form for most
characters, so substitution cannot be applied consistently.

#### Inside table cells

A footnote superscript attached to a value — `48,210³` — MUST be tagged as `48,210<sup>3</sup>`.
Whether the marker stays in the cell is a separate question, answered by
Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6).

A raised marker that is itself Markdown punctuation is tagged **and** escaped:
`<sup>\*\*</sup>` — see Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4).





#### Related

- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — where a footnote marker inside a cell belongs
- Chemical Molecules (§13.1) — formulas with subscripts
- Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4) — when the raised marker is itself Markdown punctuation, it is escaped as well as tagged

#### 7.2.12 Underlined Text

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-underlined-text` · Tags: text, formatting, inline

> **✅ Normative**
> Underlined text MUST be wrapped in `<u>…</u>`. The output MUST NOT use `<ins>`, and MUST NOT use
> `_ text _`.

```text
subject to the <u>prior written consent</u> of the lessor
```

Markdown has no underline of its own, so the HTML element is used.

#### Why not the alternatives

`<ins>` means *inserted text* — an edit-history claim that a plain underline on a page does not
make. `_ text _` collides with Markdown emphasis and renders as italics.

#### Underline in a redline

An underline-only replacement in a redlined table — a new figure underlined in place of a struck
one — is still written `<u>1.335</u>`, next to the struck value. See
Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) for how the pair is encoded.





#### Related

- Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1) — the full inline-markup table
- Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) — the redline pair of a struck value and its underlined replacement
- Bold and Italics (§7.2.1) — the other inline styles, which do use Markdown syntax

#### 7.2.13 Verse and Hard Line Breaks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-verse-and-hard-line-breaks` · Tags: text, formatting, line-breaks

> **✅ Normative**
> Text whose line breaks carry meaning — verse, song text, deliberately broken lines — MUST be
> written one printed line per source line, separated by a plain newline, and MUST NOT be reflowed
> into running prose. No trailing spaces, no `<br>`, no fenced block: the same spelling as
> Line Breaks Inside a Block (§6.2).

Poetry, song text, addresses and deliberately broken lines carry meaning in their line breaks.
Markdown joins single newlines into one paragraph when it renders, so the breaks vanish on screen
unless they are marked.

```text
your honor
since i've been convicted of murder
and have taken time to digest
just what that means
```

A plain newline keeps every printed line in the Markdown source, which is what the output is
judged on; a rendered view that joins the lines is a display artefact. Trailing spaces are invisible
and fragile, `<br>` puts markup on every line, and a fenced block turns the verse into code and loses
its bold and italics. Inline marks stay per line: a bold line is `**line**`.

Prose has the opposite rule: a line break inside a paragraph is typesetting, and the sentence is
joined. The question is only how to mark the lines when the break *is* the content. A verse line
that is too long for its column and wraps is still one line: the wrap is joined like prose.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a poem beside a biography

*(Source image bag-verse.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

The left column is verse, set in bold: short lines, no punctuation at most line ends, each break
intentional. Three lines are too long for the column and wrap (`… through every` / `weather!`,
`… on your lowest` / `stones`, `… that never` / `wavers — I think`); each is one verse line. The
right column is ordinary prose that wraps, then a QR code with its URL printed across two lines
beneath it.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, the verse column</summary>

```markdown
**old lighthouse**
**since I first walked this shingle as a girl**
**and have taken forty winters to notice**
**just what your light means**
**after counting the boats it has turned home**
**and how it reaches farther than any bell**
**or horn**
**you keep the same slow turn through every weather!**
**and never once hurried**
**in a calm, patient, unblinking manner**
**never asked the sea for its reasons**
**and never bent your beam to spare the rocks**
**which is a kind of honesty**
**I have only lately learned to keep**
**I have started to notice small things about you:**
**the gull that nests each spring on your gallery rail**
**the salt rings the tide leaves on your lowest stones**
**the rust blooming quietly at your door**
**the way fog softens your beam into a halo**
**the long calm between one flash and the next**
**the lamp-room ladder worn pale by other hands**
**the paint the keepers layer on each spring**
**feeling that this steadiness is a kind of instruction**
**and that there must**
**be something to learn from a light that never wavers — I think**
**patience is a shore we can still reach**

<!-- … -->
```

</details>

### 7.3 Marks on the page

#### 7.3.1 Clipped Text

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-clipped-text` · Tags: text, fidelity, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> Text cut off at the page edge MUST be rendered as the characters actually visible. A clipped word
> MUST NOT be completed, and an ellipsis or marker that the page does not print MUST NOT be
> appended to it.

A page whose content runs past the printable edge: the last letters of a label, the end of a
sentence, the right-hand column of a table are simply absent. Nothing is overprinted or redacted;
the ink was never there.

```text
Research and developmen        49,294     ← the final t is off the page
Selling, general, and administrative     41,515
Note: … These measures ar
not in compliance with … different from po
forma measures …
```

#### Requirements

- The visible fragment MUST be kept, verbatim — see Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3). Dropping it loses
  printed content; completing it adds content that is not printed. See
  Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2).
- The clipping itself MUST NOT be marked inside the text. A producer MAY record that a page is
  clipped outside the Markdown.
- A clipped line inside a paragraph is joined to the next line like any other wrapped line; the
  fragment stays as printed.

the note lines that reach the right edge lose their last characters.

```markdown
  <!-- … -->
</table>

Note: The company provides pro forma financial data as an alternative for understanding its operating results. These measures ar not in compliance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, and may be different from po forma measures used by other companies
```

#### 7.3.2 E-Signature Tags

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-e-signature-tags` · Tags: text, marks, forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A field that carries only an e-signature tag is unsigned and MUST be rendered as a blank, `[blank]`.
> A tag that prints a word — SIGN, INITIAL — MUST be rendered as that word, separately beside the
> field, and MUST NOT be rendered as a signature or as the field's value.

Electronic signing tools print a small coloured tab beside each field the signer must complete —
"SIGN", "INITIAL", an arrow. The tab is not a signature and not part of the form; it is an
instruction to a future signer, often left in the exported file.

```text
QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN'S   │ QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN'S   │ DATE
SIGNATURE                       │ PRINTED NAME                    │
▸SIGN                           │                                 │
```

#### Requirements

- The field MUST be rendered as unsigned: `[blank]`, as for any blank field — see Fill-Ins (§10.4.4).
- A tag's printed word MUST be kept, verbatim, beside the field and outside the field's value. The
  samples below place it on its own line directly after the field.
- A tag that prints no word adds nothing to the text.
- A page on which the signature fields carry only tags is unsigned. `[signature]` MUST NOT appear
  for such a field — see Signatures (§7.3.10).

in the first cell of each; every cell is otherwise empty.

```markdown
- **QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN’S SIGNATURE**: [blank]
  SIGN▸
- **QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN’S PRINTED NAME**: [blank]
- **DATE**: [blank]
```

</details>

#### 7.3.3 Handwritten Annotations

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-handwritten-annotations` · Tags: text, marks, handwriting

> **✅ Normative**
> A handwritten note on a printed page MUST be rendered as `[handwritten: legible words]`, in a
> block of its own next to the content it annotates. Its legible words MUST be kept; words that
> cannot be read MUST NOT be reconstructed.

A note written on a printed page: an exhibit reference in the margin, a circled item, an arrow with
a word, a reviewer's initials. Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5) settles handwriting that *replaces* a
printed value inside a table; a note in the margin of prose replaces nothing.

```text
    … to confirm the absence of cyclonic flow.

                                      2                     Attach. B   ← red pen
                                                       SAQB 193        ← Bates stamp
```

#### Requirements

- The note adds information to the printed page, so it MUST be kept, and MUST be kept apart from
  the body text: it MUST NOT be spliced into the sentence beside it.
- The block MUST sit next to the content the note annotates in reading order.
- Legible fragments MUST be kept verbatim. Characters that cannot be read are left out, never
  guessed.

Bates number `SAQB 193`. The page's own number, `2`, is centred above.

```markdown

A pretest meeting will be held with agency staff not less than fifteen days prior to the scheduled test date. Results will be submitted in a final report within forty-five days of test completion, together with process data logs covering the full duration of each run.

[handwritten: Attach. B]

SAQB 193
```

</details>

#### 7.3.4 Iconography and Symbols

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-iconography-and-symbols` · Tags: text, images, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> An icon that carries meaning MUST NOT be dropped. It MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic tag
> in the icon's position: one lower-case word naming what the icon means — `[yes]`, `[no]`,
> `[locked]` — with `: degree` where the icons are graded (`[water: 3]`, `[sun: partial]`), and
> `[icon: shape]` naming the shape
> where the meaning is unclear (`[icon: sun]`). The vocabulary is open: the word is whatever names
> the meaning on this page.

Small symbols and images that stand in for a value rather than decorate — a tick in a
feature-comparison column, a padlock, a sun or water icon used as the cell content itself.

#### Rendering

The icon is read the way the page intends it, and that reading is written in brackets:

```text
| Feature | Basic     | Pro   |
| SSO     | [locked]  | [yes] |
```

- Each icon MUST produce one tag, in the position the icon occupies.
- Where an icon has no clear meaning in context, the tag MUST describe what is drawn —
  `[icon: sun]` — rather than guess a value.
- Where the icons are graded, the tag MUST carry the **degree**, not just the presence:
  `[sun: full]` / `[sun: partial]`, `[water: 3]` / `[water: 1]`. A tag that distinguishes the
  values beats a prettier glyph that does not.

#### Why a tag, and an open vocabulary

A tag reads back unambiguously and does not depend on a glyph existing, where the nearest Unicode
character or emoji may not exist or may carry a different meaning. Its word is not drawn from a fixed
list: no list would cover every icon, so the word is whatever names the meaning on this page, in
lower case, used the same way throughout the document.

#### Why it matters

When the icon *is* the value, dropping it empties the table. A feature matrix or a scorecard whose
marks are gone says nothing at all. This is the same failure as Color as the Value (§9.6.4), where a
coloured fill with no text becomes an empty cell and the table stops meaning anything.

##### ❌ **Counter-sample** — graded icons flattened to one glyph

*(Source image iconography-example.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A plant-list table with two icon-valued columns — **Sun** and **H₂O**. The printed page on the left
uses graded symbols: a filled, a half-filled or an empty sun, and one, two or three water droplets.
The parse preview on the right renders both columns as a single ☀️ and a single 💧.

**That is the failure this rule exists to prevent.** The icons were not dropped — they were
*flattened*. A plant needing three droplets and one needing a single droplet come out identical,
so the column still looks populated while the information it carried is gone. The columns are
the whole point of the table: *Sun* and *H₂O* are the two facts a reader consults it for. The
expected Markdown reads the empty sun as `[sun: none]`; the red outlines around the two columns
are highlighting added to the figure, not part of the page.

<details>
<summary>Non-conforming output</summary>

```markdown
<table>
  <tr> <th>Common Name</th> <th>Size</th> <th>Sun</th> <th>H<sub>2</sub>O</th> <th>Comment</th> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Marigold</td> <td>1' x 1'</td> <td>☀️</td> <td>💧</td> <td>Full sun, one droplet…</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Larkspur</td> <td>2' x 1'</td> <td>☀️</td> <td>💧</td> <td>Partial shade, two droplets…</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Fernwort</td> <td>1.5' x 1'</td> <td>☀️</td> <td>💧</td> <td>Shade only, three droplets…</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Coastal Sage</td> <td>3' x 2'</td> <td>☀️</td> <td>💧</td> <td>Drought tolerant…</td> </tr>
</table>
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · printed table (left)</summary>

```markdown
<table>
  <tr> <th>Common Name<br/>Botanical Name</th> <th>Size</th> <th>Sun</th> <th>H<sub>2</sub>O</th> <th>Comment</th> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Marigold<br/><em>Tagetes hybrida</em></td> <td>1' x 1'</td> <td>[sun: full]</td> <td>[water: 1]</td> <td>Full sun, one droplet: light, infrequent watering.</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Larkspur<br/><em>Consolida ajacis</em></td> <td>2' x 1'</td> <td>[sun: partial]</td> <td>[water: 2]</td> <td>Partial shade, two droplets: moderate, regular watering.</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Fernwort<br/><em>Pteris umbrosa</em></td> <td>1.5' x 1'</td> <td>[sun: none]</td> <td>[water: 3]</td> <td>Shade only, three droplets: keep evenly moist.</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Coastal Sage<br/><em>Salvia litoralis</em></td> <td>3' x 2'</td> <td>[sun: full]</td> <td>[water: 1]</td> <td>Drought tolerant once established.</td> </tr>
</table>
```

</details>

#### Icons standing in for labels

An icon that clearly supplies a field's label — a pin before an address, a handset before a phone
number — MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic label beside its value: `[address]`, `[phone]`,
`[web]`. The nearest word (`Address:`) MUST NOT be substituted: it is not printed. An icon whose
function is unclear is described by its shape instead of guessed.

#### 7.3.5 Margin Banners

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-margin-banners` · Tags: text, marks, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> Rotated text printed along a side margin MUST be rendered once, as a furniture block of its own
> outside the body flow, with its words kept — branding included. It MUST NOT be tagged as a
> watermark unless it actually overlays the content.

Text printed rotated along the page margin, outside the content area: an archive stamp, a brand
line, a firm mark. Unlike a watermark (§7.3.13) it does not overlap the content, and unlike a
page header it is not in the top or bottom margin.

```text
 U │                                         │
 S │  Overview of Risk Ranking Symbols       │
   │                                         │
 E │  One way to rank environmental impacts  │
 P │  …                                      │
 A │                                         │
```

#### Requirements

- The words MUST be kept. Some banners are document metadata — "US EPA ARCHIVE DOCUMENT" tells the
  reader the document is superseded, the same kind of fact "DRAFT" carries. Branding is printed
  text too, and MUST NOT be dropped as decoration.
- The banner MUST be one block of its own, rendered once on the page, and MUST NOT be spliced into
  a body sentence, table or list.
- The `[watermark: …]` marker MUST NOT be used for text that does not cross the content.
- The rotation MUST NOT be described. The words are the content.
- The samples place the banner at the start of its page's content.

nowhere else.

```markdown
Downloaded via VARENBROOK UNIV on February 22, 2021 at 01:49:16 (UTC).
See https://pubs.velmora.example/sharingguidelines for options on how to legitimately share published articles.

```

#### 7.3.6 Overlapping Text

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-overlapping-text` · Tags: text, marks, legal

> **✅ Normative**
> Where two printed strings overlap, each legible string MUST be rendered whole, in a block of its
> own, with the stamp first. Legible fragments MUST be kept; characters hidden by the overlap MUST
> NOT be reconstructed.

Two printed strings occupy the same space. The common case is a court e-filing stamp — `Case
1:19-cv-00892  Document 36  Filed 04/04/19  Page 2 of 2` — laid across a header the page already
had, so the two texts interleave character by character.

```text
4/4/2019   PresCase 1:19-cv-00892-KSC Document 36 Filed 04/04/19 Page 2 of 2ates | The White House
           ↑ browser print header             ↑ filing stamp, printed over it
```

The stamp is the more important string — it identifies the exhibit — but the underlying header is
still printed content.

#### Requirements

- Every legible string MUST be kept: the stamp and the text beneath it are both printed. Keeping
  only the more legible one drops content.
- The strings MUST NOT be interleaved into one line. Each is rendered whole, in its own block.
- At the overlap, the stamp MUST come first, as its `[stamp: …]` marker (see Stamps (§7.3.11)), followed by the
  string it is printed over.
- Characters that the overlap hides MUST be left out rather than guessed; the legible part of the
  string is kept — see Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2).

header line, and the two are unreadable as one string. Read apart, both are legible. The footer URL

```markdown
https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/presidential-proclamation-declaring-national-emergency-concerning-southern-border-united-states/ 2/2
```

#### 7.3.7 QR Codes and Bar Codes

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-qr-codes-and-bar-codes` · Tags: text, images, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> A QR code or bar code MUST be rendered as an image reference whose alt text holds the decoded
> content and whose target holds the literal label: `![decoded content](QR Code)`,
> `![decoded content](Bar code)`. The code MUST also be an element of its own, carrying the decoded
> value and a box around the code.

#### The rendering

```text
![content of qr code](QR Code)
![content of Bar code](Bar code)
```

So a code that decodes to a tracking URL becomes `![https://example.com/t/9F2K](QR Code)`.

The alt-text and target slots are used in the reverse of the usual Markdown convention: the content
goes in the alt slot, the literal label in the target slot. That is deliberate.

#### Why this form

It is the only encoding where the Markdown alone is useful. A reader gets the decoded payload —
usually a URL or a tracking number — without following an element reference. The code's own
element still carries the scan value, and its box locates the code for anyone who needs the image.

#### When the code does not decode

A payload MUST NOT be invented. A code that does not decode MUST be rendered with the label alone
and an empty alt text, and is still its own element with its box:

```text
![](QR Code)
```

#### Example

##### ✅ **Sample** — a QR code closing a product page

*(Source image corpus-qr-code.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A QR code printed at the foot of a product page, beside the line *"Pour découvrir d'autres
exemples, c'est ici :"* — the prose leads directly into it, so dropping the code leaves a sentence
pointing at nothing. The code on this page does not decode, so the alt text stays empty; had it
decoded, its payload would fill the alt slot. The code is its own element, with a box around the
code alone.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, foot of the block</summary>

```markdown
<!-- … -->

**Pour découvrir d'autres exemples, c'est ici :**

![](QR Code)
```

</details>
