#### 7.3.8 Redacted Text

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-redacted-text` · Tags: text, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> Each contiguous redacted span MUST be rendered as one `[REDACTED]` marker, in the position the
> suppressed text occupied. Visible text and any printed exemption code MUST be kept; the hidden
> characters and their count MUST NOT be inferred.

Text blacked out or boxed over in the source document.

#### The rendering

The marker sits where the suppressed text was, so the surrounding line still reads correctly:

```markdown
Account holder: [REDACTED]
```

Where only part of a value is covered, the marker MUST replace only the covered part, and the
visible characters MUST be kept verbatim — not normalised, padded or reconstructed. Printed masking
characters are visible characters, escaped where they are Markdown syntax (see
Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4)):

```markdown
Account number: \*\*\*\*-\*\*\*\*-\*\*\*\*-4471
```

When boxes are requested, a redacted span has a box like any other printed region — see
Boxes and Granularity (§3.3).

#### Why a positive marker beats silence

A redaction is an assertion: something was here and was deliberately removed. If the output emits
nothing, a reader cannot tell "the field was blank" from "the field was suppressed" — a meaningful
difference in a legal or regulatory document.

`[REDACTED]` is the same bracketed-placeholder shape used for Signatures (§7.3.10) (`[signature]`) and
for QR Codes and Bar Codes (§7.3.7) (`![](QR Code)`).

#### Exemption codes

A redacted region that prints an exemption code MUST be rendered as `[REDACTED: code]` —
`[REDACTED: (b)(5)]` — with the code copied exactly, once. Unrelated text near the region MUST stay
outside the marker.

#### 7.3.9 Seals and Round Stamps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-seals-and-round-stamps` · Tags: text, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> A seal or round stamp MUST be rendered as `[seal: printed text]`, holding all of its legible rim
> and centre text in reading order, in a block separate from body prose. The bare `[seal]` MUST be
> used only when none of its text is legible.

A round or oval impression — an auditor's firm seal, a notary seal, a court seal — printed or inked
on the page, usually beside a signature. Its text runs around the rim.

```text
   ╭────────────╮        For, Caldrivane & Rao LLP
  ( CALDRIVANE &    )       Chartered Accountants
  (  RAO LLP     )       [signature]
   ╰────────────╯        A. N. Bhatt
```

#### Requirements

- The seal MUST NOT be dropped. It is the page's proof of authority, the same kind of fact as a
  signature, and its text is often the only place the firm's name is printed.
- Its text MUST be kept verbatim and in a readable order — in the samples, upper rim, then centre,
  then lower rim — including a word the rim cuts short. Illegible characters are left out, never
  guessed.
- The seal MUST be its own block, never part of a sentence beside it.
- A stamp that lands on a table is kept out of the grid — see Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5).
- A signature written across the seal is a separate mark — see Signatures (§7.3.10).

#### 7.3.10 Signatures

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-signatures` · Tags: text, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> A handwritten signature MUST be rendered as a bracketed placeholder: `[signature:{name}]` when its
> glyphs are genuinely legible, the bare `[signature]` otherwise. A name MUST NOT be guessed.

A handwritten signature over a signature line.

#### The rendering

A signature whose name can be read from its glyphs:

```markdown
[signature:Mariana Augusta de Figueiredo Lacerda e Souza]
```

A signature whose name cannot:

```markdown
[signature]
```

A half-readable signature MUST get the bare `[signature]` form.

#### Why

A signature is semantically meaningful — the document *is signed* — but it is not text. The
placeholder records the fact without asserting a transcription that could be wrong, and the
name-carrying form preserves the value when the glyphs really are readable.

This is the same shape as `[REDACTED]` in Redacted Text (§7.3.8): a bracketed tag standing in for a
non-text region.

#### Edge cases

- Two signatures on one line MUST get two placeholders, one each, in reading order — even when
  both are illegible.
- A signature that is also a stamp, or that overlaps a printed grid, follows
  Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5).

#### On a form

A signature field follows the same shapes, with one addition: an **unsigned** field is a blank
fill-in, `[blank]`, not a missing signature.

```markdown
- **Your signature**: [signature:John Doe]
- **Spouse's signature. If a joint return, both must sign.**: [blank]
- **Date**: [blank]
- **Your occupation**: Accountant
```

A signature line's date and occupation companions are ordinary fill-ins — see Fill-Ins (§10.4.4).

#### A signature with its name printed beside it

The name in `[signature:{name}]` is read off the signature's own glyphs. Many documents print the
signer's name directly under the signature line.

A name printed under or beside an illegible signature MUST NOT fill `[signature:{name}]`: the
signature is the bare `[signature]`, and the printed name is rendered as the text it is. The tag
records only what the strokes show — the printed name is not always the signer, as when someone
signs on another's behalf — and the name is kept as text beside it, so nothing is lost.

<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, the signature block</summary>

```markdown

**For, Caldrivane & Rao LLP**
**Chartered Accountants**
**Firm Registration No. - 118427W/W100284**

[signature]

**A. N. Bhatt**
Partner
Membership No. 084213
UDIN: 26084213MZQPKT2231

<!-- … -->
```

#### Initials on every page

Handwritten approval initials MUST be rendered as `[signature]` on every page that carries them,
with the initials inside the placeholder only when their glyphs support it. The placeholder MUST
be kept outside body sentences.

#### Typed names on signature lines

A name typed in a plain face on a signature line, or a conformed `/s/` signature, is not a
signature: it is printed text. It MUST be rendered as that text, verbatim — `/s/` included — and
MUST NOT be given a `[signature]` placeholder, which would assert handwriting the page does not
show.

#### 7.3.11 Stamps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-stamps` · Tags: text, marks, legal

> **✅ Normative**
> Ink applied over or beside the printed page — overprinted, boxed or rotated, or in a different
> ink — MUST be rendered as `[stamp: its words]`, exactly as printed, at its place in reading order.
> A stamp with no legible words MUST be rendered as `[stamp]`. The page's own printed text is never a
> stamp, however official it looks.

A stamp records an act on this page: `FILED`, `RECEIVED`, `PAID`, `APPROVED`, a court e-filing line
laid across the header, a clerk's dated box. It was added after the page was printed, and it is
recognised by that: it overprints the page's text, sits in a box or at an angle the page's layout
does not use, or is in a different ink.

#### Requirements

- A stamp is written with the protocol's bracket marker, `[stamp: …]`, carrying its words exactly
  as printed; a stamp on several lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
- It keeps its place in reading order. Where it overprints other text, the marker comes first,
  then the text beneath it — see Overlapping Text (§7.3.6). Over a table it stays outside the table —
  see Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5).
- A stamp whose words cannot be read is the bare `[stamp]`.
- A **round seal** is `[seal: …]` — see Seals and Round Stamps (§7.3.9). A **watermark**, background text
  that describes the whole document, is `[watermark: …]` — see Watermarks (§7.3.13). The three share one
  bracket shape because each is ink laid on the page; they keep separate names because a watermark
  describes the document while a stamp or seal records an act on this page.
- Header text that the page prints itself — a filing header, an official form number — is ordinary
  text, not a stamp.

#### 7.3.12 Text Colors

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-text-colors` · Tags: text, formatting, color

> **✅ Normative**
> Text colour MUST be carried only when it is the only thing distinguishing some text from the rest,
> written as `<font color="NAME">…</font>` around exactly the coloured words, with the nearest HTML
> colour name. Colour that is decoration MUST NOT be rendered.

Coloured text in the source document.

#### Decoration or meaning

Most coloured text is styling: a blue heading, a brand-coloured lead paragraph, a page printed in
one colour. The words are kept and the colour is not rendered.

Colour becomes content when it is the **only** thing distinguishing some text from the rest — an
insertion printed in red with no underline, a figure in red meaning negative, a status word whose
colour is the status. There the colour MUST be carried:

```text
… will testify. <font color="red">Before or promptly after the notice or subpoena is served …</font> A subpoena …
```

- The element wraps exactly the coloured words, so the output says which text carries the colour.
- The colour MUST be the nearest HTML colour name — not a hex value and not an invented label.
- Text whose colour is doubled by another mark — red *and* underlined, red *and* bold — is already
  distinguished; the colour is decoration there and is not carried.

#### The extreme case

A cell that is a coloured fill with *no text at all* — a risk-matrix square, a heat-map grid —
becomes an empty cell if the colour is dropped, and the whole table stops meaning anything. See
Color as the Value (§9.6.4) for that situation specifically.

#### Staying consistent

Highlighting already has a settled encoding built on the same vocabulary:

```text
<mark style="background-color: HTML_COLOR_NAME">…</mark>
```

Text colour uses the nearest HTML colour name too, so there is one colour vocabulary for both:
`<mark style="background-color: NAME">` for a highlight, `<font color="NAME">` for coloured text.

Every word on the page, headings included, is set in dark red. Nothing is distinguished from
anything else by the colour, so it is decoration and the output carries none of it.

The actual subpoena (Official Form 16) should include a reference to the application and the clerk's office where it is filed. An accurate statement of the title of the court and action, including docket number, is required by subparagraphs (i) and (ii) both for completeness of the record in Halvana and to enable the deponent to obtain copies of the pleadings if necessary. The term “proceeding” is used to make clear that the rule is not limited to civil actions but may be used to obtain depositions for use in probate, administrative, or criminal proceedings if the law of the other jurisdiction so provides. The statement of the action required by subparagraph (iii) should indicate briefly the factual basis of the plaintiff's claim or other matter. Pertinent discovery provisions of the law of the other jurisdiction should at least be summarized and a proper citation given.

```markdown
<!-- … -->
```

#### 7.3.13 Watermarks

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `text-watermarks` · Tags: text, marks, layout

> **✅ Normative**
> A watermark MUST NOT be deleted and MUST NOT be left inside the body text. It MUST be rendered once
> per page that prints it, as its own element at the top of that page's content:
> `[watermark: DRAFT]`.

Diagonal or background text stamped across the page — "DRAFT", "Redline Version", "CONFIDENTIAL",
"VOID".

*(Source image watermark.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

#### Requirements

- The watermark is its own element, not a phrase inside the text it happens to cross.
- It is written as the protocol's bracket marker, `[watermark: …]`, carrying its words exactly as
  printed, and placed first in the page's content — not in the middle of the paragraph or table row
  it physically overlaps.
- A watermark printed on several lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
- It is recorded on every page that prints it, and not carried onto a page that does not.

```markdown
[watermark: Redline Version]
```

#### Why not simply drop it

A watermark says something about the whole document, and it is often the single most important fact
on the page. "Redline Version" says that every figure in Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) is in play;
"VOID" invalidates everything underneath it. Removing it silently loses real information.

#### Why not leave it inline

The watermark overlaps body text physically. Rendered in place, it injects a stray phrase into the
middle of a sentence or splits a table row — corrupting content that was otherwise clean.

Keeping it as a separate element gets both: the fact is recorded and the text stream stays intact.
The bracket marker is the same shape as the protocol's other marks laid on a page — `[seal: …]`,
`[logo: …]`, `[signature]` — see Markdown Rendering (§3.2).

## §8 Lists

### 8.1 Bullets and Sub-Bullets

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `lists-bullets-and-sub-bullets` · Tags: lists

> **✅ Normative**
> A top-level bulleted item MUST be rendered with the `*` marker and a sub-item with the `-`
> marker. The two markers carry the nesting and MUST NOT be interchanged.

A printed list: items led by a bullet glyph or a number, sometimes with indented sub-items beneath
them.

```text
• Top-level item
   – Sub-item beneath it
   – Another sub-item
• Next top-level item
```

```markdown
* Top-level item
  - Sub-item beneath it
  - Another sub-item
* Next top-level item
```

#### Ordered lists

- A printed numbering MUST be kept verbatim, including its style: `1.` `2.` `3.`, `a.` `b.` `c.`,
  `(i)` `(ii)` and `1)` `2)` differ on the page and MUST differ in the output. The numbering is
  often cited elsewhere in the document.

#### Deeper nesting

- Where the page shows more than two levels, each further level MUST be carried by indentation.
- The relative structure MUST be preserved: a three-level list MUST NOT be flattened into two.

#### Lists inside table cells

A cell holding a vertical list is governed by Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3): `<ul><li>`
and `<br>•` both conform inside a cell, and parallel lists across several columns of one row MUST
NOT be collapsed — they become one row per printed line.

#### Bridge text between lists

An unbulleted line printed between two runs of bullets, such as `partially offset by`, MUST be
rendered as a paragraph between the two lists. It MAY be rendered as indented continuation text
only when it belongs to one specific list item.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a line between bullets that is not a bullet

*(Source image bag-release-bullet-interjection.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Four bulleted increases, then `partially offset by` on its own unbulleted line, then one more
bullet. The interjection is a paragraph between two lists.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt</summary>

```markdown
<!-- … -->

GAAP diluted EPS for fiscal 2024 were $11.44, a 6% increase over $10.77 for fiscal 2023. Excluding a $0.51 and $1.28 decrease for business optimization costs in fiscal 2024 and 2023, respectively, and a $0.38 increase for a gain on an investment in fiscal 2023, adjusted EPS were $11.95, a 2% increase over $11.67 in fiscal 2023. The $0.28 increase in EPS on an adjusted basis reflects:

* a $0.19 increase from higher revenue and operating results;
* a $0.05 increase from lower share count;
* a $0.05 increase from a lower effective tax rate; and
* a $0.02 increase from higher non-operating income;

partially offset by

* a $0.03 decrease from higher noncontrolling interests.
```

</details>

#### Bullet glyphs that carry meaning

- A printed bullet glyph that carries meaning — a tick for *acceptable*, a cross for
  *unacceptable* — MUST be kept as the first content token after the Markdown marker:
  `* ✓ Bank statement`.
- A decorative bullet shape (•, ◦, ▪, ➢) MUST be normalised to the Markdown marker and MUST NOT be
  transcribed.

## §9 Tables

### 9.1 What counts as a table

#### 9.1.1 Borderless Whitespace Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-borderless-whitespace-tables` · Tags: tables, detection, ocr, borderless, whitespace

> **✅ Normative**
> A whitespace-aligned block with columns MUST be rendered as a table. Its column tracks MUST be
> read off the widest row, every value MUST be placed in the track it sits in, and the block MUST
> NOT be rendered as preformatted text.

Typewriter and fixed-width reports where the columns exist **only as alignment** — no column rules,
no fills, no shading. Nothing on the page shows where one column ends and the next begins except
the whitespace.

```text
DURATION    LAPSE     EXPENSE
   1        12.0%       48.00
   2         8.5%       22.50     ← columns are pure whitespace
```

#### Reading the tracks

1. The column tracks are taken from the widest, most populated row.
2. Every remaining row is checked: each value MUST start inside one track.
3. Where they all do, the block is a table with those columns.
4. Where a value drifts toward a neighbouring track, or straddles two, it MUST be placed in the
   track its left edge is closest to. The block is still a table.

A printed header line (a row of labels, often underlined) is strong evidence that columns are
intended, and a reason to look harder for consistent tracks. It is not on its own a licence to
create columns that the body rows do not support (**never invent**).

#### Why the alignment test, and not a guess

Columns guessed wrong produce silently misaligned data — a lapse rate filed under expense. The
alignment test is how the columns are read, not a reason to give up on them: the widest row fixes
the tracks, and every other value is placed by where it starts. A preformatted block would keep the
characters but lose every number to anything that consumes structure, which is the worse loss — so
it is never the conforming output.

A purely visual "it must have printed rules" reading of Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) would exclude this
entire class by construction. It does not: these are tables when the alignment holds.

#### 9.1.2 Chart With a Printed Data Grid

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-chart-with-a-printed-data-grid` · Tags: tables, charts, orientation

> **✅ Normative**
> When a chart prints its data grid beside or beneath the canvas, the output MUST render that grid
> exactly as printed — same orientation, same headers, same row order — and MUST NOT render any
> other table for the chart.

Some charts print their numbers as a small grid next to the canvas: a bar chart with bucket-columns
× metric-rows underneath, for example. That printed grid is often **transposed** relative to the
`[Category, Value]` shape a chart is usually reasoned about in.

```text
Printed under the bar chart:            Transposed reconstruction — non-conforming:
| Metric   | $0–1k | $1k–5k | $5k+ |    | Bucket | Avg Premium |
| Avg Prem | 412   | 388    | 351  |    | $0–1k  | 412         |
                                        | $1k–5k | 388         |
```

#### Requirements

- The table representing the chart MUST open with `<table data-source="chart">`, including when
  its values come from the printed grid.
- The grid MUST be transcribed in its **printed orientation**. Metrics that run across the top stay
  across the top.
- The grid MUST NOT be transposed, and its rows and columns MUST NOT be reordered into a more
  natural shape.
- The output MUST NOT add a second, reconstructed version alongside it. One grid is printed; one
  grid is rendered.
- Values MUST NOT be re-keyed off the chart canvas — bars, points and axis ticks are not the
  source. Only what is printed as text in the grid counts.

A transposed version is non-conforming even when it reads better, in the same way that rewriting a
cell's text is non-conforming.

#### Why as printed

This is the verbatim posture the whole protocol takes: transcribe what is on the page, do not
improve it (see Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3), Accounting Number Formats (§9.6.1)). A second reconstructed copy
also creates the duplication described in Duplicated Tables (§9.2.4) and Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) —
two tables where the page printed one (**never invent**).

Each chart prints a four-row grid under its bars — one row per series, one column per quarter,
with the year as a spanning row between the quarters and the values. The grid is the rendering; the
bars are not re-keyed.

#### 9.1.3 Empty Pre-Printed Grids

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-empty-pre-printed-grids` · Tags: tables, forms, degenerate

> **✅ Normative**
> A printed grid with no values entered MUST be rendered as a table, with its headers and **every
> printed empty row** as a row of empty cells. It MUST NOT be skipped, and MUST NOT be reduced to its
> headers alone.

A blank form table — full ruled structure, headers printed, no values entered anywhere.

```text
| Name | Date | Amount | Signature |
|      |      |        |           |
|      |      |        |           |
```

#### Requirements

- The grid MUST be rendered as a table. The headers are the content: they are what the form asks
  for.
- Every printed empty row MUST be rendered, as empty cells. An empty cell is a cell.
- The headers MUST NOT be emitted on their own. A headers-only output is the degenerate shape ruled
  out in Header-Only Tables (§9.1.4); here the printed empty rows are the body, so keeping them avoids
  that shape.
- The table MUST NOT be skipped because it has no data. A page with a printed form on it is not
  blank.
- A long run of identical empty rows — dozens of them — MUST be rendered in full, never trimmed to a
  representative few.

#### Why

A reader of a blank form is asking "what fields does this form ask for?", and the structure answers
that question completely. Returning nothing gives nothing for a page that is manifestly not blank.

The row count is the awkward part: reproducing forty empty rows is faithful and repetitive,
reproducing one is compact and unfaithful. **Faithful wins** — trimming cannot be undone
downstream, while ignoring extra empty rows can be (**never drop**).

#### Related

#### 9.1.4 Header-Only Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-header-only-tables` · Tags: tables, degenerate, failure-mode

> **✅ Normative**
> The output MUST NOT contain a table that is a header with no body. A header row MUST either be
> rendered together with its body or, where no body can be joined to it, rendered as ordinary text —
> never as an orphan header row standing as a table.

The failure: a header row becomes a table of its own while the rows it describes end up in a
neighbouring region as plain text. The result claims there is a table with no data in it, and
separately claims there is a run of loose numbers with no meaning.

```text
Emitted:   | Duration | Factor |     ← header-only table…

           1   0.94                  ← …its body rendered as plain text
           2   0.91                    from the neighbouring region
```

#### Joining a header to its body

A header row with no rows under it belongs to the body immediately below or beside it. The header
and body MUST be rendered as one table **only** when all three hold:

- the body is **immediately adjacent** — the next thing on the page, not across a gap of other
  content;
- the **column bounds match** — the body's columns line up under the header's;
- **nothing sits in between** — no paragraph, no other table, no unrelated band.

If any condition fails, the merge MUST NOT be made (**never invent**): the stray header line MUST be
rendered as text rather than as a one-row table.

How large a gap is too large is not fixed. A gap large enough to put the adjacency in doubt counts
as a failed condition, and the header is not merged.

#### The related shape

A single row of labels on its own is not a table. Neither is a small table folded into the middle
of another table's body — see Side-by-Side Mini Tables (§9.2.8) for that one.

#### The one exception

A blank pre-printed form is headers plus empty rows, and there the structure genuinely is the
content: it MUST be rendered, rows included — see Empty Pre-Printed Grids (§9.1.3). That case has a body
of printed empty rows. It is not a header standing alone.





#### Related

- Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9) — when a header legitimately covers fragments with a gap
- Empty Pre-Printed Grids (§9.1.3) — the one case where headers plus empty rows are the whole content
- Side-by-Side Mini Tables (§9.2.8) — a small table inside another's body
- Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) — a lone label row fails the relation test

#### 9.1.5 Is This Even a Table

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-is-this-even-a-table` · Tags: tables, detection, boundaries

> **✅ Normative**
> A region MUST be rendered as a table when, and only when, its rows and columns **encode a
> relation** — when the position of a value in the grid is what gives the value its meaning. A
> region that encodes no relation MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

This is the first decision about a region, and every other table rule depends on it. A single page
often shows the whole spectrum at once: real grids, gridded legends, ungridded `label: value` spec
stacks, address blocks, and two-column prose that looks like a grid but is not.

```text
Same page, three regions:

┌─────────────┬───────────────┐      Motor: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← ungridded spec
│ (1) Premium │ Base rate …   │      Speed: 3-speed              stack: table? text?
│ (2) Losses  │ Incurred …    │
└─────────────┴───────────────┘      Acme Corp
  ↑ gridded legend: table?           123 Main St    ← address block: never a table
```

#### The test

The question is: **would this be a `<table>` in well-written HTML, or a `<div>` positioned with
CSS?**

A border alone does not make a region a table, and alignment alone is not always enough either. The
relation decides.

| Strong evidence it **is** a table | Strong evidence it is **not** |
| --- | --- |
| explicit row **and** column headers | running prose, however neatly it is set in columns |
| repeated records under a shared schema | address blocks |
| a printed grid, or consistent column tracks running down the block | text sitting beside a logo |
| a legend printed as label/definition records **inside a grid** | decorative alignment with no record schema behind it |

a table, and the output MUST NOT invent the missing header row.

#### Legends and static key-value references are tables

The "Column | Description" box under a rate grid, explaining what (1)–(11) mean, MUST be rendered as
a table.

```text
| Column | Description     |
| (1)    | Earned premium  |
| (2)    | Incurred claims |
```

It looks decorative, but it maps one thing to another, and a mapping is a relation. Omitting it
drops real content off the page.

#### Prose and address blocks are never tables

Two-column running prose only *looks* like a grid — its columns carry no meaning, they are a
typesetting choice. The same holds for an address block, or a caption stacked beside an image.
These MUST NOT be rendered as tables.

#### Label / value blocks without a grid

Two columns of labels and values with no ruled grid are a table or key-value content depending on
the **data**, not the layout. The same two whitespace tracks can hold either.

| The rows are… | Rendering | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Records of one kind** — every label is paired with the same kind of value (an amount per component, a factor per year) | a table, even with no header row and no ruled grid | a *Working Capital* panel (see Borderless Whitespace Tables (§9.1.1)); the *Trend Factors* block of `wwa` below |
| **Different kinds of fact** — each label names its own field (a filing number, a state, a date) | key-value content — see Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1) | filing metadata, a spec sheet, a biography's `Name:` / `Affiliation:` lines |
| **Headline figures** — labelled KPIs set as tiles or a highlight panel | stat tiles — see Stat Tiles (§5.11) | `Out-of-home +26.5%` |

A bold label with its value flowing after it — blower spec sheets and similar — is the second kind.

```text
**Motor**: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← no ruled grid, value flows after the label
**Airflow**: 1,200 CFM
```

A stack whose labels name different kinds of fact MUST NOT be rendered as a table unless a ruled
grid is printed around it; it is key-value content, and every line of it MUST still appear in the
output. A stack whose rows are records of one kind MUST be rendered as a table.

#### Form intertwined with a grid

Rate-filing pages that are half form, half table.

```text
Insurer: [blank]   NAIC #: [blank]     ← form fields…
| Year | Rate change |
| 2024 | +4.2%       |               ← …and a genuine grid, same page
```

The ruled grid region MUST be rendered as a table and the form fields as key-value content, so that
nothing printed is lost. The table MUST NOT be stretched to swallow the form fields, and the grid
MUST NOT be dropped because the page as a whole reads like a form.

#### Cases the relation test does not settle on its own

The relation test alone MUST NOT decide these cases; each is governed by its own rule:

- forms and ungridded key-value (Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1))
- trailing totals outside a frame (Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1))
- a printed data grid under a chart (Chart With a Printed Data Grid (§9.1.2))
- detached aligned cells

#### Why the cost runs both ways

A missed legend makes a real relation vanish from the output (**never drop**). A decorative box
rendered as a table asserts structure the page never claimed (**never invent**). Neither error is
recoverable downstream, which is why the relation test — not the border, not the alignment —
decides.

##### ❌ **Counter-sample** — two-column author biographies

*(Source image corpus-two-column-bios.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

values beneath them, separated by horizontal rules top and bottom. Every visual cue says table:

The label/value blocks inside each column are ungridded key-value content — see

#### Related

- Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1) — where ungridded label:value content goes instead
- Borderless Whitespace Tables (§9.1.1) — the "no rules at all" end of the spectrum
- Table of Contents (§6.10) — a column-shaped region with its own rendering
- Header-Only Tables (§9.1.4) — degenerate outputs that follow from getting this decision wrong

### 9.2 Boundaries

#### 9.2.1 Bands Inside the Grid

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-bands-inside-the-grid` · Tags: tables, boundaries, headers

> **✅ Normative**
> A full-width band inside a grid — a date line, a section line, a change of shading — MUST NOT end
> the table. The rows above and below it MUST stay in one table, and the band MUST be rendered as
> one row whose single cell spans every column.

The signal is the column headers. If the headers are **not** re-declared under the band, the table
never closed: the band is an internal divider, not a boundary.

```text
| Product   | Premium | Losses |
| As of December 2024 (bold band, headers NOT repeated) |
| Term Life | 1,204   | 887    |
| As of December 2023                                   |
| Term Life | 1,150   | 902    |

→ one table, with the two "As of…" lines as full-width band rows
```

#### Date and section bands

A bold "As of December 2024" line inside a grid whose column headers are not repeated is a **band
row spanning all columns**, not a boundary. The rows above and below it MUST stay in the same
table.

Splitting here is the most expensive boundary error. On a dense financial page, splitting per year
turns two tables into four and throws away most of the page's value — every resulting fragment is
wrong even though every cell in it is right.

The band's single cell MAY be a header cell (`<th colspan=N>`) or a body cell (`<td colspan=N>`);
both conform, and a document MUST use one form throughout — see
Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2). An in-frame **title** band is a spanning header cell (see
Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3)), so the header cell is the default where nothing else decides.

#### Shading, zebra striping, colour changes

Shading MUST NOT be treated as a table boundary.

```text
| A | 1.10 |   ← white rows
| B | 1.25 |
| C | 1.31 |   ← gray rows start here: still the same table
```

Shading is a readability aid applied by the typesetter. It makes no claim about what the rows mean,
so it cannot start a new table.

#### What does justify a split

Only a **semantic** signal justifies a split:

- a new subject
- a new schema
- a key that stops continuing

Appearance alone MUST NOT split a table.

#### Cohort bands with no column headers anywhere

```text
FEMALE                 ← band; no column headers anywhere
| 25 | 1.02 | 1.10 |
MALE
| 25 | 1.08 | 1.15 |
```

This one resolves the other way: **one table per cohort, with the band as that table's header
row.** The band is the only thing naming what the rows below it are. See
Group and Cohort Bands (§9.2.5).

#### Group bands over one shared row spine

```text
|        | Loss of Income | Other         |  ← two boxed bands
| (1)    | (2)   | (3)    | (4)   | (5)   |  ← full-width numbered tier
| 2019   | 1,204 | 887    | 310   | 95    |  ← one shared row spine
```

**One table.** A full-width numbered tier running across the whole width shows that all those
columns describe one row — splitting there destroys the row identity that crosses the groups. See
Group and Cohort Bands (§9.2.5).





#### Related

- Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7) — a band with the headers printed again does open a new table
- Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) — in-frame title bands use the same spanning header cell
- Group and Cohort Bands (§9.2.5) — bands that head a table rather than divide one
- Row-Label Hierarchy (§9.5.5) — a parent label inside one column, the other reading of `Precision`

#### 9.2.2 Column Continuation

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-column-continuation` · Tags: tables, boundaries, continuation

> **✅ Normative**
> One long series printed as side-by-side blocks SHOULD be rendered as **one table per printed
> block**, each carrying its own copy of the headers, including repeated blocks inside one frame.
> A checker MUST accept source-supported joined equivalents without losing or reassigning records.

A long series — states A–Z, durations 1–36 — printed as two or three blocks beside each other under
one title, with the headers repeated over each block and the key continuing from one block to the
next.

```text
Printed:   | State | Rate |   | State | Rate |
           | AL    | 1.10 |   | MT    | 0.95 |

Rendered:  one table for the left block, one table for the right block,
           each with its own | State | Rate | header.
```

#### Requirements

- Each printed block SHOULD be its own table, in reading order, with its own copy of the headers
  exactly as printed above it.
- Stacking the blocks into one table — the second block's rows appended under the first block's
  header — carries the same rows and is an accepted equivalent (see Accepted Alternatives (§A.1)); a
  document MUST use one form consistently throughout.
- **Do not invent a wide grid.** For separately framed blocks, zipping row *i* of each block into one wide row MUST NOT be done: it pairs `AL`
  with `MT` and asserts a relationship between two unrelated records. A row reading
  `STATE | AVAILABILITY | WITHDRAWAL | STATE | AVAILABILITY | WITHDRAWAL` built from separate blocks
  is non-conforming unless that wide grid is itself printed inside one enclosing frame.
- Repeated copies of the same schema inside one enclosing frame SHOULD also be split into one
  table per printed block. The outer frame and continuous horizontal rules do not make records
  with different keys belong to the same row. Keeping that source-printed wide grid is an
  accepted equivalent; splitting is preferred because each series can be traversed directly.
- A shared title MUST remain attached to the whole group. It MAY appear once outside the group;
  a title band MAY instead be repeated over each block with its span reduced to the block width.
  Actual shared row keys, non-repeating column groups, and cells carrying relationships across
  blocks MUST NOT be split by this rule.
- A shared key column MUST NOT be duplicated into both halves' output. It adds nothing and breaks
  the link between cells and their position on the page.

#### The case that looks the same but is not

Blocks with **different super-headers** over the same rows are one genuinely wide table, not a
continuation. They MUST be rendered as a single table with each super-header spanning its columns.

```text
| Non-Tobacco | Tobacco |     ← different super-headers over the same
| Age | M | F | M | F   |       ages: ONE genuinely wide table
```

The discriminator: in a continuation the blocks are the *same* columns with the key continuing
onward; here the blocks are *different* columns describing the same rows.

#### Related

- Horizontal Slicing (§9.2.6) — the transpose of this case
- Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9) — the inverse: header printed once, not repeated
- Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7) — a header repeated below, rather than beside, data rows
- Side-by-Side Mini Tables (§9.2.8) — independent schemas, including grids with no repeated continuation schema

#### 9.2.3 Continued in the Title

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-continued-in-the-title` · Tags: tables, continuation, captions

> **✅ Normative**
> A continuation marker — `(cont'd)`, `(continued)`, `Table 5 — … (cont.)` — is printed text and MUST
> be kept verbatim in the title. The fragment on this page MUST be rendered as a table in its own
> right.

```text
Table 5 — Lapse Rates (cont'd)     ← explicit continuation marker
| Duration | Rate |
```

#### Requirements

- The title MUST be transcribed exactly as printed, marker included. The marker MUST NOT be
  stripped to tidy the title, nor rewritten into a fuller form.
- The table on this page MUST be rendered as a table in its own right. Its rows MUST NOT be fused
  with a fragment on a previous page (unless the join option of Output Options (§3.5) was requested).
- The kept marker is what records that the fragment continues an earlier table. It is the
  strongest continuation evidence a page can give — far stronger than the indirect signals other
  fragments offer.

#### Why this is the easy end of a hard problem

Everywhere else in Cross-Page Tables (§4.3), continuation has to be inferred from weak signals: a
missing header, a first row that starts mid-key, rows running right to the page edge. Here the
document says it outright, so there is nothing to infer — only a statement not to throw away.

Keeping the marker settles the fidelity half of the question however the fragments are eventually
joined: the words are printed on the page, so they survive (**never drop**). The fragment stays on its
own page and is flagged as continued — see Cross-Page Tables (§4.3).

#### 9.2.4 Duplicated Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-duplicated-tables` · Tags: tables, fidelity

> **✅ Normative**
> Every printed occurrence of a table MUST be rendered, in reading order, each as its own table —
> including a table the page prints twice. Transcription is not summarisation: page content MUST
> NOT be deduplicated.

```text
Page prints:                    Non-conforming:
[Table X]  …  [Table X again]   [Table X]     ← second copy silently dropped
```

#### Requirements

- Identical repeats MUST NOT be collapsed into one, and the second copy MUST NOT be replaced with a
  note that it repeats the first (**never drop**).
- Duplication MUST be judged from the rendered page. A table seen once on the page is there once,
  whatever the underlying text layer says (**never invent**).

#### The trap

A PDF's text layer can carry a phantom second copy of a run — from a shadow effect, an overprint, or
a quirk of whatever generated the file — that never appears on screen. Judged from extracted text
rather than from the page as rendered, a duplicate can be "found" that does not exist, or two
visually identical blocks can be missed as both printed.

The rule that resolves it is the one in Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) and
The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1): **the image is the authority, the text layer is a hint.**

#### Repeated template is not duplication

Blocks with an identical header schema but different numbers are separate tables with real,
distinct content — not copies. Three panels of the same shape showing 89%/11%, 100%/0% and so on are
three tables, and none of them is a duplicate of another. The data, not the layout, decides.

#### 9.2.5 Group and Cohort Bands

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-group-and-cohort-bands` · Tags: tables, boundaries, headers

> **✅ Normative**
> Bands over stacked grids resolve on one question: **is there a shared row spine?** Grids sharing
> one spine MUST be rendered as one table. Grids with no shared spine and no column headers MUST be
> rendered as one table per band, with the band as that table's header row.

| | Shared spine | No shared spine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Row spine | one continuous spine, shared label column | repeated, independent per band |
| Column headers | present, often with a numbered tier | **absent entirely** |
| **Rendering** | **one table** | **one table per cohort**, band becomes its header row |

The row spine is checked first, then the column headers. Those two signals decide it; the bands
themselves look identical in both cases.

#### Group bands over a shared spine — one table

Two boxed group headers sitting over **one continuous row grid that shares a left label column**
MUST be rendered as a **single table**.

```text
|        | Loss of Income | Other         |  ← two boxed bands
| (1)    | (2)   | (3)    | (4)   | (5)   |  ← full-width numbered tier
| 2019   | 1,204 | 887    | 310   | 95    |  ← one shared row spine
```

##### The decisive signal

> **A full-width numbered tier is proof of single-table semantics.**

If `(1)…(13)` runs across the whole width, the page is asserting that all those columns describe
one row. Splitting there loses the row identity that spans the groups — the fact that 2019's
Loss-of-Income figures and its Other figures belong to the same year.

- The group bands MUST be rendered as spanning cells over their column ranges.
- The numbered tier MUST be kept as a header row, not dropped as decoration. See
  Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — dropping the numbered tier as noise also destroys the
  evidence that the table is one table.

#### Cohort bands with no column headers — one table per cohort

Same-shape grids stacked under cohort bands, **with no column headers anywhere**:

```text
FEMALE
| 25 | 1.02 | 1.10 |
MALE
| 25 | 1.08 | 1.15 |
```

> **One table per cohort. The band becomes that table's header row.**

Fusing these into a single table loses the row headers: with the bands demoted to ordinary rows,
nothing says which block is female and which is male.

The band is a header here precisely *because* nothing else is — it is the only thing naming what
the rows below it are.

#### Keeping the two apart

The two shapes look alike from a distance and resolve in opposite directions, so both checks are
run deliberately:

- Does the left label column run continuously through both bands, unrepeated? → one table.
- Does each band restart the same labels under it, with no column headers printed anywhere? → one
  table per band.

Date bands and shading changes inside a single grid are a different question again — see
Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1).





#### Related

- Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1) — bands that divide one grid rather than head a new one
- Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — the numbered tier that proves the shared spine
- Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7) — blocks that each re-declare their headers are separate tables

#### 9.2.6 Horizontal Slicing

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-horizontal-slicing` · Tags: tables, continuation, boundaries

> **✅ Normative**
> A table too wide for the page, printed as stacked column blocks, MUST be rendered as one table per
> printed block, each keeping its repeated row-label column. The blocks MUST NOT be re-widened into a
> single wide table.

A table too wide for the page is printed as column blocks stacked vertically, with the row-label
column repeated in each block.

```text
| State | Jan | Feb | Mar |
| AL    | 1.1 | 1.2 | 1.2 |

| State | Apr | May | Jun |   ← same rows, next columns
| AL    | 1.3 | 1.3 | 1.4 |
```

#### Requirements

- Each printed block MUST be rendered as its own table, top to bottom.
- The repeated row-label column MUST be kept in every block. It is printed in each one, and it is
  what makes the blocks joinable later.
- The blocks MUST NOT be re-widened into a single `State | Jan…Jun` table, even though the repeated
  key makes the join look obvious.

#### How to recognise it

The blocks share their **rows** and differ in their **columns** — the same keys reappear down each
block, with new column headers over them. That is the opposite of Column Continuation (§9.2.2), where the
blocks share their columns and the key runs onward from one block to the next.

If the row keys do **not** line up across the blocks, it is not a slice of one wide table at all:
the blocks are separate tables, with no join to look for.

#### The asymmetry worth noticing

In Column Continuation (§9.2.2), widening is the one shape that is always wrong: it pairs unrelated
records with each other. Here it is the *appealing* option, because the repeated key column gives a
reliable join and no record gets paired with a stranger. The rendering nevertheless stays one table
per printed block: the page printed blocks, and the join is left to whoever consumes the output.





#### Related

- Column Continuation (§9.2.2) — the transpose: blocks side by side, key running onward
- Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) — blocks split by a page break instead of by width
- Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7) — a header printed again below data rows opens a new table

#### 9.2.7 Repeated Headers and Title Bands

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-repeated-headers-and-title-bands` · Tags: tables, boundaries, headers

> **✅ Normative**
> Within one page, a column-header row printed again after data rows MUST close the table and open
> a new one at the repeat. Header repetition is the table-boundary signal.

```text
| State | Rate |
| AL    | 1.10 |
| State | Rate |   ← header printed again after data rows:
| MT    | 0.95 |     the first table ends, a second starts here
```

#### Requirements

- A re-declared header row MUST start a new table. The rows under it belong to that new table, not
  to the one above.
- An entity or geography band that reappears as a title bar before each block likewise MUST open a
  new table each time it appears.
- The repeated header MUST be kept: it is printed, so it is the new table's header row.
- Two tables separated by a repeated header MUST NOT be fused, even where they read as one series
  broken up for layout.

*(Source image zoo-2021-q3-consensus-poll-calculation.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Four period blocks that look like one table whose headers reappear after each data group. Each
block has its own `Period` title and participant count above its header, so each is a **wholly
separate table** — the title and count form its opening `<caption>` rather than data rows.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, block 1 of 4</summary>

```markdown
<table>
  <caption><strong>Period</strong> Q3 2031
<em>Number of participants:</em> 9</caption>
  <tr> <th> </th> <th>Sales million EUR</th> <th>Gross profit margin %</th> <th>EBIT margin %</th> <th>Net result million EUR</th> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Average</td> <td><strong>142.6</strong></td> <td><strong>39.4%</strong></td> <td><strong>18.6%</strong></td> <td><strong>25.7</strong></td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Median</td> <td><strong>144.0</strong></td> <td><strong>39.3%</strong></td> <td><strong>19.0%</strong></td> <td><strong>25.1</strong></td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>High</td> <td><strong>147.2</strong></td> <td><strong>39.8%</strong></td> <td><strong>20.4%</strong></td> <td><strong>36.9</strong></td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Low</td> <td><strong>118.3</strong></td> <td><strong>39.0%</strong></td> <td><strong>14.2%</strong></td> <td><strong>15.6</strong></td> </tr>
</table>
```

</details>

#### Read it against the mirror case

If two fragments share a header that is **not** repeated, they are one table — see
Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9). Together, the two rules make header repetition the single
boundary signal, decidable from what is printed without judging what the rows mean. An exception
for a case that "obviously" continues weakens both rules and MUST NOT be made.

#### Across a page break

Across a page break, a repeated header is routine and says nothing about whether the table ended.
That case is governed by Cross-Page Tables (§4.3), not by this rule; within one page, a repeat is a
boundary.





#### Related

- Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9) — the mirror case: an unrepeated shared header joins fragments
- Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) — a header repeated after a page break is not a boundary
- Column Continuation (§9.2.2) — side-by-side blocks, each with its own header copy

#### 9.2.8 Side-by-Side Mini Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-side-by-side-mini-tables` · Tags: tables, boundaries, failure-mode

> **✅ Normative**
> Boxes sitting side by side with **their own titles and their own schemas** MUST be rendered as
> separate tables — even when their rows line up perfectly. Neighbouring tables MUST NOT be woven
> together, and a small side table MUST NOT be folded into the middle of another table's body.

```text
Printed:  [Box A]      [Box B]        Woven output (non-conforming):
          | a1 | a2 |  | b1 | b2 |    | a1 | a2 | b1 | b2 |
          | a3 | a4 |  | b3 | b4 |    | a3 | a4 | b3 | b4 |
                                        ↑ rows from unrelated boxes glued together
```

Weaving is not merely mis-structured. It asserts that `a1` and `b1` belong to the same record,
which the page never said (**never invent**).

#### Requirements

- Each box MUST be rendered as its own table, with its own title and its own header stack.
- Row alignment MUST NOT be used as a grouping signal. Boxes are top-aligned for looks, so their rows
  land at the same heights by accident.
- The title and the schema decide: its own title and its own columns means its own table.
- A small side table MUST NOT be absorbed into another table's body. A "12pt / 3 Year" side panel is
  not three extra rows in the claims grid beside it.

#### Header attribution is per column, not per table

A header owns the columns printed under it, not everything to its right. A title like "Reported
Claims" sitting over the claim-count columns does not also claim the year labels beside them. A
spanning header MUST span exactly the columns it sits above.

#### Contrast with the cases that DO merge

The neighbouring cases pull the other way, which is why the title and schema are checked rather than
a blanket "boxes are always separate":

- Column Continuation (§9.2.2) — side-by-side blocks that **are** one series: same schema, headers
  repeated, key continuing onward
- Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9) — fragments that **must** merge: one header, printed once

The discriminator is own title / own schema. If each box declares what it is and how its columns
are named, it stands alone.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a two-sided balance sheet in one frame

*(Source image bag-two-sided-balance-sheet.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

#### Related

- Column Continuation (§9.2.2) — side-by-side blocks that continue one series
- Split Tables Sharing a Header (§9.2.9) — fragments that share one printed header and merge
- Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) — boxed panels that are not tables at all

#### 9.2.9 Split Tables Sharing a Header

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-split-tables-sharing-a-header` · Tags: tables, boundaries, headers, proposed-rule

> **✅ Normative**
> Fragments that share a header row or a label column printed only once MUST be rendered as **one
> table**. The missing header is the proof that the second fragment was never meant to stand alone.

A grid is sometimes printed as two or more visually separated fragments — a gap, a page-design
break, a divider — with the header row or the label column printed **once** and not repeated in the
second fragment. Read on its own, the second fragment is unreadable without the header above it, so
it is not a separate table. Emitting it as a separate headerless table, or dropping it, loses the
meaning of every value in it (**never drop**).

```text
Printed:   | Age | Rate M | Rate F |     ← header printed once
           | 25  | 1.10   | 1.05   |

              (visual gap / band)

           | 45  | 1.42   | 1.31   |     ← no header repeated: same table
           | 55  | 1.80   | 1.66   |
```

This is the mirror of the repeated-header test in Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7): a repeated
header starts a new table, an unrepeated one continues the current one. Between them, header
repetition is the single boundary signal on a page, read before gaps, rules or bands.

#### Two cases that need judgement

**Something sits in the gap.** A band row, a caption or a paragraph between the fragments does not
automatically break the table. The fragments MUST be merged as long as the second one still depends
on the header above it; a heading printed in the gap becomes a band row inside the one table.

**The shared piece is the label column.** Side-by-side fragments with the row labels printed once
on the left and value blocks separated by a gutter follow the same test: the value blocks cannot be
read without those labels, so they MUST be rendered as one table. Every printed value MUST be kept,
with the blocks placed as further columns of the labelled table.

##### ✅ **Sample** — one label column, two value blocks

*(Source image corpus-shared-label-column.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A quarterly summary printed as **one row-label column on the left** — *Revenue*, *Gross profit*,
*Selling, general and administrative expenses*, *EBIT*, *Non-controlling interests*, *Net income* —
feeding **two separately boxed value blocks**: `C$ millions` and `(% of revenue)`, each with its
own `Q2 2025 / Q2 2024` header pair.

The right-hand block has **no row labels of its own**. Read on its own it is ten unnamed values,
which is the proof that the two fragments were never meant to stand apart. The same structure is
printed again below for the year-to-date figures, with its header rows repeated, so that block is a
second table.

The blocks do *not* share a header row: each has its own. It is the **label column** that is
printed once — the mirror sub-case. The em-dashes in the *Non-controlling interests* rows are
values, not blanks (Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6)), and `(% of revenue)` is a units line in the
header (Units Row (§9.3.5)). The empty gutter between the blocks is not a column (Gutter Columns (§9.4.1)).

#### Related

- Repeated Headers and Title Bands (§9.2.7) — the mirror: a header printed again opens a new table
- Column Continuation (§9.2.2) — side-by-side blocks that each carry their own header copy
- Header-Only Tables (§9.1.4) — the failure this rule prevents
- Cross-Page Tables (§4.3) — the same dependency across a page break, rendered per page

### 9.3 Headers

#### 9.3.1 Barely-Existing Columns and Headers

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-barely-existing-columns-and-headers` · Tags: tables, columns, headers, drops

> **✅ Normative**
> The output MUST transcribe what is printed and add nothing. A column or a header MUST NOT be dropped
> because it is empty, plainly styled or easy to miss, and a label MUST NOT be invented for a cell
> that has none.

```text
|        | Current | New Program² |
| Rate A | 1.10    |              |    ← all-blank column, proven only by its
| Rate B | 1.25    |              |      header: it exists, keep it
  ↑ blank corner: leave it blank, do not invent "Category"
```

Four situations look like nothing and are routinely lost. All four are the same failure in one of
two directions — a **drop** or an **invention** (Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2)).

#### An all-blank body column proven only by its header

A column whose body is entirely empty still exists. It MUST be kept as an empty column, and any
marker on its label MUST be kept — a superscript such as `New Program²` is part of the header
text, not decoration.

#### A numbered tier `(1) (2) (3)…` across the columns

```text
| State | Premium | Losses |
| (1)   | (2)     | (3)    |   ← a header row: render it
```

A numbered tier running across the columns is a header row, not decoration, and MUST be rendered.

Dropping it costs twice. The tier also runs the full width of the grid, which is the evidence that
every column below belongs to one row — the proof Group and Cohort Bands (§9.2.5) and
Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1) rely on to show that banded blocks are a single table. Without the tier,
both the header *and* the boundary signal are lost.

#### Header bands that are not bold

A band naming a section is a header row even when it is set in plain type. "Lending" over a block
of lending figures, or a `CA|PPO` line above its rates, are headers; demoting them to body rows is
non-conforming.

```text
| Lending    |       |   ← plain-styled band naming a section: still a header
| Commercial | 120.5 |
```

Boldness MUST NOT decide what is a header. Headers are recognised from position, span and what the
line does for the rows beneath it — Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) shows styling is applied
unreliably in both directions and cannot carry this judgement.

#### Blank space beside or below a header label

```text
| 34 | S |          | [rowspan=3]34     | S |
|    | M |    vs    | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE | M |
|    | L |          | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE | L |
```

A region that is visually blank beside or below a labelled cell MUST be rendered as **separate empty
cells**. The label's `rowspan` or `colspan` MUST NOT be extended over it unless the cell is
*genuinely merged* — when the print says so, not when it is inferred.

##### Telling a real merge from adjacent blankness

| Genuine merge — **extend** | Adjacent blankness — **separate empty cells** |
| --- | --- |
| No ruling divides the region: it is printed as **one box** | Ruled cell borders continue through the blank region |
| The label is **centred across** the whole span | The label sits in the first cell, blank cells follow |
| A stub label spanning the header tiers (`<th rowspan="2">UW Category</th>`) | A header label that simply has nothing under it |

**The stopped-divider test.** A ruling line that *stops* is as informative as one that continues.
On a bundle-credit rate table the divider beneath `Number of Additional Policies` stops before the
`Factor` column: that stopped rule is positive evidence that the group covers `Car` and `Other`
only, and that `Factor` is a genuinely merged cell spanning both header tiers. What looks like
"blank space above Factor" is in fact inside a visibly merged two-row header cell. Where a divider
stops, the cell beside it spans.

Most blank-adjacency cases have no such geometry. Absent a stopped divider or an equivalent printed
signal, nothing proves a merge — which is why the default is *do not extend*.

**Carve-out.** A stub label that spans the header tiers (Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3)) still takes a
`rowspan` across those header rows. That is a logical merge and this rule does not touch it.

**Why this way.** A span mirrors what is printed, never what is inferred. A blank cell asserts
nothing; a span asserts "this label owns that region", which needs printed evidence. Making merge
the default would teach the reflex *when in doubt, rowspan* — exactly the habit
Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4) exists to suppress. It is also the simpler question: *"is this cell's
printed content empty?"* rather than a semantic judgement, the same test Blank and Spacer Rows (§9.5.1)
uses in the table body.

#### The through-line

Every case here is a drop or an invention. One principle covers all of them, the one also stated in
Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4): **never emit less data than went in, and never invent what was not
printed.**





#### Related

- Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4) — the same never-drop, never-invent discipline in the body
- Header Body Column Count Mismatch (§9.4.2) — columns that seem to disappear between header and body
- Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3) — the stub rowspan carve-out
- Blank and Spacer Rows (§9.5.1) — the empty-content test applied to rows

#### 9.3.2 Header Wrap vs Real Tier

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-header-wrap-vs-real-tier` · Tags: tables, headers, heuristic

> **✅ Normative**
> A header line with a rule beneath it, standing over two or more self-standing leaf labels, is a
> real tier and MUST be rendered as its own header row. Fragments that simply stack with no border
> and read as one phrase are a wrapped label and MUST be joined with a space into a single header
> cell.

**As printed:**

*(Source image header-wrap-vs-tier-1.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

**As parsed — the failure:**

*(Source image header-wrap-vs-tier-2.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Only **"Common Stock"** is a real tier here: it has a rule beneath it and spans two self-standing
leaves, *Shares* and *Amount*. The other three are **single wrapped labels** — "Capital in Excess of
Par Value" is one column heading broken across two lines to fit. Treating all four the same way
splits every wrapped label into a phantom two-row tier, which is the error this rule prevents
(**never invent**).

Wrapped header text looks **exactly** like a two-row tier, so the test is run deliberately rather
than by eye.

```text
Wrap (one header, join with a space):     Real tier (parent phrase over leaves):
| Published    |                          | (Paid as of 12-31-2020) |
| Availability |                          |   2018    |    2019     |
  ↑ fragments concatenate, no border        ↑ spans two sub-columns
```

#### The test

1. **A rule beneath the upper line.** A printed border under a label, with columns continuing below
   it, points to a tier.
2. **The lower labels on their own.** If each stands as a complete column heading — *Shares*,
   *Amount*, *2018*, *2019* — the line above is a tier over them. If the lines only make sense
   concatenated, they are one wrapped label.
3. **The span.** A tier covers two or more leaf columns. A label that sits over exactly one column
   is a wrap, whatever its line count.

#### The case that catches people out

A parent phrase can be wrapped *and* be a tier. "(Paid as of 12-31-2020)" is broken across lines
**and** spans its sub-columns — so "it wrapped" never settles the question on its own. The span
does: a phrase that covers more than one leaf column MUST be kept as a tier with its exact colspan,
however many lines it takes. A phrase that covers one column is joined into that column's label.

#### A label broken inside a word

A space join assumes the break falls between words. When a narrow column breaks **inside** a word
— `Distributio` / `n`, `Appointe` / `d` — the fragments MUST be joined with nothing:
`Distribution`, `Appointed`. A wrap with a printed hyphen inside a word (`per-` / `form-` / `ance`)
is joined the same way, dropping the hyphens. A hyphen that belongs to the word, as in a compound,
stays — see Line-End Hyphenation (§7.2.7). Only a break between words gets a space.

#### Related

- Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3) — how real tiers are encoded once recognised
- Units Row (§9.3.5) — a units line under a header is a different case
- Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — header rows that must not be dropped
- Line-End Hyphenation (§7.2.7) — which printed hyphens survive a join

#### 9.3.3 Multi-Row Header Tiers

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-multi-row-header-tiers` · Tags: tables, headers, encoding

> **✅ Normative**
> Every printed header tier MUST be rendered as its own header row, with exact colspans. A group
> header MUST span only its data columns; the row-label stub takes a `rowspan` across the header rows
> instead.

```text
Printed:  |            BI          |            PD          |
          | Indicated  | Proposed  | Indicated  | Proposed  |
```

#### Every real tier is kept

Both rows are rendered with their spans — `[colspan=2]BI` over `Indicated | Proposed`, and so on.

The stack MUST NOT be flattened into one row of concatenated labels: "BI Indicated", "BI Proposed"
is non-conforming, not a stylistic choice. It destroys the grouping that the page printed and makes
the number of header rows depend on the producer rather than the page.

A wrapped parent phrase is still a tier. "(Paid as of 12-31-2020)" broken across two lines and
spanning its sub-columns is a genuine tier — "it wrapped" does not demote it. The span, not the
line count, decides; Header Wrap vs Real Tier (§9.3.2) has the full test.

#### The group header stops at the first data column

A group super-header spans its data columns and **never the row-label stub**. The stub takes a
`rowspan` across the header rows:

```html
<th rowspan="2">UW Category</th><th colspan="3">Inception to Date</th>
<!-- then: -->  Earned Premium | Incurred Claims | Loss Ratio
```

> **The group's colspan MUST equal its leaf count, exactly.**

The printed rule under the group starts at the first data column. The stub is not part of
"Inception to Date" — the stub says *which row*, the group says *which measure*. Different axes, so
they do not share a span. Spanning the stub as well is the most common way this goes wrong.

#### Reconciling the tracks

The leaf-column tracks **N** of the table are counted. For each header row, the expanded colspans,
occupied **plus explicit blank** tracks, MUST add up to N.

A mismatch shows which kind of error was made, before anything else is inspected:

1. a missed column
2. a wrong span
3. two tables fused into one
4. a header line read as the wrong kind of thing

#### Period stacks in financial statements

```text
| $ in millions |       Average for the        |  ← corner note; apex tier
|               | Three Months Ended | Year …  |
|               | December | December | Dec…   |  ← stacked "December"/"2024"
|               | 2024     | 2023     | 2024   |    is ONE leaf label
```

Period headers follow the same rules, with a few fixed calls of their own — apex qualifiers,
stacked month-over-year labels and the "$ in millions" corner note. They are set out in
SEC Period Tiers (§9.3.4), which governs 10-K and 10-Q header stacks.

#### 9.3.4 SEC Period Tiers

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-sec-period-tiers` · Tags: tables, headers, sec

> **✅ Normative**
> A financial period stack MUST be rendered as its printed tiers: period groups over their own date
> leaves, an apex qualifier above them, a stacked month and year joined into one leaf label, and the
> units note kept verbatim as the corner header cell.

This is the header stack of every 10-K and 10-Q. It looks ambiguous, but every part of it has a
fixed answer.

```text
| $ in millions |       Average for the        |  ← apex qualifier
|               | Three Months Ended | Year …  |  ← sibling period groups
|               | December | December | Dec…   |  ← stacked month/year =
|               | 2024     | 2023     | 2024   |    ONE leaf, joined
```

| The page shows | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| "Three/Six Months Ended…", "Year(s) Ended…" | MUST be **sibling group tiers** over their own date leaves |
| An apex qualifier like "Average for the" | MUST be a tier **above** them, spanning the period groups |
| Stacked "December" / "2024" | MUST be **one leaf label**, the lines joined |
| Bold on the current-period column | **styling, not structure**: the header structure MUST NOT change; the bold is marked per cell as printed |
| "$ in millions" in the stub corner | MUST be **the corner header cell**, kept verbatim |

#### Why the stacked month and year join

"December" and "2024" are not two levels of anything — no other column shares a "December" parent.
The typesetter broke one label across two lines to fit a narrow column, so it is a wrap. A tier is
kept only for a label that genuinely spans more than one leaf column, as
Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3) requires.

#### 9.3.5 Units Row

*⚖️ Equivalent forms · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-units-row` · Tags: tables, headers

> **⚖️ Equivalent forms**
> A units line under the header MAY be rendered as a **second header row**, or folded into the
> header label above it ("Premium ($000)"). Both forms conform, and a document MUST use one of them
> throughout (see Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2)). A units line MUST NOT become the first body
> row.

```text
| Premium | Losses | Ratio |
| ($000)  | ($000) | (%)   |   ← units line: a header tier, or folded into
| 1,204   | 887    | 73.6  |     the labels as "Premium ($000)"
```

#### Recognising it

A units line sits directly beneath the header, carries no values, and repeats the same kind of
token across the columns — `($000)`, `(%)`, `(millions)`, `(points)`. Every entry describes how to
read the column below it rather than reporting a measurement.

#### The two conforming forms

**Second header row.** The line is kept as its own header row, aligned to the columns it describes,
and the values below stay bare. This is closest to what is printed.

**Folded into the label.** The unit is appended to the header text — "Premium ($000)". This is the
most useful for downstream extraction, because the unit travels with the field. It does edit the
header string, which sits awkwardly beside the verbatim posture of Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3), so the
second header row SHOULD be preferred when a document uses units lines heavily.

#### The outcome to avoid

A units line MUST NOT be rendered as a body row. It is not merely inelegant: a reader of the first
body row then gets `($000)` as a premium value. Where the choice between the two conforming forms
is unclear, the second header row is the default.

### 9.4 Columns

#### 9.4.1 Gutter Columns

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-gutter-columns` · Tags: tables, columns, currency

> **✅ Normative**
> A currency glyph or a separator typeset in a column track of its own SHOULD be rendered in the
> same cell as the value it belongs to — `$ 277.09`, `$1,200 — $1,800`. A marker numeral such as
> `(i)` or `(ii)` SHOULD be rendered in a column of its own.

Financial PDFs frequently typeset `$` in its own column track, and print ranges as `value — value`
with the dash in a track of its own. Those tracks are real in the typesetting, but they are layout,
not data.

```text
Printed tracks:  $ | 1,200 | — | $ | 1,800
Rendered as:     $1,200 — $1,800   (one cell)
```

#### Currency and separators: merged into the value

- A currency glyph printed in its own track SHOULD be rendered in the cell of the number it
  belongs to. The glyph MUST NOT be dropped: where the page prints `$` only on some rows, only
  those rows' values carry it.
- A separator between the two ends of a range (a dash, `+/-`, `to`) SHOULD be rendered in one cell
  with both ends.
- A `$` kept in a cell of its own beside its value, as a pair of cells, also conforms; the single
  cell is the preferred form.

*(Source image zoo-some.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

The `$` sits in its own boxed column track in the image, which looks like a column of its own. It is
not: the glyph belongs to the value, so the first value cell reads `$274`. The *Second Quarter* and
*January - June* spanners printed above the header are part of the table.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · table 1 of 5</summary>

```markdown
<table>
  <tr> <th> </th> <th colspan="3">Second Quarter</th> <th colspan="3">January - June</th> </tr>
  <tr> <th>Main Indicators</th> <th>2Q06</th> <th>2Q05</th> <th>Change</th> <th>2006</th> <th>2005</th> <th>Change</th> </tr>
  <tr> <th>Million US dollars</th> <th>(1)</th> <th>(2)</th> <th>(1)/(2)</th> <th>(3)</th> <th>(4)</th> <th>(3)/(4)</th> </tr>
  <tr> <td>Net Revenue</td> <td>$274</td> <td>207</td> <td>32.3%</td> <td>515</td> <td>409</td> <td>26.07%</td> </tr>
  <tr> <td>EBITDA</td> <td>$53</td> <td>49</td> <td>7.7%</td> <td>105</td> <td>111</td> <td>19.05%</td> </tr>
</table>
```

</details>

#### Marker gutters: kept as a column

```text
| (i)  | Base salary … |     ← one column for the numeral, one for the text
| (ii) | Bonus …       |
```

A marker numeral such as `(i)` / `(ii)` SHOULD be rendered in a column of its own. A merged
`(i) Base salary …` cell also conforms, but the separate numeral column is the preferred form.

#### Why the two resolve opposite ways

A currency symbol is *part of the value*. A marker numeral is a *reference label*: it is cited
elsewhere on the page ("see (ii)"), so it has an identity of its own and earns a column.

A gutter this rule does not name is decided by the column-count test: a track gets its own column
only if a competent person modelling this data in a spreadsheet would give it one. That is the same
appeal to how a person would model the content that decides Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) — judge by the
data, not by what is inked.

#### 9.4.2 Header Body Column Count Mismatch

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-header-body-column-count-mismatch` · Tags: tables, columns, repair

> **✅ Normative**
> Every row of a table MUST carry the full column count. Where the header and the body disagree,
> the short side MUST be padded with empty cells, one per missing position, and MUST NOT be padded
> with a duplicated or invented value.

```text
Header:  | Duration | Factor | Trend |     ← 3 columns
Body:    | 1        | 0.94   |             ← Trend all-blank → body reads as 2
         | 2        | 0.91   |
```

#### Header wider than the body

The usual cause is a column whose body is uniform or empty — all `1.000`, all blank, all `—`. The
column MUST be restored as cells, empty where the page prints nothing, and its header label MUST be
kept: a column proven only by its header still exists
(Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1)).

#### Header narrower than the body

The usual cause is a missed span in the header: a group label that carries a `colspan`, or a stub
that takes a `rowspan`. The header's spans SHOULD be re-read against the page before the body is
treated as the side that is short.

#### Padding

- Padding MUST be individual empty cells, one per missing position — not a span across the gap. A
  span claims the page merged those cells; it did not, they were simply not printed. The same
  reasoning pads a jagged half cell by cell in Triangles and Matrix Tables (§9.8.2).
- Body cells MUST NOT be fabricated or duplicated to reach a count. An empty cell asserts nothing;
  a copied value asserts something false about the page. Where it cannot be decided which side is
  wrong, the output renders the cells that are printed and pads with empty cells rather than guess
  at content.

### 9.5 Rows and cells

#### 9.5.1 Blank and Spacer Rows

*⚖️ Equivalent forms · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-blank-and-spacer-rows` · Tags: tables, either, rows, disputed

> **⚖️ Equivalent forms**
> A genuinely printed blank row inside a table MAY be rendered as an empty row or left out; both
> forms conform, and a document MUST use one of them throughout. A blank row that is the only thing
> separating two groups of rows SHOULD be rendered as an empty row.

```text
| ROU assets total   | 10,234 |
|                    |        |   ← printed blank row: on this page it is the
| Lease liabilities: |        |     only section boundary — rendered as an empty row
```

#### When the blank row is load-bearing

On a page with no rules, no bands and no repeated headers, the whitespace *is* the structure.
Dropping a blank row there merges two sections the page deliberately kept apart — as in a lease
note where a single blank line is all that separates the right-of-use totals from "Lease
liabilities:".

- A blank row whose removal would change how a reader groups the rows around it SHOULD be rendered
  as a row of empty cells, in its printed position.
- A purely decorative blank line — even spacing between every row, padding at the foot of a block —
  carries no such meaning and MAY be left out.
- An empty row MUST NOT be rendered where the page prints none: the row is kept because it is
  printed, never added to make groups easier to read.
