#### Encoding an empty region

> **The encoding of an empty region is free. Its existence is not.**

- An empty region inside a table body MAY be encoded as individual empty `<td>` cells or as one
  blank cell spanning it (`colspan` / `rowspan`): three leading empty `<td>`s per row and one
  `colspan="3" rowspan="8"` blank block render identically, and both conform. Where the page draws
  no separation inside the empty region, neither encoding is preferred.
- **Carve-out:** in a loss triangle or similar matrix, every empty position MUST be its own empty
  cell, never part of a span — each is a distinct, meaningful absence. See
  Triangles and Matrix Tables (§9.8.2).
- **The half that is not free:** the cells and columns MUST exist. A column proven only by its
  header still exists (Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1)), and every value in it MUST stay
  reachable. Encoding is a choice; deletion is an error.
- Blank space beside a *header* label is not free: it MUST be rendered as separate empty cells, not
  as an extended span, unless the page prints a genuinely merged cell. See
  Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1).





#### Related

- Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1) — the other way a page marks a section boundary inside a table
- Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — empty cells beside header labels, and columns proven only by a header
- Empty Pre-Printed Grids (§9.1.3) — rows that are blank because the form is unfilled, all of which are kept
- Triangles and Matrix Tables (§9.8.2) — the one place empty positions are never spanned

#### 9.5.2 Nested Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-nested-tables` · Tags: tables, encoding, rare

> **✅ Normative**
> A small grid printed inside one cell of a table MUST be rendered by subdividing that cell into the
> outer table's own grid: the inner grid's cells become rows and columns of the outer table, and the
> neighbouring cells span them. The output MUST NOT contain a nested `<table>` element, and MUST NOT
> flatten the inner grid into text.

A cell that itself contains a small grid: a fee schedule inside a plan-comparison cell, a
mini-table of components inside one row of a summary.

```text
| Plan | Fees                          |
| A    | ┌ admin │ 0.25% ┐            |
|      | └ fund  │ 0.10% ┘   ← a table inside the cell
```

#### Recognising a nested table

The inner grid has its own alignment: two or more columns of its own, sometimes its own header row,
and its own row boundaries that do not line up with the outer table's rows. That is what separates
it from a cell that merely holds several lines of text, which is governed by
Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3).

#### Rendering

The inner grid's cells MUST become **real cells of the outer table**, and every cell alongside it
MUST span the rows it now occupies:

```html
<tr>
  <td rowspan="2">A</td>
  <td>admin</td><td>0.25%</td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td>fund</td><td>0.10%</td>
</tr>
```

`A` is printed once and genuinely covers both fee rows, so `rowspan="2"` is a true statement about
the page — the same test Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4) applies everywhere else.

- **No nested `<table>`.** A nested table makes the inner grid invisible to anything that walks the
  outer one: cell counts, column arithmetic and per-cell boxes all stop at the `<td>` boundary.
  Subdividing keeps every value addressable at the same level as the rest of the table, and the
  outer grid still reconciles — see the leaf-track check in Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3).
- **Pairs MUST survive.** The pairing inside the inner grid is the data: `admin` goes with `0.25%`
  and `fund` with `0.10%`. An encoding that lists all the labels and then all the values has
  destroyed the table; so has flattening the cell to `<br/>`-separated text.

This is one of several cases that need HTML tables rather than pipe tables, which cannot express the
spans this rule depends on (see Markdown Rendering (§3.2)). The others are spans in
Multi-Row Header Tiers (§9.3.3), full-width band rows in Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1), and level markers on
the stub in Row-Label Hierarchy (§9.5.5).

#### 9.5.3 Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-record-groups-and-multi-line-cells` · Tags: tables, encoding, rowspan

> **✅ Normative**
> Independently printed records MUST each be rendered as their own row, with `rowspan` only on
> cells the page genuinely merged. One prose cell MUST stay one cell, with `<br/>` between its title
> and its paragraph. In a boxed row holding lists in several columns, lines that pair up one-to-one
> MUST be separate rows, and a list whose neighbours print a single value for the whole list MUST
> stay in one cell, `<br/>`-joined, beside that value.

```text
Printed boxed row:        Rendered:
| Products   | States |   | MoneyGuard | AL         |
| MoneyGuard | AL     |   | MG II      | AK<br/>AZ  |
| MG II      | AK     |
|            | AZ     |
```

#### A record spanning several printed lines

Each printed line of the record MUST be its own row, and the cells genuinely shared across those
lines MUST carry a `rowspan`.

- The record's lines MUST NOT be `<br/>`-joined into one row.
- A blank continuation cell MUST NOT stand where a `rowspan` belongs.
- The lines MUST NOT be rewritten — `Owner:` and `Extended` printed on two lines do not become
  `Owner: Extended`. The verbatim line structure is part of the output.

#### Parallel lists across several columns of one boxed row

When one boxed row holds several columns, each with its own vertical list, what decides the
rendering is how the lines pair up across the columns:

- **Lines that pair up one-to-one** — line *i* of one column beside line *i* of the next, each
  line a record of its own (`English Language Paper 1 · 0815 – 0925 h · 1 h 10 min`) — MUST each be
  their own `<tr>`. `<br/>`-joining them destroys which value belongs to which line.
- **A list whose neighbours print a single value for the whole list** — eight papers beside one
  time and one duration; two states beside one product — is one record: the list MUST stay in one
  cell, `<br/>`-joined, beside that single value. Splitting it into rows would attach the value to
  the first line only.
- A boxed row may hold both: `MoneyGuard` pairs with `AL` one-to-one, while `MG II` is printed once
  beside the list `AK`, `AZ`.

This is not the same as a line break inside a single cell, which follows.

#### In-cell lists and line wraps

These are inside **one** cell, and here more than one rendering conforms:

| Printed | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **Bullet list in a cell** | `<ul><li>…</li></ul>` or `<br/>•` before each item; both conform |
| **Two deliberate printed lines** in a label | kept as `<br/>` |
| **Incidental word-wrap** in a label | flattened to one string, joined with a space |
| **Break the page does not settle** | either rendering conforms |
| **A label and its value packed into one cell**, where the page does not settle whether they are two columns (`N =`, `Z =`) | one cell or two existing columns; both conform |

None of this licenses collapsing lines that pair up one-to-one across columns: `<br/>`-joining that
case is an error.

#### When rowspan is right and when it is wrong

Rowspan is the required rendering here and the error in Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4). The
discriminator is whether the page **actually merged** the cell: a value printed once against
several lines takes a `rowspan`; a value printed separately on each line is that many cells.

#### A row label that wraps

The one-row-per-printed-line requirement is about records. A stub label that merely wraps —
`Increase (Decrease) in Accounts Payable` / `and Accrued Liabilities`, value on the second line —
MUST be **one row, its label joined with a space**. The tell is that the wrapped lines read as one
phrase and only one of them carries values.

#### A cell holding a title and a paragraph

A single ruled prose cell MUST stay one cell in one row. Its title keeps its printed emphasis and
MUST be separated from its paragraph by `<br/>`; values stacked in the adjacent cell are kept in
that cell, joined with `<br/>`. Only independently printed records are split into rows.

#### Related

- Repeated Identical Values (§9.5.4) — where a `rowspan` is the error
- Nested Tables (§9.5.2) — a grid inside a cell, not lines of text
- Row-Label Hierarchy (§9.5.5) — the level of a wrapped or indented stub label

#### 9.5.4 Repeated Identical Values

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-repeated-identical-values` · Tags: tables, rowspan, failure-mode

> **✅ Normative**
> A `rowspan` MUST be used only where the page genuinely merged the cell. A value printed *k* times
> at *k* distinct vertical positions MUST be rendered as *k* cells; repeated content MUST NOT be
> merged.

"82.13%" printed nine separate times, "Data Page" repeated down a column, the same rate on every
row — the temptation is to collapse them into one spanning cell. That output is non-conforming.

```text
Printed (9 separate lines):    Non-conforming output:
| 1 | 82.13% |                 | 1 | [rowspan=9]82.13%  |
| 2 | 82.13% |                 | 2 | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |  ← merges a value
| … | 82.13% |                 | … | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |    printed 9 times
```

#### Why merging is wrong, not just different

A `rowspan` is a claim about the *page*: "these cells are one cell." When the page printed nine
cells, that claim is false — the **never invent** failure. Anyone counting records downstream then
gets one where the document has nine, and the loss is invisible because the output still looks
well-formed. A span that cannot be pointed to on the page is an error even when the values under
it are right.

#### Deciding from the geometry

The decision MUST be taken from where the value is printed, not from how the column reads:

- **one printed occurrence** spanning several rows → one cell with a `rowspan`;
- **distinct vertical positions** → separate cells, one per row.

A column of identical values is exactly where the eye stops resolving lines, so the word positions
on the page, not an impression of the column, settle it (see Boxes and Granularity (§3.3)). For the
opposite case — where the page really did merge a cell across a multi-line record — see
Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3).

#### Related

- Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3) — where `rowspan` **is** the required rendering
- Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — the same never drop, never invent discipline for columns
- Header Body Column Count Mismatch (§9.4.2) — never duplicate a value to fill a position

#### 9.5.5 Row-Label Hierarchy

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-row-label-hierarchy` · Tags: tables, rule, hierarchy, encoding

> **✅ Normative**
> Where a table's row labels are indented to show nesting, every label cell MUST carry its
> **absolute level** as a `data-level` attribute: `<td data-level="2">iPhone</td>`. Level `0` is the
> leftmost label position in the stub column, `1` the next indent step, and so on — counted from the
> left edge of the column, never from the row above.

Financial statements and rate manuals encode hierarchy by indenting the row label. Flattened,
"iPhone" and "Total net sales" read as siblings.

```text
Printed stub:                     Rendered as:
Revenue                           <td data-level="0">Revenue</td>
  Products                        <td data-level="1">Products</td>
    iPhone          205,489       <td data-level="2">iPhone</td>
Total net sales     383,285       <th data-level="0">Total net sales</th>
```

A table whose indented labels all come out at the same level is the failure this rule exists to
prevent.

#### Why flattening is dangerous

The flattened output is well-formed and looks correct. Nothing signals that a parent/child
relationship was dropped, so a reader summing the column double-counts: `iPhone` is *inside*
`Total net sales`, and the flattened table gives no way to know it. The damage is silent, which is
why the indentation MUST be preserved even where the choice of encoding seems secondary.

#### Reading the level

- The level MUST be the number of indent steps between the left edge of the stub column and the
  start of the label as printed. The leftmost label position is `0`; each further indent step adds
  one. A level can therefore be checked against a single row without reading any other.
- The label text MUST stay verbatim and the rows MUST stay in printed order.
- Where a table carries levels, every label cell in its stub that prints a label MUST carry one,
  level-`0` rows included. A table whose stub shows no nesting — no indentation, no "of which"
  rows — and has no labelled total carries none.

##### Absolute, not relative

A level is read off the print, never inherited from the row above:

- A row following a level-`2` row is level `3` only if the page indents it further. At the same
  indent it is another level-`2` sibling.
- A row MAY jump back several levels at once. `Total net sales` returning to `0` after an `iPhone`
  at `2` is normal and needs no marker of its own.

##### Not from the numbers

A level MUST NOT be deepened because the arithmetic suggests a row is a component, and MUST NOT be
flattened because the arithmetic does not add up. The indentation is the evidence; the values are
not. A page whose sub-items do not sum to their parent is transcribed as printed.

##### Not as leading whitespace

The level MUST be carried as an attribute, not as leading spaces or `&nbsp;`: the first trim,
Markdown render or CSV round-trip removes whitespace and the structure goes with it. Where an output
format cannot carry a cell attribute, the level SHOULD go into a dedicated level column rather than
into whitespace.

#### Recognising a child row

A child is indented relative to the row above it, and its value is a *component* of a figure
elsewhere in the column rather than an independent record. Phrases such as "out of which", "of
which" and "within which" state the same relationship in words; a row introduced by one MUST be
rendered as a child even where its indentation is slight. The same page may present a breakdown as
an indented stub or as a row that decomposes into sub-rows; both are the same phenomenon and are
rendered the same way.

A total row takes a level like any other row, usually `0`; how its label cell is marked is defined
in Total and Subtotal Rows (§9.5.6).

#### Two more stub shapes

##### Two-column stubs

Where a table sets sub-labels in a second stub column to the right of the parent label, one per
line, each with its own values, the output MUST render a two-column stub: the parent label in the
first column, spanning its children with a `rowspan` where the page prints it as one cell, and each
sub-label in the second column on its own row.

#### Related

- Total and Subtotal Rows (§9.5.6) — the aggregate row at the top of the hierarchy, and its label cell
- Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells (§9.5.3) — multi-line labels that are one cell, not parent and child
- Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) — weight and slant that often accompany a hierarchy, rendered per cell

#### 9.5.6 Total and Subtotal Rows

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-total-and-subtotal-rows` · Tags: tables, rule, semantics, rows

> **✅ Normative**
> In a total or subtotal row, the label cell MUST be a `<th>` and the value cells MUST stay `<td>`.
> The label cell MUST carry the row's absolute level as `data-level`, read as for the stub
> hierarchy — a top-level total is `data-level="0"`. Label and values MUST be kept exactly as
> printed, bold only where the page prints them bold.

```text
| iPhone          | 205,489 |
| Mac             |  29,357 |
| **Total**       | 234,846 |   ← bold + a double rule above it
```

#### The rendering

```html
<tr><td data-level="1">iPhone</td><td>205,489</td></tr>
<tr><td data-level="1">Mac</td><td>29,357</td></tr>
<tr><th data-level="0">Total</th><td>234,846</td></tr>
```

- The `<th>` states that the cell labels rather than reports.
- `data-level` records the printed absolute indentation of the label, counted from the left edge of
  the stub as in Row-Label Hierarchy (§9.5.5); because a total carries a level, every label cell of its
  stub carries one too.
- The level MUST be the printed one even where it contradicts the apparent grouping — a total set
  further right than the items it sums keeps that deeper level. Arithmetic membership MUST NOT be
  inferred from indentation, and indentation MUST NOT be adjusted to fit the arithmetic.
- A total row whose label position prints nothing has no label cell to mark: it MUST be rendered
  with an empty `<td></td>` there — never an invented `Total` and never an empty `<th>`.

#### A `<th>` is a per-cell decision

A row can be part header, part data, and a total row is exactly that: a heading cell on the left
and reported values to its right. Marking the whole row `<th>` would claim the numbers are headings;
marking none of it loses the distinction between the cell that names the aggregate and the cells
that report it. Both are non-conforming.

The same holds in reverse for a full-width band or divider row, where **every** cell is heading and
none is data — see Bands Inside the Grid (§9.2.1) and Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3).

#### Recognising one

A total or subtotal row usually carries three tells at once: a label that names an aggregate
("Total", "Total net sales", "5 YR. TOTAL"), a rule or double rule printed above it, and bold or
otherwise emphasised type. Any one alone is weak evidence — bold is applied unreliably in both
directions (Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2)) — but together they are reliable.

#### Row order and table sections

- Every row MUST stay in printed order. A total MUST NOT be moved to fit a table section.
- `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` wrappers MAY be used or omitted; they do not change the cells
  or their values, and `th` versus `td` is still decided per cell.
- Totals printed outside the table frame are governed by Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1).

#### Related

- Row-Label Hierarchy (§9.5.5) — the levels a total's label shares with the rest of the stub
- Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1) — totals printed outside the table frame
- Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2) — bold on a total is transcribed per cell, as printed

### 9.6 Cell values

#### 9.6.1 Accounting Number Formats

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-accounting-number-formats` · Tags: tables, fidelity, numbers

> **✅ Normative**
> Every number in a cell MUST be transcribed exactly as printed — parentheses, currency dashes,
> separators and change markers included. The output MUST NOT carry a normalised twin of the value
> beside it, and MUST NOT replace the printed form with a normalised one.

Accounting pages print numbers in shapes that look as if they ask to be tidied up. They do not: the
cell is copied character for character.

```text
Printed:     (1,204)    $—     n/m     1.204,50 (EU)     △2.5%
Verbatim:    (1,204)    $—     n/m     1.204,50          △2.5%
Normalized:  -1204      0?     null?   1204.50           +2.5%? -2.5%?
```

#### Requirements

| Printed form | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| **Parenthesised negative** — `(1,204)`, `(2.0)%`, `($8.75)` | MUST keep its parentheses; MUST NOT be rewritten with a minus sign. |
| **Leading minus** — `-50.009` | MUST stay a leading minus; MUST NOT be converted into parentheses. The page's convention is the one recorded. |
| **Currency and percent dashes** — `$—`, `— %` | MUST stay dashes, with their currency or percent sign. |
| **Placeholders** — `n/m`, `NM`, anything printed in place of a figure | MUST be transcribed as written. |
| **Separators** — `1.074.778`, `1.204,50` | MUST stay as printed: thousands points stay points, a decimal comma stays a comma, and no separator is removed or swapped for the other convention. |
| **Change markers** — `△2.5%` | MUST stay attached to the number, in the same cell. |

Spacing printed inside a value — `3.8 %`, `$ 17,565.8` — is part of the printed form and is kept.

#### Why no normalised twin

A cleaned-up value beside the printed one looks free to produce and saves every consumer the same
work. It is refused for two reasons.

**Normalisation here is not a transformation, it is a guess.** A "clean" column would have to decide
things the page does not say: is `$—` zero, or not applicable? Is `n/m` null, an empty string, or a
string literal? Does `△2.5%` mean up or down — the triangle's direction is conventional and the sign
is not printed at all. A twin column would carry three guesses dressed as data, and nothing
downstream distinguishes a guessed value from a read one.

**A second value is a second thing to be wrong.** The printed form is verifiable against the page;
the derived form is verifiable only against whatever rules produced it. A consumer that needs a
number applies its own conventions to the printed string — and it knows its own conventions, which
the producer does not.

Hence: **one value per cell, and it is the one on the page.** Verbatim leaves the interpretation to
whoever consumes the table, the only place it can be made safely.

#### Related

- Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) — the general rule that the page, not the text layer, decides what a cell says
- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — when a dash alone in a cell is a value
- Gutter Columns (§9.4.1) — a currency sign typeset in a column track of its own
- Units Row (§9.3.5) — units printed once for a column rather than in each cell

#### 9.6.2 Bold and Italic Inside Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-bold-and-italic-inside-tables` · Tags: tables, formatting

> **✅ Normative**
> Inside a table, bold, italic and underline MUST be marked per cell, and only where the printed
> glyphs of that cell are heavier, slanted or underlined. A whole column or a whole header row MUST
> NOT be styled on principle. Inside an HTML table cell, bold MUST be written `<strong>`, italic
> `<em>` and underline `<u>`.

The same holds for strikeout and coloured text: they are properties of the glyphs in one cell, not
of the role that cell plays.

```text
Page bolds one column:        Over-bolded output:
| **Doc** | Status |          | **Doc** | **Status** |
| **A-1** | Filed  |          | **A-1** | **Filed**  |
```

The block on the right is the error this rule exists to prevent: the page bolds a single column,
and every cell came back bold.

#### Markup inside a cell

Emphasis inside a table cell is written with HTML elements, not Markdown `**` and `*`. Strikeout inside a cell follows Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7).

| Printed | Rendering in a cell |
| --- | --- |
| Bold | `<td><strong>Net sales</strong></td>` |
| Italic | `<td><em>P. abyssalis</em></td>` |
| Bold and italic | `<td><em><strong>All other plans</strong></em></td>` |
| Underlined | `<th><u>Rx Claim Information</u></th>` |
| Styling on part of a cell | only that run: `<td><em>ZRK2</em> kinase inhibitor</td>` |

- `**…**` and `*…*` MUST NOT be used inside a table cell.
- The markup MUST cover exactly the styled run. A cell that is bold throughout wraps its whole
  content; a cell with one bold word wraps that word.

#### Header rows

A `<th>` cell states the cell's role, not its weight. Where every cell of the header rows is printed
in the same weight, that shared weight SHOULD NOT be repeated as `<strong>` in each header cell —
that styles the header row on principle. A header cell whose glyphs **differ** from the rest
of the header — an italic stub heading, an underlined label, one bold heading among regular ones —
MUST carry that difference.

#### Deciding cell by cell

1. The structure — rows, columns, header tiers — is read first, blind to weight and slant.
2. Styling is then taken from the glyphs of each cell, one cell at a time.

Weight differences are often subtle, so a cell is judged against its neighbours rather than on its
own. Where it cannot be told whether a cell is heavier, the cell SHOULD be left unstyled: an
unmarked cell loses a nuance, a wrongly marked one asserts something the page does not say.

#### The same error, seen from both ends

Over-styling comes from reasoning about the category — "this is a header, headers are bold" —
instead of from the glyphs. The mirror image is in Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1): a band
that is not bold gets missed because a header is expected to be bold.

Both are prevented by the same discipline: **detect structure blind to styling, and take styling
from the glyphs.**





#### Related

- Bold and Italics (§7.2.1) — the same rule outside tables, in Markdown syntax
- Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) — the mirror error: structure missed because it is not bold
- Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) — strikeout is also a per-glyph property
- Total and Subtotal Rows (§9.5.6) — bold total rows are styled from their glyphs, cell by cell
- Highlighted Text (§7.2.5) — highlighting inside tables follows the same per-cell discipline

#### 9.6.3 Cell Text Fidelity

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-cell-text-fidelity` · Tags: tables, fidelity, ocr

> **✅ Normative**
> The text of a cell MUST be what the rendered page shows — not the text layer, not OCR, and not
> what the value ought to be. A character that cannot be read at any zoom MUST be written as
> `[illegible]`, never as a plausible guess.

The text layer and the rendered image disagree at the character level far more often than
expected, and the cost of a single wrong digit depends entirely on who reads the table. The text
layer is a hint about roughly what is there; the image decides.

#### Three cells that were read wrong

In each of these the transcription and the OCR agreed with each other — and a zoomed view of the
page proved both wrong:

```text
printed 0.99        → transcribed 0.98      (Age-to-Ultimate factor)
printed 2012.5-(A)  → transcribed 2013.5-(A)
printed 1.0400^(W)  → transcribed 1.04009^(W)
```

A disputed cell SHOULD be settled from a zoomed crop of the cell or from the word coordinates, and
MUST NOT be settled by plausibility. "Plausible" is exactly what produced all three errors above:
`0.98` is a perfectly reasonable factor.

#### What is printed is what is written

- **Typos stay.** A word misspelled inside a cell MUST keep its misspelling.
- **Numbers are copied digit by digit**, with thousands and decimal separators exactly as printed.
  See Accounting Number Formats (§9.6.1).
- **Wrapped codes are not fused with their neighbours.** In a narrow column a code can wrap onto two
  lines, or two short codes can sit in neighbouring cells and look like one. The column boundaries
  and the cell's span decide: fusing `B-2` with `VC`, or `TR-1` with `TR-2`, is an error, and it
  also throws off the column count of the whole row.
- **A blank cell stays empty.** A cell that prints nothing MUST be rendered empty; a dash MUST NOT be
  supplied because the column has dashes elsewhere.

#### Characters the image cannot tell apart

Some characters are visually identical and no zoom separates them: µ (U+00B5) and μ (U+03BC), a
non-breaking space and an ordinary space, a minus sign and a hyphen.

- The output MUST keep the visible form and the character count exactly as printed, and SHOULD use
  the character normally typed for that glyph.
- The text layer MUST NOT be used to break the tie: it is a hint about the content, never the
  authority on it.
- A consumer or checker MUST treat the members of each family below as equal, so the choice among
  them cannot make an output non-conforming.

| Family | Written as |
| --- | --- |
| µ (U+00B5) ≡ μ (U+03BC) | either |
| non-breaking space ≡ ordinary space | an ordinary space |
| minus sign (U+2212) ≡ hyphen-minus | `-` |
| non-breaking hyphen ≡ hyphen-minus | `-` |
| figure dash, en dash ≡ hyphen, inside a numeric range | either |

The image outranks every other source on **what is printed**. Where two codepoints are
indistinguishable there is no fact about the page for it to be authoritative over — µ and μ *are*
the same ink. The visible form is fidelity and stays exact; the codepoint underneath is a
serialisation detail.

A dash that is *doing something* is not a homoglyph question. An em dash alone in a cell is a value
— see Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — and a struck-through digit is not a character variant at all.

#### What else rests on the image

- Duplicated Tables (§9.2.4) — the rendered page decides whether a repeated table is really printed twice.
- Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) — OCR silently joins a struck value to its replacement and produces
  a number that appears nowhere on the page. Only the image catches it.





#### Related

- The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1) — the principle this rule applies to cells
- Accounting Number Formats (§9.6.1) — verbatim numbers, signs and separators
- Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) — the image separates a struck value from its replacement
- Duplicated Tables (§9.2.4) — the image decides whether a table is printed twice
- Borderless Whitespace Tables (§9.1.1) — column boundaries without rules, where fused cells are most likely

#### 9.6.4 Color as the Value

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-color-as-the-value` · Tags: tables, color, marks

> **✅ Normative**
> A cell whose only content is a coloured fill MUST be rendered as an **empty `<mark>` carrying the
> colour**: `<td><mark style="background-color: red"></mark></td>`. The colour MUST be the nearest
> HTML colour name, never the meaning a legend assigns it, and the cell MUST NOT be left blank.

Risk matrices and heatmap tables put the meaning in the fill. The cell has no text at all:

```text
| Likelihood ╲ Impact | Low | High |
| Rare                | 🟩  | 🟨   |   ← the fill IS the value
| Likely              | 🟨  | 🟥   |
```

Read straight through, the body of that table is blank, and a blank body makes the whole grid
meaningless.

#### The rendering

```html
<tr>
  <td>Rare</td>
  <td><mark style="background-color: green"></mark></td>
  <td><mark style="background-color: yellow"></mark></td>
</tr>
```

- The `<mark>` MUST be **empty**: the cell prints no text, and adding some would be inventing
  content.
- The colour rides on the `style` attribute — the same mechanism as highlighted text in
  Highlighted Text (§7.2.5) and Text Formatting Conventions (§7.1). One vocabulary covers both: the nearest
  HTML colour name in `style="background-color: …"`.
- The colour MUST NOT be written as the cell's text. A cell reading `green` is indistinguishable
  from a cell whose printed content is the *word* "green" — and heatmap legends do sometimes spell
  their colours out. Text is what the page printed; the attribute is how the cell was filled.

The rendering degrades correctly. A consumer that ignores attributes sees an empty cell, which is
truthful — the page printed no text there. A consumer that reads them gets the value. Neither is
misled.

#### Why not the meaning

Writing "Low risk" instead of "green" means reading a legend, and the legend is routinely elsewhere
on the page or on another page entirely. A rendering that depends on material outside the region
would be a guess whenever that material is out of reach. The colour name needs no legend, stays
faithful to the page, and leaves the interpretation to whoever reads the table.

#### Colour that is not the value

The two cases MUST be kept apart:

| The cell prints | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **A fill and text** | The text is the value; the fill is decoration or revision tracking. The text is transcribed and the fill is not carried. |
| **A fill and nothing else** | The case of this rule: an empty `<mark>` with the fill's colour. |

#### Shading that means "not applicable"

A grey fill over cells the page does not compute MUST be rendered the same way: an empty `<mark>`
per shaded cell with the nearest colour name, e.g.
`<td><mark style="background-color: gray"></mark></td>`. The fill is what the page printed there,
and a consumer ignoring attributes still sees an empty cell. The shaded region MUST NOT be rendered
as a `colspan` or `rowspan`: the page prints the cells separately.

#### Related

- Text Colors (§7.3.12) — coloured text, as opposed to a coloured fill with no text
- Highlighted Text (§7.2.5) — the same `background-color` vocabulary for highlighted runs
- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — printed marks (ticks, dots, icons) that stand in for a value
- Iconography and Symbols (§7.3.4) — icons outside tables
- Rotated and Diagonal Content (§9.8.1) — the diagonal corner cell of the risk-matrix sketch

#### 9.6.5 Handwriting and Stamps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-handwriting-and-stamps` · Tags: tables, marks, redline

> **✅ Normative**
> **Handwriting over a printed value** MUST keep both, the struck-through printed value first:
> `~~60~~ 55` — the same markup as a printed redline replacement. **A stamp** over a table MUST keep
> its text and MUST be rendered **outside the table**, as page-level content; it MUST NOT be
> assigned to a cell.

Filled-in ledgers and approved/void stamps put ink on top of a grid that was printed empty.

```text
| Qty | Description | Amount |
| 2   | Widget      | ~60~ 55 (handwritten) |  ← replaces? joins? annotates?

     [ APPROVED ]   ← stamp overlapping three cells: which cell gets it? any?
```

#### Handwriting over a printed value

The cell MUST hold the printed value struck through, then the handwritten one:

```text
page shows:   60 (printed, crossed out)   55 (handwritten)
rendered as:  ~~60~~ 55
```

**This is deliberately the same markup as Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7).** A printed correction and
a handwritten one are the same act — a value replaced in place — and the ink used to make the
change is not what a consumer needs to know. One encoding covers both, so nothing downstream has to
distinguish a pen from a strikethrough font to read the cell.

The printed and the handwritten digits MUST NOT be merged into one number. OCR readily runs them
together and produces a number that appears nowhere on the page and looks entirely reasonable; the
image decides which glyphs are printed and which are written, and they are recorded as two values.

Handwriting that adds a value where the printed cell was empty is simply the cell's content.

#### Stamps

A stamp belongs to the page, not to a cell. It overlaps cells only because of where it landed, so
any cell it could be assigned to is arbitrary — and putting its text inside a cell corrupts a value
that is otherwise correct.

- The stamp MUST be kept and rendered **outside the table**, as its `[stamp: …]` marker — see
  Stamps (§7.3.11).
- Its letters MUST NOT be distributed across the cells it crosses, and it MUST NOT be dropped for
  having nowhere obvious to go.

Assigning a stamp to a cell fails in both directions: it corrupts the cell's value, and it makes the
stamp's own text unreadable by splitting it. Every candidate cell is equally arbitrary, which is the
tell that the cell level is the wrong level.

No example page exercises either case yet; the sketches above stand in for one.





#### Related

- Struck and Replaced Values (§9.6.7) — the same `~~old~~ new` markup for a printed replacement
- Watermarks (§7.3.13) — the other page-level mark rendered outside the content it overlaps
- Stamps (§7.3.11) — the `[stamp: …]` marker
- Seals and Round Stamps (§7.3.9) — round seals and their `[seal: …]` marker
- Handwritten Annotations (§7.3.3) — handwriting in a margin, which replaces nothing
- Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) — the image, not OCR, separates printed from written glyphs

#### 9.6.6 Marks and Symbols in Cells

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-marks-and-symbols-in-cells` · Tags: tables, marks, encoding

> **✅ Normative**
> A footnote marker MUST stay in the cell of the value it is attached to. An em-dash alone in a
> cell is a value and MUST be kept; a cell printed blank MUST stay blank. A cell whose content is a
> symbol or icon MUST be rendered as a bracketed transcription of what the mark asserts, and MUST
> NOT be replaced by an emoji.

*(Source image marks-in-cells.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A sun/water requirements table where the **icons are the values** — a full sun versus a partial sun,
one droplet versus two. A rendering that leaves those cells empty says nothing at all.

```text
| Subscribers¹ | 48,210³ |   ← superscripts attached to a value
| Dividend     | —       |   ← an em-dash standing alone in a cell
| Approved     | ✓       |   ← a checkmark standing in for a value
```

#### Footnote superscripts

- A footnote marker MUST stay in the same cell as the value it is attached to, rendered with
  `<sup>`: `48,210<sup>3</sup>`, `New Program<sup>2</sup>` — see Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11).
- The marker MUST NOT be stripped, and MUST NOT be given a column of its own. It points at one
  number; separated from that number it points at nothing.

#### The em-dash

- An em-dash alone in a cell is a value and MUST be rendered as `—`. In accounting it means *zero,
  and we checked* — a different claim from an empty cell, which means *nothing here*.
- The rule holds in both directions, and the second is the one most often broken: a cell printed
  blank MUST be rendered as an empty cell, and a dash MUST NOT be supplied for it, however many of
  its neighbours carry one (**never invent**).

The same reasoning makes the structural blank meaningful in Triangles and Matrix Tables (§9.8.2) and the
coloured fill meaningful in Color as the Value (§9.6.4) — a non-value that is a value.

#### Checkmarks, crosses and icons

- A mark that stands in for a value MUST be rendered as a bracketed word stating what it asserts:
  `[yes]`, `[no]`, `[checked]`, `[locked]`, `[icon: present]`.
- The nearest emoji MUST NOT be substituted. An emoji looks faithful and is not: it carries a shape
  rather than the claim the page makes, and no two producers pick the same one.
- Where a symbol is glued to a value rather than standing in for one — `▲ 512.40`, a bare `+` or `-`
  carrying a superscript — the glyph MUST stay with the value in the cell, as printed. See
  Iconography and Symbols (§7.3.4) for marks outside tables.

```text
| Feature | Basic | Pro |
| SSO     | 🔒    | ✓   |   → | SSO | [locked] | [yes] |
```

##### A repeated mark is a scale

Some columns grade a value by printing the mark more than once — one droplet for low water, two for
high; one star, three stars.

- A repeated mark MUST be transcribed **once per printed mark**: `[water]`, `[water][water]`. The
  count is the value; collapsing the pair to one token loses the distinction the column exists to
  draw.
- A count notation such as `[water:2]` MUST NOT be used.
- The vocabulary MUST distinguish every distinct mark the scale prints. A sun column printing a
  solid, a half-filled and an outline glyph is a **three**-step scale; a rendering with two names
  for it has lost a step.

#### Related

- Iconography and Symbols (§7.3.4) — the same marks outside tables
- Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11) — how a footnote marker is tagged
- Color as the Value (§9.6.4) — a fill that is a value, like the em-dash
- Triangles and Matrix Tables (§9.8.2) — a blank that is meaningful, and must not be filled
- Accounting Number Formats (§9.6.1) — dashes and brackets as number notation

#### 9.6.7 Struck and Replaced Values

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-struck-and-replaced-values` · Tags: tables, redline, ocr, failure-mode

> **✅ Normative**
> A cell holding a struck value and its replacement MUST render both, struck first —
> **`~~1.316~~ 1.335`** — and MUST NOT merge them into one figure. The `~~` MUST cover exactly the
> glyphs struck on the page: `1.~~316~~ 335` when only the digits are crossed out.

A cell holds an old value crossed out plus its replacement. A text layer joins them without a trace:

```text
page shows:  1.316 (struck)  1.335
text layer:  1.316335        ← this number does not exist on the page
```

That is the worst outcome available on a table: not a drop and not a garble, but a fabricated number
that looks entirely plausible and that nothing downstream can catch. Struck cells MUST be read from
the rendered page, never from the text layer — see Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3).

#### Writing the cell

- A struck value and its replacement MUST be rendered `~~old~~ new`, which keeps the two readings
  distinct and marks which one is superseded.
- Where the page marks the change with an underline instead of a strike, the replacement MUST be
  rendered `<u>1.335</u>`, recording what is actually drawn.
- A handwritten correction over a printed value MUST use the same markup — see
  Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5). A printed strikethrough and a pen stroke are the same act, so a
  consumer never has to tell them apart.
- The output MUST NOT restructure the table into "Previous" and "Current" columns. Where the page
  itself prints the old and new figures in separate tables or columns, each MUST be rendered where
  it appears rather than folded into one cell.

##### ✅ **Sample** — `strike`

#### The strike span mirrors the printed strike

Where the strike starts and stops is printed information, and the markup carries it: exactly the
struck glyphs, no more, no less.

```text
whole value struck:      1.316 (all struck)  335        →  ~~1.316~~ 335
only the digits struck:  1.316 (316 struck)  335        →  1.~~316~~ 335
```

The unstruck `1.` sits **outside** the `~~`, because that is where it sits on the page. Nothing is
reconstructed and nothing is invented — the prefix is transcribed because it is printed and was
never struck.

`1.~~316~~ 335` gives a reader everything needed to arrive at `1.335` without the output asserting
it. The `1.` is printed, unstruck, and therefore still part of the value; the replacement digits
follow. The reading falls out of the transcription instead of being asserted on top of it.

That is why the span must be exact. `~~1.316~~ 335` for a page that only struck `316` throws away
the prefix a reader needs, and `1.~~316~~ 335` for a page that struck the whole value claims ink
that is not there. Both are losses, in opposite directions.

#### One struck cell puts the column in play

Strikes are thin and reproduce badly at page zoom, so a struck cell is easy to miss. One struck cell
means the column is a redline column: every other cell in it MUST be read for a strike before the
column is rendered.

#### Redline in prose

- Deleted text MUST be rendered `~~…~~` and inserted underlined text `<u>…</u>`, each over exactly
  the printed span.
- Where colour distinguishes revisions or authors, the colour MUST be preserved as well. Insertion
  MUST NOT be inferred from colour alone where the page marks nothing else.

#### Related

- Handwriting and Stamps (§9.6.5) — the handwritten equivalent uses the same markup

### 9.7 Titles and edges

#### 9.7.1 Bottom Edge Totals and Islands

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-bottom-edge-totals-and-islands` · Tags: tables, drops, boundaries

> **✅ Normative**
> Content printed below or beside a table MUST NOT be dropped, even when it sits outside the ruled
> frame. Where it continues the table's ruled grid it MUST be rendered as rows of that table; where
> it stands apart as its own unbordered block it MUST be rendered as its own small key-value table.

The bottom edge is where content goes missing most often, because everything here sits past the
last rule of the frame — and it is usually the numbers the reader actually wanted.

```text
| Item   | Qty | Rate | Amount |
| Widget | 2   | 30   | 60     |
└──── ruled frame ends ────────┘
               Subtotal    60      ← outside the frame:
               Shipping    10        footer rows of the table? its own KV
               Total       70        table? dropped entirely?
```

#### The frame decides

The block under the table is placed by one question: does it sit **inside** the ruled frame, or
visually continue the table's ruled column grid?

| Block under the table | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **Inside the frame**, or continuing its ruled column grid | footer rows of that table, each value in its printed column |
| **Standing apart** as a separate unbordered block — even if its columns loosely line up under the table's rightmost columns | its own key-value table: one row per printed line, a label cell and a value cell |

The block MUST NOT be omitted, and a block that is not part of the grid MUST NOT be padded into the
main table as extra footer rows. This is the frame test of Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3), applied at
the other edge of the table. Footnotes are the one exception — see Footnotes Inside the Frame (§9.7.2).

  <tr> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> </tr>

  <tr> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> </tr>
  <tr> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> </tr>
  <tr> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> <td> </td> </tr>

#### Trailing aligned summary lines

Lines such as "Selected …" or "Reserve to Surplus Ratio:" whose values land under real columns are
rows of the grid. They MUST be rendered as rows, each value in its printed column — not as prose
after the table.

```text
| Year | Reserves | Surplus |
| 2023 | 1,204    | 887     |
Selected             1,190     ← values align under real columns:
Reserve/Surplus:     1.36        rows of the table
```

#### Invoice-style totals blocks

A Subtotal / Discount / Shipping / Total block printed below the line-item table and outside its
frame MUST be rendered as its own key-value table: label and value, one row per printed line.

This is a deliberate exception to the treatment of ungridded key-value regions in
Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1). Trailing totals are a numeric continuation of the table's data, and
a table whose totals are missing has lost the part of the page most people read first.

#### Detached cell islands

A small offset group of cells that lines up with a table's column tracks is content. It MUST be
rendered; it is not decoration.

```text
| (1) | (2) | (3)  |
| 100 | 82  | 0.82 |

            | 0.79 |   ← "(8) Benchmark" offset box, aligned
                         with column (3)'s track
```

Where it goes is decided by one test: **does the island line up with an existing table's column
tracks?**

- **Yes** → it belongs to that table and MUST be appended as an extra row: the label in the stub
  column, the value in the column whose track it lines up with.
- **No** → it MUST be rendered as its own small table.

Column-track alignment is the typesetter saying "this value belongs under that heading". A floating
box that lines up with nothing makes no such claim, so it stands alone.

#### Alignment on its own is not proof

Alignment places an island once it is known to belong to the table; it cannot by itself prove that
an out-of-frame line is a footer row. On a premium-tax page an underline closes a
`Premium Tax / Total` mini-table, and the `3. DCCE to Loss Ratio` line printed beneath it sits under
the same columns while belonging to neither table.

The frame test MUST be applied first, and alignment used only to place what it hands over — not
the other way round.

#### Where the frame is genuinely ambiguous

Some pages have no ruled border either way. There, both encodings — footer rows of the table, or
a separate key-value table — conform, provided every printed line is kept. A document MUST use one
of them throughout. See Accepted Alternatives (§A.1) and Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2).





#### Related

- Total and Subtotal Rows (§9.5.6) — totals printed inside the grid
- Footnotes Inside the Frame (§9.7.2) — the one bottom-edge block that never becomes a row
- Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) — the same frame test at the top edge
- Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1) — the key-value treatment this rule makes an exception to

#### 9.7.2 Footnotes Inside the Frame

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-footnotes-inside-the-frame` · Tags: tables, captions, boundaries

> **✅ Normative**
> A table footnote MUST be rendered outside the table, as footnote text placed after it — even when
> the page prints it inside the table's ruled border. It MUST NOT be rendered as a row of the table.
> It retains the Footnote class and MUST NOT be wrapped in `<caption>`. This is a deliberate
> exception to the frame test.

A footnote line printed within the table's own ruled border:

```text
| Rate A     | 1.10¹   |
| Rate B     | 1.25    |
| ¹ Excludes riders    |   ← printed INSIDE the ruled frame
```

#### Why the frame test does not decide footnotes

The frame test — ink inside the border is a row, ink outside it is a caption — decides titles and
banners in Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) and totals blocks in Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1). It
is worth having because it is mechanical.

A footnote is where it gives the wrong answer. **The line names no columns and carries no values**,
so rendering it as a row asserts something false about the table: a consumer counting records gets
one too many, and the row's single cell has no relationship to any column above it. Where the
typesetter drew the border is a layout accident — the footnote is commentary on the table either
way.

The carve-out costs the frame test its single-signal property, and that price is paid
deliberately: **the frame decides titles and banners; it does not decide footnotes.**

#### Rendering the footnote

- **Wherever the border falls, the footnote MUST be footnote text placed immediately after the
  table.** It MUST be transcribed verbatim, including its leading marker, and MUST stay attached to
  the table it annotates rather than drifting into the surrounding prose.
- A line opening `¹`, `*`, `(a)` or `Note:` that refers to a marker printed in a cell above it is a
  footnote, not a row.
- Superscript markers **inside** cells MUST stay attached to their values — see
  Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6). The footnote body leaving the table does not take the reference
  with it, so `1.10¹` in the cell and `¹ Excludes riders` after the table still point at each other.
- **The text MUST survive either way.** Only its placement is decided here; dropping it is never
  conforming.

#### Related

- Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3) — the frame test that decides titles and banners, and does not decide footnotes
- Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1) — the frame test applied to totals and islands at the same edge
- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — the in-cell marker that points at the footnote

#### 9.7.3 Titles Banners Captions

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-titles-banners-captions` · Tags: tables, captions, headers

> **✅ Normative**
> For a table-only title, the frame and the fill decide. A band that shares the table's border or
> fill MUST be rendered as a header row **inside** the table; a table-only title outside the ruled
> frame MUST be rendered as `<caption>` inside the table HTML. Table and chart captions MUST be
> the first or last content inside `<table>` according to reading order and MUST appear once.

```text
22. Consolidated Income Statement        ← title line above the table:
| Revenue | 2024 | 2023 |              ## heading? first header row? both?

| [colspan=3]LAWNS & ANNUALS |       ← band sharing the table's border/fill:
| Name | Water | Sun |                 header row inside, or heading outside?
```

#### Structural statement titles

A table-only caption is first told apart from a principal financial-statement or numbered schedule
title using Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7). A principal statement title can be a document
heading, and a company line printed directly above it joins that heading (see Stacked Headings (§6.9));
a units line cannot. A numbered schedule title printed within a grid keeps its structural role, but
its text MUST stay in the table once and MUST NOT be duplicated as an outside heading. The frame
test below applies to ordinary table captions and bands.

#### The frame test

The position of the ink relative to the ruled border, and whether the band carries the table's
fill, decide:

| The band… | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **shares the border or the fill** | a header row inside the table. A coloured "LAWNS & ANNUALS" band that runs to the table's own edges is a `<th colspan=N>` banner row. Such bands MUST NOT be omitted — they carry the heading for everything under them. |
| **sits outside the ruled frame** | `<caption>` inside the table HTML, first or last according to reading order |

Only text that belongs to the table alone counts. A page heading that happens to sit above a table,
and would still make sense if the table were removed, is not a title band.

A **bold caption with paragraph spacing directly above a bordered mini-table** follows the same
rule: it MUST be the first `<caption>` inside the table HTML.

#### An in-table title is one full-width cell

A title band rendered as a row MUST be a **single full-width `<th colspan=N>`** — never the title
in one column with empty cells padded beside it.

```text
| [colspan=3]Table 13 — Scale G2 |    vs    | Table 13 — Scale G2 |  |  |
                                             ↑ padded: a spurious record
```

A full-width single-value row is recognised as a title and set aside; the padded form reads as a
real data row with missing values, and adds a row that the table does not have.

A table-only title therefore has two forms, chosen by its printed role: **a full-width header
row** for an in-frame band, or **`<caption>`** for a caption outside the printed frame.

#### A title appears once

A title MUST appear once, in the form selected by the frame test. A `<caption>` MUST NOT also
appear as a paragraph outside the table or as a header row.

#### Banner colspan follows the region, not the ink

A centred band title MUST span **the region it heads**, not the pixels its letters happen to cover.

```text
|      Proposed      |            ← ink covers 4 of 14 column tracks:
| c1 | c2 | … | c14 |              colspan=4 or colspan=14?
```

A "Proposed" banner over a 14-column table is `colspan=14`, even though its ink reaches only the
middle four. Centred text shrinks toward the middle whatever it spans, so measuring the glyphs
measures the font, not the structure.

#### Section-divider rows

A divider row that **names no columns** — "Part I — Financial Information" and the like — SHOULD
be rendered as a bold body row (`<td colspan=N>`); a `<th>` row MAY be used instead. A document
MUST use one of the two for every visually identical band — see
Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2). Whichever tag is used, a divider MUST NOT be promoted into the
column-name tier: it labels a region, not a column.

```text
| Part I — Financial Information |   ← names no columns
| Item 1 | 10-Q | 45 |
```

Bold `<td>` is the preferred form because a `<th>` claims "this labels the cells below it", and a
section divider makes no such claim.

#### How a caption is rendered

A table or chart caption MUST be rendered once as `<caption>…</caption>` inside the HTML table
that represents its object. Reading order determines its position in the HTML source:

- A caption read **before** the table or chart MUST be the first content line after the opening
  `<table>` tag, before any rows or table-section wrappers.
- A caption read **after** the table or chart MUST be the last content line before `</table>`,
  after all rows and table-section wrappers.
- A chart's table MUST still open with `<table data-source="chart">`.

```text
caption before the table:
<table>
  <caption>Table 5 — Lapse Rates</caption>
  <!-- rows -->
</table>

caption after the chart:
<table data-source="chart">
  <!-- rows -->
  <caption>Figure 2 — Annual losses</caption>
</table>
```

The first/last requirement concerns the serialized HTML, including captions after the final row.
Source notes, footnotes and nearby prose retain their own roles and MUST NOT be turned into
captions. Captions of objects that are not represented by tables retain their adjacent paragraphs.

In the element list, a caption MUST be attached to the table or chart it describes wherever the
association is clear from the page. It retains the Caption class and its own box even when its
rendering is nested inside `<table>`; the table or chart box follows Block Boundaries (§5.2). When
the association is unclear, the output MUST NOT invent an attachment.

##### Caption formatting is content

Captions are rarely plain text, and their styling is printed content like any other. It MUST be
preserved as printed, per run:

```text
printed:      Figure 2. Predicted vs True Tree count on the test set.
              ^^^^^^^^^ bold          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ plain
output:       <caption><strong>Figure 2.</strong> Predicted vs True Tree count on the test set.</caption>

printed:      FIG.2.3. Electric and non-electric energy growth rate (from [1]).
              ^ all italic
output:       <caption><em>FIG.2.3. Electric and non-electric energy growth rate (from [1]).</em></caption>
```

Three shapes recur: **fully italic**, a **bold label followed by plain text**, and a caption set in
a heading-like face. A bold run stays bold, an italic run stays italic, and a mixed caption keeps
the boundary between them. Styles MUST NOT be normalised to one, and MUST NOT be dropped because
the text survives without them. The per-run discipline is the one that governs styling inside
tables — see Bold and Italic Inside Tables (§9.6.2).

**A caption MUST NOT be converted into a heading**, even when it is set in a heading-like face. A
`##` heading above the table asserts a document section that the page did not print, and it
survives into any structure derived from the headings. A caption names an object; a heading opens
a section.

This is the placement rule only. Whether a given piece of text is a caption at all, or a title band
inside the table, is settled by the frame test above.

### 9.8 Special table types

#### 9.8.1 Rotated and Diagonal Content

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-rotated-and-diagonal-content` · Tags: tables, orientation, headers

> **✅ Normative**
> A rotated table MUST be read in **its own orientation**, never in page orientation. A diagonally
> split corner cell MUST stay **one cell** holding both labels separated by a slash —
> `Region \ Year` — the label across the top first.

*(Source image diagonal-corner-cell.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

One printed cell carrying two labels: **MONTH** across the top, **COUNTRY** down the side, split by a
diagonal rule. There is only one cell to put them in.

#### A landscape table on a portrait page

- A table printed sideways MUST be rendered as a reader would read it after turning the page: rows
  are rows as the table reads, not as the page is filed.
- Sideways text MUST NOT be transcribed in page order.

#### Vertical column headers

Labels printed at 90° over narrow columns are ordinary headers. Each MUST be rendered as normal
header text, upright, in the column it heads.

```text
| ⤴A⤴ | ⤴B⤴ | ⤴C⤴ |   ← headers printed vertically
| 1   | 2   | 3   |
```

Nothing about the rotation changes the structure — it is a typesetting choice made because the
column is narrow.

#### The diagonally split corner cell

```text
| Region ╲ Year | 2023 | 2024 |   ← one printed cell, two labels
| East          | 40   | 44   |
```

- Both labels MUST survive: one names the stub column, the other names the header row, and losing
  either leaves an axis unnamed.
- There is one printed cell, so it MUST stay one cell, the two labels separated by a slash —
  `Region \ Year` — in the reading order the diagonal implies: the label across the top first, then
  the one down the side.
- The corner MUST NOT be split into two header cells.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a landscape page in a portrait document

*(Source image corpus-rotated-page.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A paper page rendered sideways: the body text, both tables and the *Table 3* caption read
bottom-to-top. Upright, the two tables are ordinary tables; nothing about them is special except
that a reader has to turn the page. The page is cut off after the *Kestrel 33B* row of the second
table, so nothing below it is rendered.

What makes this the useful case is that **the rotation is not marked anywhere**. There is no
landscape flag; the only signal is that the text runs the wrong way. A rendering in page orientation
transposes headers and rows and still looks structurally plausible.

Note also the blank corner cells above both stub columns, and the en-dashes standing in for missing
benchmark scores — see Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1) and Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6).

#### 9.8.2 Triangles and Matrix Tables

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `tables-triangles-and-matrix-tables` · Tags: tables, encoding, empty-cells

> **✅ Normative**
> **Every row MUST carry the full column count.** The jagged half MUST be padded with **individual
> empty cells** — one `<td></td>` per missing position. A `colspan` or `rowspan` over the empty region
> MUST NOT be used, and a `0` or any other value MUST NOT be invented.

Loss development exhibits and similar matrices are jagged on purpose. The missing half is
**meaningfully** empty — that development period has not happened yet — not data that failed to be
read.

```text
Accident yr | 12mo | 24mo | 36mo |
| 2021      | 450  | 512  | 530  |
| 2022      | 470  | 528  |      |  ← structurally empty,
| 2023      | 465  |      |      |    not "failed to read"
```

#### Requirements

- **The shape MUST be kept.** Every row has the full column count; the cells past the end of the row
  are present and empty. Rows MUST NOT be truncated.
- **One empty cell per missing position.** Four unhappened periods are four `<td></td>`, not one
  `colspan="4"`. The span would say *"this region is one thing"*, and it is not — it is four distinct
  coordinates that each have not happened yet.
- **The empty half MUST NOT be padded with values.** Filling it with `0`, `n/a` or a repeat of the
  last figure destroys the only thing the triangle asserts.
- **A printed value MUST NOT be read as structural emptiness either.** Some pages print `0` across
  the future half. A zero is a claim and a blank is an absence; the output MUST render whichever the
  page prints.
- A cell that is empty because it cannot be read is a different situation — see
  Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3).

#### Why a span is wrong here, when it is free elsewhere

Blank and Spacer Rows (§9.5.1) leaves the encoding of an unruled empty region free: leading empty cells
and one blank spanning block render identically, and neither is preferred.

**A triangle is the carve-out.** Every empty cell sits at a real coordinate — an accident year
crossed with a development period — and *"12 months has not elapsed for the 2023 year"* is a
separate fact from the same statement about 24 months. Collapsed into one span, those coordinates
stop being addressable: a consumer can no longer ask what the 2023 row holds at 24 months, because
the cell it would look in no longer exists.

Elsewhere the empty region is one undifferentiated blank. Here it is a set of individually
meaningful absences that happen to be adjacent.

This is the same principle that settles blank space beside a header in
Barely-Existing Columns and Headers (§9.3.1): **a span is a claim that the page merged something.** The
page did not merge these.

#### Why the blank matters more here than elsewhere

In most tables, blank versus an explicit empty marker is cosmetic. In a loss triangle the blank
carries actuarial meaning: it asserts *this development period does not exist yet*, which is a fact
about the world, not a gap in the transcription. That is the same argument that makes the em-dash a
value in Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) and the coloured fill a value in Color as the Value (§9.6.4) — a
non-value that is a value.





#### Related

- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — the em-dash and the blank as values
- Blank and Spacer Rows (§9.5.1) — where the encoding of an empty region is free
- Header Body Column Count Mismatch (§9.4.2) — padding short rows to the column count

## §10 Forms

### 10.1 Forms and Key-Value Regions

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-forms-and-key-value-regions` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> Fill-in fields and checkbox regions are key-value content, not tables: they MUST be rendered as
> the key-value list of The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) and MUST NOT be rendered as a table. The output MUST
> NOT contain a two-column key/value table that the page does not print as a ruled grid.

Form controls printed on the page — labels waiting for a value, checkbox rows, signature and date
lines — look tabular because they line up in columns. They are not tables: the alignment is
typesetting, not structure.

```text
Insurer: ________        NAIC #: ________
☒ Renewal     ☐ New business
```

```markdown
- **Insurer:** [blank]
- **NAIC #:** [blank]
- [x] Renewal
- [ ] New business
```

#### Fillable or static

A region is **form content** when it prints labelled fields to fill, checkboxes, or blanks —
**even when its layout looks like a plain grid of labels and values**. Such a region MUST be
rendered as a key-value list.

A **static key-value reference** — a legend, a specification sheet, a summary box, filing
metadata — prints fixed labels and values and **nothing to fill in and no checkbox**. It is not a
form. The test is whether anything on it was meant to be filled in.

#### The border test for static key-value blocks

A page that raises this question is usually half form, half grid, so the decision is made region
by region. For each static block of `label: value` pairs:

| The block | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **Printed inside a ruled border** (a gridded key/value block) | It MUST be rendered as a table, per Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5); leaving it out drops a table. |
| **Not ruled** — a specification stack, a cluster of `Label: value` fields above a table, an address block, a prose-line legend | It MUST be rendered as text in reading order and MUST NOT be rendered as a table. |

A totals block printed under a table is the one exception: it belongs to the table above it, not
to the surrounding fields — see Bottom Edge Totals and Islands (§9.7.1).

#### Why not a small table

A two-column key/value table built from an unruled block creates a record that exists nowhere on
the page — the **never invent** failure of Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2). It teaches whatever learns
from the output that structure can be conjured from whitespace. Rendering the block as text or as a
key-value list loses nothing, because nothing there was ever printed as tabular.





#### Related

- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) — how form content is transcribed once it is recognised
- Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5) — the test a ruled static block goes through
- Marks and Symbols in Cells (§9.6.6) — checkbox glyphs used as values inside a real table cell
- Empty Pre-Printed Grids (§9.1.3) — a fully blank ruled form, where the structure is the content

### 10.2 Repeated and Unlabelled Fields

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-repeated-and-unlabelled-fields` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> Field groups that repeat without a printed heading MUST be kept as anonymous groups in printed
> order, separated by a blank line in the Markdown. The output MUST NOT invent a heading, label or
> positional id — no `Vehicle 1`, no `Child 2` — for a group or field the page does not name.

#### Repeating unlabelled record blocks

Insurance-application premises, vehicle and applicant blocks, and family-court residence blocks
repeat the same field set several times and **print no heading of their own**.

*(Source image form-vehicle-blocks.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

- Each repetition MUST be rendered as its own group of key-value lines, in printed order.
- Consecutive groups MUST be separated by one blank line in the Markdown; when a sidecar is
  produced, each group MUST be its own nested group of items.
- A heading, number or label that the page does not print MUST NOT be added to tell the groups
  apart.

#### Where non-field text goes

Instructions, preambles and fine print MUST be transcribed at their printed reading position,
between the fields they accompany — see Fields Outside the Form (§10.5.1).

#### Unlabelled entries with no id

An entry with neither a printed id nor a printed label MUST be rendered as its bare value, or as a
bare `[blank]` when it is empty. A label or positional id MUST NOT be invented for it.

### 10.3 The output format

#### 10.3.1 Ids and Labels

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-ids-and-labels` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A field's **id** is its printed designator, written exactly as printed in escaped brackets outside
> the bold label. Its **label** is the printed caption, verbatim. A label MUST NOT repeat the id, and
> a caption MUST NOT be written as an id.

#### The distinction

An **id** is a short printed designator that indexes into the form — `1a`, `e`, `H1`, `Part III`.
It is what a reader cites when they say "see line 12a".

A **label** is the caption. **A caption is never an id.** On a 1099, only the numbered boxes have
ids; `PAYER'S TIN` is a label with no id.

```markdown
✅  - \[1a\] **Total amount**: 4,200
❌  - **1a Total amount**: 4,200      ← id folded into the label
❌  - \[PAYER'S TIN\] **...**          ← a caption is not an id
```

#### Nothing is cleaned up

A label MUST keep its abbreviations, capitalisation and punctuation exactly as printed. A label
MUST NOT be renamed, expanded or tidied: `FAX (A/C, No)` stays `FAX (A/C, No)`.

#### Implicit numbers

When a printed id carries an **implicit** number, the id MUST include it.

*(Source image form-implicit-ids.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A block printed `35a` then `b`, `c`, `d` has the ids **`35a`, `35b`, `35c`, `35d`** — not `35a`,
`b`, `c`, `d`. The `35` is implied by position and is part of how the field is cited; dropping it
makes three of the four ids unusable for reference.

#### Escaping

`\[x\]` is a printed id "x"; `[x]` is a checked box. The escape is what keeps them apart — see
The Key-Value List (§10.3.2).





#### Related

- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) — the line format ids and labels sit in
- Fill-Ins (§10.4.4) — fields with an id but no label
- Form Reading Order (§10.5.2) — ids set the order of the fields

#### 10.3.2 The Key-Value List

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-the-key-value-list` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> Fillable form content MUST be rendered as a Markdown key-value list, not as a table. Every field
> MUST be one list item using the `-` marker.

#### The shape

```markdown
### \[Part I\] Information About the Partnership

- \[A\] **Partnership's employer identification number**: 27-4162308
- \[D\] **Check if this is a publicly traded partnership (PTP)**: [ ]
- **CONTACT NAME:** Melinda Clayton
- **FAX (A/C, No):** [blank]
- \[G\]
  - [x] General partner or LLC member-manager
  - [ ] Limited partner or other LLC member
- **Your signature**: [signature: John Doe]
```

#### The line format

```text
- \[id\] **Label**: value
```

- The id and the label MUST each appear **only when printed**. A field with no printed id carries
  no brackets.
- An id MUST be written in **escaped** square brackets — `\[1a\]` — **outside** the bold label.
- An empty fill-in MUST be rendered as `[blank]`. A checkbox MUST be rendered as `[x]` (checked) or
  `[ ]` (unchecked).
- An option line MUST be box-first: `- [x] Single`.
- A printed section heading MUST be rendered as a Markdown heading. A box whose id covers several
  fields MUST be rendered as a parent list item with the fields nested beneath it.

#### Why the id is escaped

`\[x\]` is a printed field designator "x"; `[x]` is a **checked box**. Without the escape the two
cannot be told apart, and a field id silently becomes a tick.

#### Colons

- When the printed label ends in `:`, the colon MUST stay **inside** the bold label:
  `- **CONTACT NAME:** Melinda Clayton`.
- When the value is not printed on the same line as its label — a caption printed under its
  line, an answer area below its question — the `:` after the label MUST be omitted:
  `- **SIGNATURE OF DEPONENT** [blank]`.





#### Related

- Ids and Labels (§10.3.1) — what counts as an id and what as a label
- Values Are Verbatim (§10.3.3) — what goes after the label
- Fill-Ins (§10.4.4) · Checkboxes (§10.4.2) · Option Groups (§10.4.5) — the field shapes
- Forms and Key-Value Regions (§10.1) — deciding that a region is form content at all

#### 10.3.3 Values Are Verbatim

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-values-are-verbatim` · Tags: forms, fidelity

> **✅ Normative**
> Entered content MUST be transcribed exactly as it appears on the page. A value MUST NOT be
> rounded, reformatted, computed or summarised.

This is Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) applied to what someone wrote into a field.

| Printed | Output | Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `29,513` | `29,513` | `29513`, `29,513.00` |
| `590.50` | `590.50` | `590.5` |
| `1.0000000000 %` | `1.0000000000 %` | `1.0%`, `1` |
| `-599,459` | `-599,459` | `(599,459)` |
| `(284,791)` | `(284,791)` | `-284,791` |

A negative amount MUST keep the form the page printed: a leading minus stays a minus, parentheses
stay parentheses. Converting between them is a reformat, and a reformat is how a value stops
matching the document it came from.

#### Identifiers are not normalised either

An entered SSN, TIN, policy number or account number MUST be transcribed exactly as printed. It
MUST NOT be rewritten to a canonical mask such as `XXX-XX-XXXX` or re-grouped to a standard shape.

This holds however the form splits the digits. A social security number printed across three
boxed groups is the printed digits, in the grouping the page uses:

```markdown
- \[E\] **Partner's SSN or TIN**: 27-4162256
```

Normalising an identifier looks harmless because the canonical form is *more* readable. It is the
same failure as rounding a number: the output stops matching the document, and a reader verifying
a value against the page finds a string that is not on it. A consumer that needs a canonical form
can derive one; it cannot recover the printed one.

#### Split dollar and cent columns

A form that prints dollars and cents in two ruled columns holds **one value**. It MUST be rendered
as one value — `1,234.00` — and MUST NOT be split across two fields. The rule lines are
typesetting, not structure.





#### Related

- Cell Text Fidelity (§9.6.3) — the same rule inside tables
- Accounting Number Formats (§9.6.1) — negative and zero forms kept as printed
- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) · Fill-Ins (§10.4.4) — where values sit

### 10.4 Fields

#### 10.4.1 Blanks Inside Sentences

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-blanks-inside-sentences` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A sentence with fill-in gaps MUST be kept intact, with each gap rendered as `[blank]` at its printed
> position. A hint printed with a blank MUST be kept next to that blank, once.

Affidavits, declarations and notarial blocks print their fields as prose with gaps in it:

```text
The Enterprise is ______________% Black Owned using the flow-through principle …
Executed on the (date) ______ day of (month) ____________ (year) ________
```

```markdown
The Enterprise is [blank]% Black Owned using the flow-through principle …
Executed on the *(date)* [blank] day of *(month)* [blank] *(year)* [blank]
```

Fill-Ins (§10.4.4) assumes a label followed by a field. Here there is no label — the sentence is the
label, and one sentence can hold three blanks. The sentence MUST NOT be broken up into key-value
lines, and a key MUST NOT be made up from the words before a blank.

#### The sub-cases

| The page prints | Output |
| --- | --- |
| A blank inside a sentence | `[blank]` in its printed position |
| A hint inside or beside the blank | The hint as printed, next to its own blank, once |
| A caption under the line | The caption kept with that blank, once, never duplicated |
| A currency glyph before a blank | `$[blank]`, keeping the printed spacing |

#### 10.4.2 Checkboxes

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-checkboxes` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A checked box MUST be rendered as `[x]` and an unchecked box as `[ ]`. An unchecked box MUST be
> transcribed explicitly and MUST NOT be dropped.

#### What counts as checked

A box is checked when it holds a **clear, unambiguous mark inside it** — a check, a cross, a
filled box.

- Handwriting or a mark *near* a box MUST NOT make it checked.
- A box whose state is in doubt MUST be rendered `[ ]`.
- A decorative bullet (●) printed beside a required field is not a check mark.

#### The rendered page decides

A check mark can exist only as **drawn strokes with no text-layer glyph** — common on degraded
scans. The state MUST be read from the rendered page, never from the text layer: a tick the text
layer never saw is still a tick. See The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1).

#### A lone labelled checkbox

The box sits in the value position:

```markdown
- **FATCA filing requirement**: [x]
- \[D\] **Check if this is a publicly traded partnership (PTP)**: [ ]
```

#### A checkbox with its own write-in

One line — the box first, then the entered text:

```markdown
- \[3\] [x] 8888
- **Other (specify):** [x] consulting
```

#### Every box on the page

A checkbox MUST be included wherever it sits — header, margin, footer: `Final K-1` /
`Amended K-1` at the very top of a K-1, `CORRECTED (if checked)` at the top of a 1099. See
Fields Outside the Form (§10.5.1).

#### Radio buttons

A radio control MUST be rendered with the same `[ ]` / `[x]` notation as a checkbox. Every option
MUST be kept, with its grouping, and a printed pick-one instruction MUST be kept as text.

#### 10.4.3 Checklists

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-checklists` · Tags: forms, checkboxes

> **✅ Normative**
> Each checklist item MUST be rendered box-first — the box before its printed label — and items
> MUST be nested under their group label. A group-level box MUST stay on its group's line. A form's
> group labels MUST NOT be promoted to document headings.

A list of items each led by a box, sometimes under a group label that carries a box of its own.
Nothing is being answered; the page is a to-do list or a required-documents list.

```text
☐ Division 9 rate filings
    ☐ Transmittal information
    ☐ Certification (EC-1, residential property)
    ☐ Rate filing checklist (Exhibit A)
```

```markdown
- [ ] **Division 9 rate filings**
  - [ ] Transmittal information
  - [ ] Certification (EC-1, residential property)
  - [ ] Rate filing checklist (Exhibit A)
```

A checklist item has no caption above it and no label before its box, so neither shape of
The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) applies unchanged: it is not an option of a captioned group, and it is not a
labelled field with a box in the value position. It is rendered box-first, like an option line.
