#### A box printed before an id

**The order of box and id.** A lettered or numbered item can print its box **before** its id:
`☐ (h) The crime of …`. It MUST be rendered box first, then the escaped id — `- [ ] \[h\] The crime
of …` — so that the box always opens the line whether or not an id follows it.

#### 10.4.4 Fill-Ins

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-fill-ins` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> Each printed entry field MUST be rendered as one line. An empty field MUST be rendered as `[blank]`
> and MUST NOT be omitted.

The blank is the word marker `[blank]`, like the protocol's other markers (`[signature]`, `[seal]`,
`[stamp]`). It replaces the older `[___]`, whose underscores pair up as emphasis whenever two blanks
share a line (`from [___] to [___]`) and vanish when the Markdown is rendered. A printed bracketed
word `[blank]` on the page is escaped, `\[blank\]` — see Escaping Printed Marks (§7.2.4).

```markdown
- \[1\] **Wages, tips, other compensation**: 29,513
- \[7\] **Social security tips**: [blank]
- \[9\]: [blank]
```

#### The shapes

| The page prints | Output |
| --- | --- |
| id + label + value | `- \[1\] **Label**: value` |
| id, no label *(shaded or unused boxes)* | `- \[9\]: [blank]` |
| neither id nor label, filled | the bare value |
| neither id nor label, empty | a bare `[blank]` |

#### An empty field is content

An empty field says *this was asked and not answered*. Dropping it loses that, and the field count
no longer matches the form — on a W-2 that is boxes 7–11, on a 1040 page 2 most of lines 17–31.

#### Adjacent boxes are separate fields

Two entry boxes printed side by side under one id are two fields and MUST NOT be fused into one
value. W-2 box 15 prints `State` and `Employer's state ID number` side by side:

```markdown
- \[15\]
  - **State**: SC
  - **Employer's state ID number**: 00-0000056
```

*(Source image form-w2-p1.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

#### A currency glyph before a blank

A currency glyph printed before an empty field MUST be kept immediately before the blank —
`$[blank]` — with any printed spacing preserved. The field's label MUST stay unchanged: the glyph is
not folded into it.

Separate blanks MUST be emitted only for fields that are separately labelled or independently
answerable.

form clearly asks for that value, even though no line, box or space is drawn. A field MUST NOT be
inferred from a colon in ordinary prose.

- Blanks Inside Sentences (§10.4.1) — blanks with no label before them
- Sections and Grouped Fields (§10.5.3) — boxes that group several fields
- Signatures (§7.3.10) — a signed signature field

#### 10.4.5 Option Groups

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-option-groups` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A question answered by ticking one or more of several printed boxes MUST be rendered as **one
> group**: the caption line, then one nested box-first line per option. Every printed option MUST
> be listed, ticked or not.

#### Pick-one

```markdown
- **Filing Status**
  - [x] Single
  - [ ] Married filing jointly
  - [ ] Married filing separately (MFS)
  - [ ] Head of household (HOH)
  - [ ] Qualifying widow(er) (QW)
```

#### A group whose caption is only its id

W-2 box 13 prints three independent checkboxes. They are one printed cluster, so they are one
group, captioned by the id alone:

```markdown
- \[13\]
  - [x] Statutory employee
  - [ ] Retirement plan
  - [ ] Third-party sick pay
```

#### Options keep their own ids and may carry a write-in

An option MUST keep its printed id — here printed before the box, and written there — and an
option with a write-in MUST carry the write-in after its box:

```markdown
- \[16\] **Tax (see instructions). Check if any from Form(s):**
  - \[1\] [ ] 8814
  - \[2\] [ ] 4972
  - \[3\] [ ] [blank]
- \[16\]: 0.00
```

The line-16 **amount** is a separate unlabelled entry that shares the printed id, rendered right
after the group. An id printed once per role appears once per role; that is not a duplicate.

#### Yes/No questions are option groups

A caption with two boxes — a virtual-currency question, K-1 items G and H1 — has the same
structure as a five-option filing status and MUST be rendered the same way.

*(Source image form-option-groups.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

```markdown
- **At any time during 2020, did you receive, sell, send, exchange, or otherwise acquire any financial interest in any virtual currency?**
  - [x] Yes
  - [ ] No
```





#### Related

- Checkboxes (§10.4.2) — the state of each box
- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) — the line format
- Ids and Labels (§10.3.1) — option ids and caption ids

#### 10.4.6 Printed Buttons and Placeholders

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-printed-buttons-and-placeholders` · Tags: forms, furniture

> **✅ Normative**
> The text of a printed button, and the caption of a box reserved for a later stamp or seal, MUST be
> transcribed as text where it sits, in reading order. A reserved box is not a fill-in and MUST NOT
> be rendered with `[blank]`.

Fillable PDFs export their widgets into the page: `Print`, `Save`, `Clear` buttons and the notice
beside them. Court forms reserve empty boxes — `[SEAL]`, `File Stamp Here`, `COURT USE ONLY` —
for something to be added by hand later.

| Printed thing | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **Buttons** — `Print` · `Save` · `Clear` in coloured pills at the page foot | their text, as text, in reading order — they are printed, so they are kept (**never drop**) |
| **Reserved boxes** — an empty ruled box whose caption says what will go in it | the caption as text, nothing else — no blank, since nothing is filled in there (**never invent**) |

### 10.5 Structure

#### 10.5.1 Fields Outside the Form

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-fields-outside-the-form` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A field printed in a header, a footer or anywhere outside the main form body MUST still be
> rendered. A field printed above the form MUST be placed before the form content; any other such
> field MUST be placed after it.

*(Source image form-outside-fields-1.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

*(Source image form-outside-fields-2.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

`CORRECTED`, `Final K-1`, `Amended K-1` sit outside the ruled form body and are easy to sweep
past, but each changes what the whole document means: a K-1 marked *Amended* is not the same
filing as one that is not.

#### Non-field text

Instructions, preambles and fine print on a form page MUST be transcribed at their printed reading
position, between the fields they accompany. They MUST NOT be gathered at the end of the region or
dropped.

##### ✅ **Sample** — an instruction between two sections

*(Source image bag-form-blue-hints.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

"Skip this section if both parties signed Section 12 above." sits between the section 13 heading
and its first field, in blue. It is not a field and is transcribed where it is printed.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown · excerpt, section 13 and footer</summary>

```markdown
<!-- … -->

### \[13\] Certificate of Service

Skip this section if both parties signed Section 12 above.

On *(enter service date)* [blank]

- **I certify that I sent a copy of this document to the other parties by:** *(select one)*
  - [ ] Borvika Courts E-Filing. *\[www.efiling.courts.bv.gov/efile\]*
  - [ ] Regular Mail, addressed to:
    *Name & full address:* [blank]
  - [ ] Other: *(explain)* [blank]
- **Signed:** [blank]

AFF 118 – Affidavit for Decree without Appearance

R: April 2, 2025

Page 3 of 3
```

</details>





#### Related

- Checkboxes (§10.4.2) — header and footer boxes are still checkboxes
- Form Reading Order (§10.5.2) — the order of the fields inside the form
- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) — the line format for these fields too

#### 10.5.2 Form Reading Order

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-form-reading-order` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> The fields of a form MUST be ordered by the form's printed indexing scheme — its ids — rather than
> by column-first or row-first geometry.

A form's ids are its intended order. Where lettered and numbered fields share a page, one scheme
MUST be read through, then the other, rather than sweeping across the page and interleaving them.

#### An id sequence stays contiguous

- Fields whose ids run in sequence MUST stay together and in order, **with no un-id'd field
  between them**.
- Unlabelled fields MUST be placed around the sequence, not inside it. A 1099-MISC is the standard
  case.

#### Sections do not interleave

Fields from different printed sections MUST NOT be mixed, even when they sit side by side on the
page.

#### Where this differs from block reading order

Reading Order (§5.9) orders *regions* on a page the way a person reads them. This rule orders
*fields* within a form, and the form's own numbering overrides visual position when the two
disagree — which on a dense tax form they routinely do. Where a group of fields prints no ids, the
order of Reading Order (§5.9) applies.





#### Related

- Sections and Grouped Fields (§10.5.3) — the sections that must not interleave
- Ids and Labels (§10.3.1) — what an id is
- Fields Outside the Form (§10.5.1) — fields outside the body go before or after it
- Reading Order (§5.9) — the order of regions, and of fields with no ids

#### 10.5.3 Sections and Grouped Fields

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-sections-and-grouped-fields` · Tags: forms

> **✅ Normative**
> A printed heading that names a group of fields opens a section. Only a printed grouping MAY get a
> parent: fields MUST NOT be wrapped in a section or group the form does not print.

A printed grouping takes one of two shapes, depending on its size.

#### Form grouping and the document outline

The Markdown headings of this rule delimit local form groups. They do not make every form label a
section of the document: a form's section labels are form content and MUST NOT be added to the
containing page's outline — least of all inside an embedded screenshot of a form. See
Recognising Ambiguous Headings (§6.7) for form furniture and real document titles.

#### Band or part headings become Markdown headings

A bold or boxed caption in the margin or spanning the page — `Part I`, `Filing Status`,
`POLICY INFORMATION`, `Sign Here` — MUST be rendered as a `###` heading, and every field printed
under or beside it MUST follow that heading.

The heading is **in addition to** the field labels inside it; both MUST be kept.

Where a printed designator sits beside a descriptive title, the designator is the id and the title
is the heading text:

```markdown
### \[Part II\] Information About the Partner

- \[E\] **Partner's SSN or TIN (Do not use TIN of a disregarded entity. See inst.)**: 38-7714902
- \[I1\] **What type of entity is this partner?**: CORPORATION
```

*(Source image form-k1-p1.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Bands with no printed ids work the same way:

```markdown
### POLICY INFORMATION

- **PROPOSED EFF DATE**: 08/23/2026
- **PROPOSED EXP DATE**: 08/23/2027
- **PAYMENT PLAN**: MONTHLY
- **MINIMUM PREMIUM**: [blank]
- **POLICY PREMIUM**: 34,259.95
```

*(Source image form-commercial-application-p1.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A section almost never holds a single field. One field under a heading usually means the heading
was invented.

#### Small captioned boxes become nested list items

A printed box whose label groups a few entries MUST be rendered as a parent list item with its
entries nested one level beneath it:

```markdown
- \[e\]
  - **Employee's first name and initial**: Joan Jackson
  - **Last name**: [blank]
  - **Suff.**: [blank]
- \[12a\]
  - **Code**: D
  - 1,500.00
- \[15\]
  - **State**: SC
  - **Employer's state ID number**: 00-0000056
```

The `12a` amount slot prints no label, so it is the bare value; an unlabelled empty entry would be
a bare `[blank]` — see Fill-Ins (§10.4.4).

#### Repeating groups without labels

Field groups that repeat without a printed heading are anonymous groups in printed order,
separated by blank lines, with no invented `Vehicle 1` heading — see
Repeated and Unlabelled Fields (§10.2).

#### Never invent a wrapper

The W-2 is almost entirely flat. It prints no `Identification` or `Employer` grouping, so neither
appears in the output. Inventing one is the same failure as inventing a table header: it adds
structure the page does not have.

- The Key-Value List (§10.3.2) — the line format inside each section
- Fill-Ins (§10.4.4) — the entries a box groups
- Form Reading Order (§10.5.2) — sections do not interleave
- Ids and Labels (§10.3.1) — the designator beside a section title

#### 10.5.4 Tables Inside Forms

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `forms-tables-inside-forms` · Tags: forms, tables

> **✅ Normative**
> Inside a form, a table MUST be used only for a **genuine grid**: one shared set of printed column
> headers over repeating rows of the same shape, or a printed row-by-column matrix. Where it is
> ambiguous, the fields SHOULD be rendered as individual field lines.

#### Numbered form lines are never table rows

A line with its own caption and one amount box is a **field line**, even when the amount boxes
align into a ruled column. It MUST be rendered as a field line, not as a table row: the alignment
is typesetting, the caption is the structure.

Dollars and cents printed in two ruled columns MUST be rendered as one value — `1,234.00` — never
split.

#### A matrix keeps its blank corner

The empty corner header of a matrix MUST be kept. Dropping it shifts every heading one column left:

```markdown
<table>
  <tr><th></th><th>Beginning</th><th>Ending</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Profit</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Loss</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Capital</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
</table>
```

This is the rule of a blank corner cell in any table (§9.3.1).

#### Cells carry the normal form notation

- A checkbox cell MUST be rendered `[x]` or `[ ]`. A blank cell *intended* to be checked is a
  checkbox; a blank cell not intended to be checked stays empty.
- Every printed row MUST be emitted, blank rows included, as full rows of empty cells. Rows MUST
  NOT be merged, reordered or added.
- Each entry belongs to its own row's rule lines, never to a neighbour's. Insurance-application
  coverage grids are the stress test.
- A cell containing form fields MUST use the normal form notation, as list items inside the cell.

```markdown
<tr><td>Jane</td><td>Doe</td><td>987-65-4321</td><td>Daughter</td><td>[x]</td><td>[ ]</td></tr>
<tr><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td>- [ ]</td><td>- [ ]</td></tr>
```

#### A table as a field's value

Some keyed entries take a grid as their value. The key MUST stay a normal field line, and the table
MUST be placed **below it, indented to the list item's content column**, with a blank line on each
side:

```markdown
- \[J\] **Partner's share of profit, loss, and capital (see instructions):**

  <table>
    <tr><th></th><th>Beginning</th><th>Ending</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Profit</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  </table>

- **Check if decrease is due to sale or exchange of partnership interest.**: [ ]
```

**The indent is load-bearing.** An indented table belongs to the list item, so the list — and the
depth of everything after it — survives. A flush-left table between bullets ends the list and
flattens everything that follows.

#### Not every table on a form page is form content

A large standalone data table that is not part of the fillable form — an embedded financial
schedule — is an ordinary table. See Is This Even a Table (§9.1.5).

## §11 Charts

### 11.1 The annotation

#### 11.1.1 Cover Every Data Point

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-cover-every-data-point` · Tags: charts, basics

> **✅ Normative**
> A chart MUST be rendered as a **chart table** that holds **every data point the chart draws**:
> every category position × every series, plus every printed callout that belongs to a position.
> A data point MUST NOT be skipped because it is hard to read; it MAY be left out only when no
> printed text can locate it or it is genuinely unreadable.

A chart is a data display, so its conforming rendering is its content — see
Images and Figures (§12.1.2). A rendering that gets a few prominent points right while the rest of the
chart is missing is not a rendering of the chart.

#### What full coverage means

| Chart | Data points the chart table MUST hold |
| --- | --- |
| Grouped or stacked bars | positions × series (the sample below: 6 years × 4 groups = 24 values) |
| Single series | one per position |
| Printed callouts and totals | one each, where a printed label can locate them — see Legend and Overlay Values (§11.2.4) |
| Multi-panel figure | every panel, without exception — see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3) |

Two kinds of position MUST still be covered:

- **A labeled position with no mark** is a data point whose value is `0` — the histogram's empty
  `1500` bin is `0` (see Bars and Histograms (§11.2.1)).
- **A position the axis does not label** is located by its axis value: `2023` on a year axis that
  ticks every third year, `2500` on a bin axis that labels every other bin. The printed, regularly
  labeled axis is the calibration; a position that no printed calibration reaches is not locatable.

#### What may be left out

The default is **in**. A data point that can be read MAY be left out only when:

- no printed text can uniquely locate it — see Labels (§11.1.2); the unnamed companion curve in
  Legend and Overlay Values (§11.2.4) is the standing example; or
- it is genuinely unreadable — too blurred, too dense, or overlapping beyond judgment.

Leaving a point out MUST NOT be replaced by invented text: a made-up series name, a made-up
category or a placeholder cell stands for nothing on the page (see Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2)).

#### The page is the only reference

Values are read from the page. A value MUST NOT be shaded towards what some parser or earlier
rendering produced, and a correct value stays correct however many renderings disagree with it
(see The Page Is the Ground Truth (§2.1)).

#### The chart table

Every table representing a chart MUST open with `<table data-source="chart">`. The
`data-source="chart"` attribute belongs on the opening `<table>` tag, including when the chart
prints a data grid that supplies the table's content (see Chart With a Printed Data Grid (§9.1.2)).
A table representing an ordinary printed table MUST NOT carry `data-source="chart"`.

**The layout of the chart table.** A chart table MUST be laid out as follows, so that every chart
table reads the same way — category down, series across:

- one HTML `<table data-source="chart">` per chart or panel, at the chart's place in reading order;
- the chart's title, subtitle or caption in `<caption>` inside that table, first or last according
  to reading order (see Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3)); its printed notes and source follow the table;
- one row per category position (axis tick, bar, bin, slice, tile, region, named point), in the
  order the axis runs — left to right, top to bottom, a pie clockwise from the top;
- a first column holding the category labels, then one column per series in legend order;
- a header row holding the printed series names, its first cell holding the printed category-axis
  title or left empty; a single series with no printed name is headed by the printed value-axis
  title; when nothing printed names any column, the table has no header row;
- a printed total that is not itself a category (a stack total above its bar) sits in a last column
  under an empty header cell;
- printed text of the chart that is not a data point — axis titles not used as headers, unit notes,
  reference-line labels, event callouts, annotation boxes, legend entries of series that carry no
  value — follows the table as plain text in reading order.

The value in each cell is governed by Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4); the labels in the first column and
the header row by Labels (§11.1.2).

#### 11.1.2 Labels

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-labels` · Tags: charts, labels

> **✅ Normative**
> The category labels and series names of a chart table MUST be text printed on the chart — an axis
> tick, a legend entry, a direct label — copied verbatim. A label MUST NOT carry unit text imported
> from elsewhere on the page, colour words, chart-type words or an expanded abbreviation, and two
> dimensions MUST NOT be merged into one label.

Each value in a chart table is located by the labels on its row and in its column, so the labels
are the lookup key of the whole table: a value under the wrong label is a wrong value.

#### Which label goes where

| Chart | Row label | Column label |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single series | the category (`Cleaners`) — see Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4) | the series name, or the value-axis title when no name is printed |
| Two-dimensional (grouped, stacked, multi-line) | the category (`China`) | the series (`Ride hailing`) |
| Grouped or nested categories | the category, with its printed group (axis tier) in a column of its own where the category alone repeats | the series |

A value MUST sit at the intersection of exactly the labels that locate it: its category's row and
its series' column. Dimensions stay independent — `2024` in the row and `Revenue` in the column,
never one label `2024 - Revenue`.

#### Verbatim, and what "no units" means

Each label is one printed string, copied whole — `SEA`, `> 15000`,
`Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS)`, `REDBIKE (Akira)`, `first-day-of-month price`. Parentheses printed
inside a legend entry are part of the legend text and MUST be kept.

The no-units requirement forbids **importing** unit text from elsewhere on the page into a label.
Where the axis corner prints `(millions of euros)` and the tick prints `2024`, the label is `2024`,
not `2024 (millions of euros)`. Likewise `Revenue`, not `Revenue (USD bn)`, when the unit prints as
an axis note rather than inside the legend entry. The unit note itself is not dropped: it stays in
the output as the chart's own text (see Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)).

A label MUST NOT be rewritten:

- no colour words — `Blue line - GDP Growth` is `GDP Growth`;
- no descriptive or chart-type suffixes — no `(line)`, no `(bars)`;
- no expanded abbreviations — `SEA` stays `SEA`.

#### Positions the axis does not label

A position on a printed, regularly labeled axis that carries no tick label of its own is labeled
by its **axis value** — `2023` on a year axis ticked every third year, `2500` on a bin axis labeled
every other bin. That label is a reading against printed calibration, not invented text (see
Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)).

#### Several charts with the same labels

Each chart or panel has its own chart table with its own printed title in `<caption>` (see
Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3)), so charts that reuse one label set are told apart by their
captions, without altering their labels. The caption appears once inside the table, first or last
according to reading order (see Titles Banners Captions (§9.7.3)).

- The twin pies in Legend and Overlay Values (§11.2.4) reuse every slice name; each pie's title
  (`Month of September 2025: $346B`, `Fiscal Year 2025 to Date: $7,010B`) is what distinguishes
  them.
- The solar panels in Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3) need nothing more: `China` with `619`
  appears only in the avoided-emissions panel.

A point that no printed label can locate is not rendered in the chart table (see
Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)); the unnamed companion curve in Legend and Overlay Values (§11.2.4) is the
standing example.

#### 11.1.3 Multiple Charts and Reference Ink

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-multiple-charts-and-reference-ink` · Tags: charts, structure

> **✅ Normative**
> Each chart or panel on a page MUST get its own chart table, and every panel MUST be covered (see
> Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)). Reference ink — labeled averages, trend lines, shaded bands, event
> callouts — draws no data points and MUST NOT be rendered as data: it gets no row, no column and
> no value in any chart table. Its printed text MUST still be kept.

#### Several charts on one page

Every chart and every panel of a multi-panel figure is its own chart table, in reading order, with
its printed title or panel heading in `<caption>`. The same one-row-per-position,
one-column-per-series coverage applies to each. Where charts share a label set, each table's
caption tells them apart (see Labels (§11.1.2)).

A caption shared by several panels MUST appear once: first inside the first panel's table when
read before the group, or last inside the last panel's table when read after the group. A shared
caption and that panel's own title are kept in printed order within the same `<caption>`.

Ink printed **once for several panels** — a shared axis title, a single legend serving every panel
— MUST NOT be lost:

- a shared legend names the series of every panel it serves, so each panel's table carries those
  series names as its column headers;
- a shared axis title is printed text of the figure and is kept once, as text.

#### Reference ink is not data

| Reference ink | Why it is not data |
| --- | --- |
| A labeled **average or trend line** (`10-year average`, a line fitted through a scatter) | it summarises the data points; it is not one of them |
| A **shaded band** or background region | it marks a span of the axis, not a value |
| An **event callout** naming a year (`1976: Tangshan Earthquake, China` — see Log Scale Charts (§11.2.6)) | it comments on a point; its value is the point's own |

A chart table that gains a column for a trend line, or a row for a shaded band, contains values
the chart never drew as data — invented content (see Never Drop, Never Invent (§2.2)). The printed
labels of reference ink are text on the page, kept as text, after the table in reading order — see
the chart table's layout in Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1).

#### 11.1.4 Values and Tolerances

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-values-and-tolerances` · Tags: charts, values

> **✅ Normative**
> Each cell of a chart table holds one of three values. A value **printed** on the chart MUST be
> copied character for character and in full. A value **not printed** MUST be estimated at the
> mark's visual centre against the mark's own axis. A mark **drawn at the baseline**, or a labeled
> position with **no mark**, MUST be `0`.

#### Printed values — copied exactly

Whatever the chart prints at, on or beside the mark is the value, in full:

- `25 (13.0%)` stays `25 (13.0%)` — not `25`, not `13.0%`, and never `25 countries (13.0%)`;
- printed formats stay: thousands separators (`11,270`), decimal commas (`2,08`), currency and
  percent marks, parentheses for negatives (`($60B)`), footnote markers (`<sup>1,2</sup>3.60`);
- printed beats geometry: where the label says `43`, the value is `43` even if the bar top measures
  a hair lower.

#### Estimated values — the visual centre

Where nothing is printed, the value is read at the mark's **visual centre** against **its own**
axis — a second axis where the series is scaled by one (see Dual-Axis and Combo Charts (§11.2.2)), the
decade bands of a logarithmic axis (see Log Scale Charts (§11.2.6)), and a stacked segment's own two
boundaries (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls (§11.2.9)).

An estimate SHOULD be a value a careful reader could defend within the readability tolerance
below — neither falsely precise nor coarser than the axis allows.

**How an estimated value is written.** An estimated value MUST be written as a bare number in the
axis's own format — its unit mark (`2.5%` on a percent axis) and its digit grouping (`17 000` on an
axis ticked `18 000`) — with no approximation marker, and no more precise than the reading
supports: at most one decimal place beyond the axis's tick labels, and two significant figures on a
logarithmic axis. Whether a value was printed or estimated is recoverable from the page and is not
marked in the Markdown.

#### Zeros

A mark **drawn at the baseline** is `0`. A **labeled position with no mark at all** is also `0` —
the histogram's empty `1500` bin is `0` (see Bars and Histograms (§11.2.1)). A stack that simply has no
segment of one series leaves that cell empty instead (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls (§11.2.9)).

#### Bars drawn in perspective

A printed bar value is copied first. Otherwise the value-bearing edge is read against the
corresponding axis plane, excluding perspective depth. Where the reference plane is ambiguous, the
value is the midpoint of the plausible readings.

#### How a checker compares values

A checker compares each cell with the value it reads off the page:

- **Printed value** — the same number, compared exactly. Formatting variants of the same number
  (thousands separators, decimal comma or point, currency and percent marks) MAY be treated as
  equal; a different number is wrong.
- **Estimated value** — accepted within a **relative tolerance** of the checker's own reading,
  chosen by how readable the mark is:

| How readable is the mark? | Relative tolerance |
| --- | --- |
| Sits on a gridline | 0.05 |
| Between gridlines, judgeable | 0.1 |
| Small, dense, or unclear scale | 0.15 – 0.2 |
| Near zero, where a relative band is too narrow | wider, as the reading demands (a `-1` read on a 10-unit grid takes 0.3) |

Most estimates fall between 0.05 and 0.15, and a tolerance above 0.2 is exceptional. The tolerance
is the range a careful eye can defend: not so tight that a second careful reading fails it, not so
loose that a wrong reading passes. For bars drawn in perspective it is widened to cover every
plausible reading.

### 11.2 Chart types

#### 11.2.1 Bars and Histograms

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-bars-and-histograms` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A bar chart MUST be rendered as a chart table with one value per bar: one row per category, one
> column per series. A histogram is a bar chart whose category is the bin: a bin the axis does not
> label MUST still get its row, labeled by its **axis value**, and a labeled position with **no bar**
> MUST hold `0`.

- A single series gives a two-column table — see the full example in Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4).
- Grouped bars give one column per legend series — see the full example in Labels (§11.1.2).
- Horizontal bars change nothing: the category axis simply runs vertically, and rows follow it top
  to bottom.
- A highlighted or average **bar** (`EU average`, shaded behind the rest) is an ordinary row. An
  average **line** is reference ink and adds nothing to the table (see
  Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3)).

#### Histogram bins

Printed bin labels are copied verbatim, catch-alls included (`> 15000`). When the axis labels only
every other bin, the unlabeled bins still exist: each gets a row labeled by its axis value — `2000`
between the ticks `1500` and `2500` on an axis labeled every $1 000. A bin that no printed
calibration reaches is not locatable (see Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)).

bar. Full coverage is 29 rows: `1500` holds `0`; the unlabeled bins are labeled by their axis values
(`2000`, `3000` …); every count is an estimate against the 20-unit grid. The catch-all keeps its
printed space (`> 15000`). The value axis title heads the single value column; the category axis
title heads the label column.

#### Progress and target bars

A goal statement with a single bar, its current value marked on it and the target at its right
end, is a **one-row bar chart**, not a chart type of its own. Its chart table MUST hold the current
value, the target and the axis end-points: the bar's meaning is relative to its scale, and `7`
against `8` or `42%` against `50%` is only legible with that scale kept.

#### 11.2.2 Dual-Axis and Combo Charts

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-dual-axis-and-combo-charts` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> Bars and lines on one canvas, or a second value axis, change only how values are **read**: each
> series' values MUST be copied or estimated against **its own** axis. The chart table is laid out
> as usual — one row per x position, one column per series — and a series name MUST NOT gain its
> mark type or axis side (no `(line)`, no `right axis`).

Before a value is estimated, the axis that scales its series is identified — from the legend order,
the mark type and the magnitudes of each axis's tick labels — and the value is traced to that axis.
A percentage series scaled by the right-hand axis read against the level axis on the left is a
wrong value, however plausible it looks.

#### 11.2.3 Gantt and Sankey Charts

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-gantt-and-sankey-charts` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A gantt chart MUST be rendered with one row per mark, giving the mark's label, its **start** and
> its **end** on the time axis — for a milestone, start and end are the same period. A sankey
> diagram MUST be rendered with one row per flow, giving its **source** node, its **target** node
> and the **value** it carries. Each family uses its one shape throughout, whatever the chart
> prints.

#### Gantt

The time axis is the value axis. Each bar's two edges are read against the printed ticks and
written as the periods the axis prints: months as month tokens (`Jan`), quarters under year headers
as quarter tokens with their year (`Q1 2025`). When the page prints exact dates for each task, those
printed dates are the start and end; when it prints them as a table beside the bars, that printed
table is the rendering and the bars add nothing to it (see Chart With a Printed Data Grid (§9.1.2)).

Nothing on the page prints the words *start* or *end*, and they MUST NOT be invented as labels of a
mark; the pair lives in the row's two period cells.

**How a gantt row is laid out.** A gantt chart MUST be one table with one row per task bar or
milestone, in the chart's top-to-bottom order: the printed label, the start period, the end period.
Its header row MUST be `Start` | `End` over the two period columns, with the first cell holding the
printed label column's title or left empty. These header cells are **protocol vocabulary**, like the markers `[blank]` or `[logo: …]`: the page does
not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to **never invent**, so that the columns
can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

**A bar edge on a period boundary.** A bar that fills January through March has its right edge on
the **April** tick. Its end MUST be the last period the bar **visibly fills** (`Mar`), and one
reading MUST be used throughout a document (see Choices Made Once Per Document (§4.2)). A checker
accepts a reading one boundary off.

#### Sankey

A flow's value is the number it carries. Where only node totals are printed, a node with a single
inflow or a single outflow gives that one flow its value, and the flow takes the same row shape. A
node that both splits and merges has no single flow its total belongs to: its total gives no flow
row, and its printed total is kept as text. A sankey that prints **no values** has no readable
flows: ribbon widths MUST NOT be estimated.

Node names in the source and target cells are copied **without** any printed node total. A ribbon
is traced from end to end before its row is written — values often print at the ribbon's start,
far from the target node, and a thin ribbon can pass under several others. A ribbon that cannot be
traced unambiguously gets no row.

**How a sankey flow is laid out.** A sankey diagram MUST be one table with one row per flow,
ordered by source from top to bottom and then by target, under the header row `Source` | `Target` |
`Value`. Each printed node total that is not any one flow's value follows the table as text, as
printed (`Industry 165`). These header cells are **protocol vocabulary**, like the markers `[blank]` or `[logo: …]`: the page does
not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to **never invent**, so that the columns
can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

#### How a checker judges spans and flows

A gantt span and a sankey flow are judged on meaning, not on a table shape: a checker accepts any
output that conveys both endpoints of a span at the granularity the axis prints — a positional grid
correctly aligned to the periods included — and accepts a span end one period boundary off. A
flow is accepted wherever the output conveys its source, its target and its value together. A
flow or span whose parts are scattered so that they can no longer be paired is not conveyed.

#### 11.2.4 Legend and Overlay Values

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-legend-and-overlay-values` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> When a chart's values are printed only in its legend or as data labels over its marks, those
> printed numbers **are** the data: every one of them MUST be in the chart table, copied exactly. A
> companion series without printed values is estimated as usual — unless no printed label can
> locate its points, in which case it has no column (see Labels (§11.1.2)).

Values print in three places, and all three are treated the same (see Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4)):

| Where the value prints | What goes in the table |
| --- | --- |
| **On or beside each mark** — bar-top numbers, slice amounts, point callouts | the printed value in the mark's cell |
| **In the legend** — `Solar (45%)`-style entries | the name part as the row or column label, the number part as the value |
| **At a direct label** — a line end stating its value (see Line Charts (§11.2.5)) | the printed value in the cell of that end position |

#### 11.2.5 Line Charts

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-line-charts` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A line chart MUST be rendered with one value per series per x position: one row per x position,
> one column per series, each series named by its legend entry or by its direct label at the line's
> end. A value printed at a point MUST be copied; every other value is read against the axis.
> Wiggles between x positions are not positions.

- A line labeled directly at its end is a named series: the printed name at the line's end heads
  its column (see Labels (§11.1.2)).
- An x position the axis does not label is labeled by its axis value (see
  Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)).
- A labeled trend, average or reference line adds no column (see
  Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3)).
- Scenario lines that share one drawn curve early on have identical values in those positions —
  correct, not a copying slip.

#### 11.2.6 Log Scale Charts

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-log-scale-charts` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A logarithmic axis changes the reading, not the chart table. Unprinted values MUST be estimated
> against the **printed decade bands**, by the mark's position inside its band, and SHOULD be given
> to no more than two significant figures.

On a tenfold-per-band axis the same visual gap covers ever larger ranges, so a value is
interpolated by **position inside the band**, not linearly: a mark a third of the way from `1 000`
to `10 000` is near `2 000`, not near `4 000`. The tolerance a checker allows is chosen by
readability like any estimate (see Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4)).

Event callouts naming years (`1976: Tangshan Earthquake, China`) are commentary: they add no row or
column, and their text is kept as text (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3)).

#### 11.2.7 Maps and Treemaps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-maps-and-treemaps` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A treemap MUST be rendered with one row per tile: the tile's label and its **printed** value.
> Tile area MUST NOT be turned into a value: no axis calibrates it. A map with **printed values
> per region** MUST be rendered with one row per printed region–value pair. A shading-only map
> with a discrete legend MUST give each region whose fill matches one swatch unambiguously that
> legend class, copied verbatim.

#### Treemaps

A tile's printed value is copied as printed. A tile that prints no value, only a comparator
(`<1%`), or a truncated label (`Re…`) gets no estimated value: its printed text is kept as it is,
and nothing is read from its area.

#### Maps

Two readable layers, each with its own place in the table (see also Geographic Maps (§12.2.4)):

- **Values printed per region or per pin** — one row per printed pair: the region or callout text
  as the label, the printed value copied as printed. A callout on a leader line (`DE 1`) is read
  like any other.
- **Shading with a discrete legend** — each region's fill is compared with the legend swatches, and
  the region takes the legend class **verbatim**. A region whose fill falls between two adjacent
  swatches is given no class.

**Where a map's classes go.** A choropleth MUST be one table with one row per region, in reading
order: the region label, its printed value when it has one, and its legend class in a last column
headed by the legend's printed title (no header row when the legend has none). A region with an
ambiguous fill has an empty class cell. Where the region names are recognised from the outlines
rather than printed, the region column's header carries `data-recognised` — see Geographic Maps (§12.2.4).

A checker judges a class on meaning: it accepts the class string, an equivalent range, or a value
inside the class's range, and treats region-name variants (`CO` / `Colorado`) as the same region.

#### 11.2.8 Scatter and Error Bars

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-scatter-and-error-bars` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A **named** scatter point MUST be rendered as one row holding its x value and its y value. Marker
> series over categories are ordinary series columns. An error bar's **centre** is an ordinary
> value, and its **whisker span** MUST be given with it: the low and high ends read at the whisker
> caps. A box plot MUST give its median, first and third quartiles, and its whisker ends when they
> are drawn. Points with no printed name have nothing to locate them and are not rendered as rows.

#### Scatter

Each named dot contributes its two coordinates, each read against its own axis (see
Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4)). A fitted trend line through the cloud is reference ink (see
Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3)).

**How scatter points, whiskers and boxes appear in the chart table.**

- A scatter chart MUST give one row per named point, a column for x and a column for y, each headed
  by its printed axis title.
- An error bar's interval MUST be written in the centre's cell, after the centre, as
  `centre (low–high)` — `3.60 (3.47–3.73)`.
- A box plot MUST give one row per box: its label, then the low whisker end, first quartile, median,
  third quartile and high whisker end in axis order, the whisker ends only where drawn, under the
  header row `Low` | `Q1` | `Median` | `Q3` | `High` (first cell: the printed label column's title,
  or empty). These header cells are **protocol vocabulary**, like the markers `[blank]` or `[logo: …]`: the page does
  not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to **never invent**, so that the columns
  can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

#### Error bars

The centre is copied when printed and estimated otherwise. The whisker ends are read at the caps
against the axis, like any estimate. A whisker whose ends cannot be read honestly is not given an
interval.

A checker judges the interval on meaning: it accepts any output that conveys it —
`3.60 ± 0.13`, `3.60 (3.47–3.73)`, separate low and high columns, prose — within the tolerance of
an ordinary estimate, and fails a centre given with no interval.

#### Related

- Values and Tolerances (§11.1.4) — coordinates and whisker ends are ordinary estimates
- Labels (§11.1.2) — named points, and the tie between two boxes over one category
- Multiple Charts and Reference Ink (§11.1.3) — trend lines and reference lines are not data
- Line Charts (§11.2.5) — named lines instead of named points

#### 11.2.9 Stacked Bars and Waterfalls

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `charts-stacked-bars-and-waterfalls` · Tags: charts, types

> **✅ Normative**
> A stacked segment's value MUST be the segment's **own span** — the size it draws between its two
> boundaries — never the cumulative height at its top edge. A waterfall step follows the same rule
> on a floating segment: its value is the rise or fall the step itself draws. Each segment series
> is a column; a printed total is a value of its own.

Writing the running total instead of the segment is the failure this family exists to catch. An
estimated segment is read at both boundaries, and its value is the difference.

- A category whose stack has no segment of one series leaves that cell empty.
- A printed total above a stack sits in the stack's row, in a last column under an empty header
  cell (see the chart table's layout in Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1)).
- A waterfall's anchor bars (start and end levels) are categories of their own; their values are
  levels, not changes.

## §12 Images and diagrams

### 12.1 Images

#### 12.1.1 Images

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `images-images` · Tags: rule, images

> **✅ Normative**
> The content of an image MUST be put into the text stream as whatever the image actually is —
> transcribed text, a table or a diagram. The output MUST NOT contain a file reference or a
> bracketed placeholder in place of an image.

An image is not a thing to point at; it is content that happens to have been rasterised. Whatever
a reader would take away from looking at it MUST end up in the output as text, or it is lost —
the **never drop** failure.

#### Decide what the image is, then encode that

| The image is really… | The output MUST contain |
| --- | --- |
| Text rendered as a picture | The text, transcribed verbatim |
| A data display (chart, plot) | A chart table — Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1) |
| A labelled schematic or conceptual figure | A suitable `diagram/<language>` block; `description` only if none can preserve it — Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5) |
| A graph of relationships or a flow | A `diagram/<language>` fenced block (for example `diagram/mermaid` or `diagram/plantUml`) — Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2) |
| A photo or decorative art | A prose description of what it shows |

The rows are tried in order. Where any text at all is legible inside the image, that text MUST be
transcribed: it is content, and describing it instead ("a chart showing quarterly revenue") drops
every number on the page.

#### When the type is not obvious

Some figures resist the table above: maps, chemical structures, electrical schematics, blueprints,
printed staves. Each has its own rule — Geographic Maps (§12.2.4), Chemical Molecules (§13.1),
Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3), Blueprints (§12.2.1), Music Notation (§13.2), Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5). Where that rule
has no settled encoding yet, the fallback is the same: every label and every legible string MUST
be preserved, and the output MUST use the encoding that loses no content.





#### Related

- Images and Figures (§12.1.2) — the same rule with equations and multi-column pages
- Iconography and Symbols (§7.3.4) — the small, semantically loaded end of the same spectrum
- Logos (§12.1.3) — what a brand mark becomes in the text stream
- Output Options (§3.5) — when a saved image may be referenced instead of described

#### 12.1.2 Images and Figures

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `images-images-and-figures` · Tags: rule, diagrams, images

> **✅ Normative**
> The output MUST NOT contain an image reference `![caption](path)` or a bracketed placeholder
> such as `[The image shows…]`. A figure's content MUST be rendered **as** text, a table or a
> diagram — whichever the figure actually is.

An output is consumed by a model or an extraction step. An image reference is a dead end to both;
the content has to be *in* the text stream.

#### Choosing the form

| The figure is really… | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| A data display (chart, plot) | A chart table — Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1) |
| A graph of relationships | A `diagram/<language>` fenced block (for example `diagram/mermaid` or `diagram/plantUml`) — Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2) |
| A labelled schematic | A suitable `diagram/<language>` block; `description` only if none can preserve it — Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5) |
| A photo or decorative art | A prose description of what it shows |
| Text rendered as an image | The text, transcribed |

#### Equations

Equations MUST be LaTeX in `$$ … $$`, inline ones included — see Inline Equations (§7.2.6). Using `$$`
uniformly keeps a stray currency symbol elsewhere on the page from opening an unterminated math
span.

#### Multi-column pages

Multi-column text MUST be unrolled into a single column in reading order. The physical column split
is a typesetting artefact, not structure, and MUST NOT be preserved — see Reading Order (§5.9).





#### Related

- Images (§12.1.1) — the general rule, with the order in which the forms are tried
- Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2) — when a figure is a graph
- Cover Every Data Point (§11.1.1) — what a chart becomes
- Layout Regions (§5.7) — separating the figure's region from the text around it

#### 12.1.3 Logos

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `images-logos` · Tags: images, furniture

> **✅ Normative**
> A logo MUST be rendered as a marker carrying its printed words, `[logo: OSTREVANE]`, at the logo's
> place in reading order. A logo that prints no legible text MUST be rendered as `[logo]`. The
> artwork MUST NOT be described.

Almost every slide and letterhead carries one: a wordmark in the corner, a symbol beside it,
sometimes a faint version behind the content. The marker keeps the printed words (**never drop**)
and tells a reader that they are a brand mark rather than a word of the body text.

#### Requirements

- The words a logo prints MUST appear inside the marker exactly as printed, case included:
  `[logo: VELTRAND LIFE]`. A wordmark set on two lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
- The marker sits at the logo's place in reading order. A logo inside a header or footer band stays
  inside that band — see Recurring Page Furniture (§4.6).
- A logo with no legible text — a symbol on its own — is the bare `[logo]`.
- A symbol printed beside its own wordmark is part of that logo; it does not get a second marker.
- A faint copy of a mark repeated behind the content is not a second logo and adds nothing; it MUST
  NOT break into the table or paragraph it lies behind. A faint background mark that carries words
  is a watermark — see Watermarks (§7.3.13).
- The artwork — colours, shapes, the apple — MUST NOT be described.

### 12.2 Diagrams

#### 12.2.1 Blueprints

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `diagrams-blueprints` · Tags: images, diagrams

> **✅ Normative**
> A floor plan or architectural drawing MUST use a faithful `diagram/<language>` encoding,
> preferring `diagram/tikz` then `diagram/svg`. If no suitable language can represent it faithfully,
> it MUST use a fenced `description` block. The output MUST preserve visible geometry, labels and
> printed measurements without inferred relationships or computed values. It MUST NOT be a table.

Floor plans and architectural drawings.

#### How the element is recognised

A drawing whose content is spatial: walls, rooms, dimensions, door swings, labels placed where the
thing they name sits. There are no rows and no columns — only positions.

#### Why a table is the wrong answer

A floor plan forced into a grid becomes a table of spatially adjacent labels that reads as data
downstream. That is worse than a description, because it is confidently wrong: nothing in the
output signals that the rows and columns were invented — the **never invent** failure. A floor plan
MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

The same trap appears in Geographic Maps (§12.2.4) (map coerced into a table) and
Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3) (circuit coerced into a graph): a spatial artefact flattened into a
linear structure that cannot carry position.

#### Encode the spatial content

Language selection follows Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2). The encoding MUST preserve visible walls,
openings, door swings, relative positions, dimensions, labels, scale bars, legends and notes.
Drawing coordinates MAY follow the visible geometry; they MUST NOT assert unprinted real-world
measurements. Inconsistent printed dimensions MUST be copied without correction. A room graph
that drops geometry is not a faithful encoding of a floor plan.

#### Description fallback

Only when no suitable language can faithfully encode the drawing, use a fenced `description`
block in this shape:

1. **What it is** — one line describing the drawing.
2. **Areas and visible structure** — one item per labelled area in reading order, its printed label
   and size verbatim, followed by visible walls, openings and spatial relationships.
3. **Dimensions and notes** — every dimension line, scale bar, legend entry, north arrow label and
   note, verbatim.

Unshown adjacency, hidden openings, computed areas and corrected dimensions MUST NOT be added.
A visible doorway or shared wall may be described as drawn; proximity alone does not establish a
connection. The description MUST distinguish what is visible from what cannot be determined.

##### ✅ **Sample** — a single-storey plan

*(Source image blueprint.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Twelve labelled areas, eight of them with a printed size, and dimension lines on all four sides. The
printed dimensions do not add up (`32'-0"`, `40'-0"` and `44'-0"` under a `62'-0"` span) and are
copied as printed.

#### Related

- Geographic Maps (§12.2.4) — the same trap of a spatial figure coerced into a table
- Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3) — a spatial figure coerced into a graph
- Images (§12.1.1) — the general rule for what an image becomes

#### 12.2.2 Diagrams and Flowcharts

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `diagrams-diagrams-and-flowcharts` · Tags: rule, diagrams

> **✅ Normative**
> A diagram or blueprint MUST use a fenced `diagram/<language>` block when a suitable language
> can faithfully represent its content. If no suitable language can do so, the output MUST use a
> fenced `description` block. A diagram that is really tabular SHOULD be rendered as an HTML table.
> A diagram MUST NOT be left out of the output.

#### Fence and language selection

The opening fence MUST identify the language actually used: `diagram/mermaid`, `diagram/plantUml`,
`diagram/dot`, `diagram/tikz`, `diagram/svg`, `diagram/circuitikz`, or another suitable
`diagram/<language>` tag. The suffix is case-sensitive; `plantUml` is the canonical PlantUML
spelling. `diagram/<language>` is a pattern, not a literal tag. Bare `mermaid`, `plantuml`,
`diagram` and `diagram/text` MUST NOT be used for diagram output.

The producer SHOULD use the following priority order, considering only languages that preserve
all the figure's content. A higher-ranked language MUST NOT be used if doing so loses information.
Different figures in one document MAY use different languages. An unlisted language MAY be used
when it preserves content the listed choices cannot. The order is a protocol preference, not a
claim that every language supports every figure in that row.

| Figure type | Preferred languages, in order | Content that decides suitability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flowchart, process, organisation chart | Mermaid → PlantUML → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG | Labels, branches, arrow directions, grouping |
| UML, sequence, class, state, ER diagram | PlantUML → Mermaid → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG | Diagram-specific symbols, relations, multiplicity, message order |
| Functional block, system or network diagram | Mermaid → PlantUML → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG | Blocks, ports, signal paths, nesting; positions when meaningful |
| Dense dependency graph or tree | Graphviz DOT → Mermaid → PlantUML → TikZ → SVG | Complete nodes, edges, directions and clusters |
| Blueprint, floor plan, geometric or spatial schematic | TikZ → SVG | Walls, openings, geometry, orientation, dimensions and label placement |
| Component-level electrical circuit | CircuiTikZ → TikZ circuit libraries → SVG | Component symbols, pins, junctions, wire crossings, topology and orientation |

Mermaid and PlantUML MAY represent a conceptual room-relationship diagram when its content is
only nodes and connections. They MUST NOT replace a spatial floor plan with an automatically
arranged graph that loses walls, openings, geometry or dimensions. A language being called
“architecture” does not make it a floor-plan encoding.

The block body MUST be valid in its named language. Every printed label, connector, direction,
meaningful grouping and spatial feature MUST be preserved, without adding inferred content.
Internal identifiers and drawing coordinates are encoding, not additional printed measurements;
coordinates MAY follow visible geometry but MUST NOT be presented as measured real-world values.
Printed measurements MUST be copied verbatim even when inconsistent.

#### Description fallback

When no suitable language can faithfully encode the figure, the output MUST use a fence whose
entire tag is `description`, not `diagram/description` or `diagram/text`. The body follows the
fixed shape in Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5), Blueprints (§12.2.1) or Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3): printed title if
present, what is visibly shown, labels and their visible features, then values and notes. It MUST
preserve all legible text and describe visible structure without guessing hidden connections,
measurements or domain meanings. Difficulty alone does not justify replacing an encodable diagram
with a description. The fallback examples below and in the specialised notes illustrate this
case; they do not require descriptions when a faithful encoding is available.

Charts, geographic maps, chemical formulae and music retain their specialised content rules.

````text
```diagram/mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Application received] --> B{Complete?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Underwriting]
  B -->|No| D[Return to applicant]
```
````

#### Preserve spatial and domain meaning

Automatic graph layout is suitable when connections carry the meaning. Where positions,
orientations or physical topology matter, the chosen language MUST preserve them. Floor plans
follow Blueprints (§12.2.1), circuits follow Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3), maps follow Geographic Maps (§12.2.4),
and structural formulae follow Chemical Molecules (§13.1). A successful render alone does not show
that an encoding preserved the source.

#### Labelled conceptual diagrams

When no suitable language can faithfully encode a labelled conceptual figure, it is rendered as a fenced
`description` block that names each element and what is visibly drawn there, so a chunker keeps the labels together —
see Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5):

````text
```description
## Detector cross-section
- **Anode**: top grid
- **S2**: secondary scintillation, produced in the gas phase
- **e<sup>-</sup>**: electrons drifting upward through the liquid
```
````

#### Examples

##### ✅ **Sample** — an organisation chart

*(Source image corpus-org-chart.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A staffing chart: boxed roles connected by rules into a strict hierarchy, five departments across
the top and two separate contracted-services blocks below.

**This is the case Mermaid is for.** The content is entirely nodes and edges — who reports to whom
— and none of the meaning lives in where a box sits on the page. Redrawn by a layout engine it
would still say the same thing, which is exactly the test that a circuit or a floor plan fails.

Two things are easy to lose and MUST be carried across: the **numbered suffixes** distinguishing
repeated roles (`事務員①`, `事務員②`), and the **annotations inside or beside the boxes**
(`週29H`, `週1×4H`) — those are hours, not decoration, and they belong to the node they sit with.
Each bracketed department label (`＜管理課＞`) names the group above it and becomes a subgraph
title. Edges follow the printed rules: each department head connects by a rule to the stack of
roles beneath it. The two lower blocks print no connecting rules, so their roles are grouped
without edges. Expected boxes: the title line, and the chart as one Picture box.

#### Language references

The preference order above is a protocol choice informed by the documented language capabilities:
[Mermaid diagram types](https://mermaid.js.org/intro/syntax-reference.html),
[PlantUML diagram types](https://plantuml.com/),
[Graphviz DOT](https://graphviz.org/docs/layouts/dot/),
[TikZ coordinates](https://tikz.dev/tikz-coordinates),
[SVG](https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG2/Overview.html), and
[CircuiTikZ](https://circuitikz.github.io/circuitikz/).

#### 12.2.3 Electrical Schematics

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `diagrams-electrical-schematics` · Tags: images, diagrams

> **✅ Normative**
> A component-level circuit schematic MUST use a faithful `diagram/<language>` encoding,
> preferring `diagram/circuitikz`, then `diagram/tikz`, then `diagram/svg`. If no suitable language
> can faithfully represent it, it MUST use a fenced `description` block. Every component symbol,
> designator, value, pin, terminal, net label and visibly drawn connection MUST be preserved.

Circuit diagrams.

*(Source image electrical-schematic.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

The figure above is an IC functional block diagram rather than a component-level circuit; it follows
Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2), using `diagram/plantUml`, `diagram/mermaid` or another suitable language
that preserves the printed blocks and signal connections. The component-level requirements below
do not apply to a functional block diagram.

#### How the element is recognised

Component symbols joined by wires, usually with a reference designator and a value beside each one
(`R1 1Ω`, `C3 10μF`). The way the components are oriented, and whether they sit in series or in
parallel, is part of the content.

#### Preserve circuit meaning

The encoding MUST preserve component orientation, pins, junctions, crossings and series/parallel
connections as drawn. An automatic graph layout that changes circuit meaning MUST NOT be used.
Functional block diagrams use the block-diagram priorities in Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2).

#### The fixed shape

When no suitable language can faithfully encode the circuit, the fallback uses a fenced
`description` block (see
Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5)).

1. **What it is** — one line: `Buck regulator input stage.`
2. **Components** — a list, one item per component in reading order (top to bottom, left to
   right): designator then value, both exactly as printed (`R1 1Ω`, `C3 10μF`). A component with no
   printed value is listed by its designator.
3. **Pins, terminals and nets** — every printed pin, terminal and net label, verbatim.
4. **Connections** — describe wires and junctions visibly drawn between identified parts. A crossing
   MUST NOT be treated as a junction unless the drawing marks it as one. Hidden or ambiguous
   connections MUST NOT be guessed.

Every printed designator, value and label is printed content and MUST be transcribed (**never
drop**). Values MUST NOT be computed, normalised or corrected.

- Chemical Molecules (§13.1) — the settled case of a domain notation preferred over a graph
- Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2) — language priorities and the description fallback
- Blueprints (§12.2.1) — another spatial drawing that a linear structure cannot carry
- Slide Diagrams (§12.2.5) — labelled figures that are not circuits

#### 12.2.4 Geographic Maps

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `diagrams-geographic-maps` · Tags: images, diagrams

> **✅ Normative**
> How a map is rendered depends on what it is *for*. A data map whose values sit in **drawn
> regions** MUST be rendered as a `Region | Value` table — the region names MAY be recognised from
> the drawn outlines when the page does not print them, and the key column is then marked
> `data-recognised`. A map of values placed only by position MUST be described, with its legend
> transcribed, and no table. A map whose content is geography MUST be described. Every printed label
> MUST be kept.

A map appearing as a figure — typically a choropleth, or a labelled regional map.

#### The test

What the figure is carrying decides the rendering:

| The map is… | Rendering |
| --- | --- |
| **A data display wearing a costume** — a shaded rate map is a `Region \| Value` table drawn on an outline; the geography is decoration, the numbers are the content | An HTML `<table data-source="chart">`, region in one column and value in another, with the legend's units kept in the caption |
| **Data placed only by position** — readings plotted at points, identified by nothing but where they sit | A description with the legend transcribed; no table |
| **A real map** — routes, adjacency, borders, position relative to other features; flattening it to a table destroys the only information it carried | A description, with every printed label, legend entry and scale transcribed |
| **Both** — shaded values *and* meaningful geography, or it cannot be told which | The description **and** the table: two encodings lose nothing, picking one loses half the figure |

#### The key column

A table needs a key. When the regions carry no printed names, the key MAY be supplied by
recognising the drawn regions — Italian regions from their outlines, US states from theirs — but
only when every value sits inside one drawn, bounded region and the region is unambiguous to a
reader of the page. A recognised key is not printed text, so the table MUST say so: the header cell
of the key column carries the attribute `data-recognised`, and a header the page does not print is
worded after the map's own caption or legend.

```html
<tr> <th data-recognised>Regione</th> <th>Prevalenza (%) …</th> </tr>
```

Values positioned only by coordinates — a scatter of point readings with no names — have no region
to recognise. They MUST NOT be tabulated by coordinate; the map is described and its legend
transcribed.

Whatever the rendering, the printed text of a map — title, caption, legend, labels, scale — MUST be
kept (**never drop**).

#### Examples

*(Source image map-as-printed.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A regional map of Italy shaded in three bands, one value printed in each region, a four-entry
legend and a caption. The geography is decoration; the values are the content, so the map is a
table. The map prints only values: each region is recognised from its outline, so the key column is marked
`data-recognised`, and its header follows the caption's wording. Basilicata is printed white (`n.d.`) with no value, so it has no
row; the caption states the gap. The table as it renders:

##### ✅ **Sample** — a map that is entirely data, with no printed key

*(Source image corpus-data-map.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

An observed-precipitation map: state outlines, and on top of them a dense scatter of numeric
readings, colour-coded by value.

*(Source image corpus-data-map-detail.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

This is a data display wearing a map, so the test says table. But it is also the case where that
answer stops being practical: the readings are positioned by latitude and longitude with **no
station names printed**, so there is no key column to put them in. The readings sit at points,
not in drawn regions, so there is nothing to recognise as a key: the legend text is transcribed,
the map is described, and no table is built.

The legend block in the top-left — title, valid time, sources and a red *"Data not fully quality
controlled"* caveat — is printed text and MUST survive whatever is done with the plotted values.
The red colour is emphasis, not a value, and is not carried. The plotted readings are too small to
transcribe reliably at this resolution and are not listed.

#### 12.2.5 Slide Diagrams

*✅ Normative · page rule*
Rule ID: `diagrams-slide-diagrams` · Tags: images, diagrams

> **✅ Normative**
> A labelled figure MUST use a suitable `diagram/<language>` encoding when one can preserve its
> content faithfully, following the language priorities in Diagrams and Flowcharts (§12.2.2). A labelled figure that no suitable diagram language can faithfully express MUST
> be rendered as a fenced `description` block in the fixed shape: one line saying what the figure is,
> then one bullet per printed label, verbatim, followed only by what is visibly drawn there, then
> printed values and notes. The block MUST NOT explain what a label means.

A slide diagram or scientific figure is a picture whose meaning lives in its **labels**: names of
parts, signal names, arrows showing direction. The labels are content and MUST NOT be lost. A
plain prose description SHOULD be used only when the figure carries no labels at all.

*(Source image slide-diagram.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

A slide: its title, a detector cross-section with labels, two small charts (`Summary`,
`Scintillation`) and two bullets. The cross-section is transcribed by the `description` block below;
the title, charts and bullets are separate elements.

#### Choose a language that fits the figure

Where the figure's content is labelled parts joined by drawn lines or arrows, it is a graph, and
Mermaid, PlantUML or another suitable language can carry it: preserve each labelled part, drawn connector, direction and meaningful position.
Where no suitable language preserves the content of a cross-section, apparatus or anatomy drawing,
use the `description` fallback block.

#### The `description` block

The block is a fenced code block tagged `description`, in the same fixed shape used for every described
figure (see Blueprints (§12.2.1) and Electrical Schematics (§12.2.3)):

1. The figure's printed title as a `##` heading, if it prints one; then **one line saying what the
   figure is**, in plain visual terms.
2. **One bullet per printed label**, in reading order, the label in bold and verbatim, followed only
   by what is visibly drawn at it — "arrow pointing down", "row of squares at the top". A label
   printed several times is listed once with its count.
3. **Printed values, scales and notes**, verbatim.

What a label *means* — "secondary scintillation signal produced in the gaseous phase" — is domain
knowledge, not printed, and MUST NOT appear (**never invent**). Text around the figure — a slide
title, bullets, small charts beside the drawing — is rendered as its own elements outside the
block; a chart becomes a chart table.

````text
```description
Cross-section of a two-layer detector.
- **Gaseous Xenon**: upper layer
- **Anode**: line to the row of squares at the top
- **S2**: in the upper layer
- **Extraction**: arrow pointing down at the boundary between the layers
- **e<sup>-</sup>** (four times): beside an arrow pointing up
- **Drift-field**: dotted arrow pointing down
- **S1**: beside a star
- **DM**: arrow pointing to the star
- **Cathode**: row of squares at the bottom
- **Liquid Xenon**: lower layer
```
````

Superscripts and subscripts inside the block stay inline as `<sup>` / `<sub>`, the same as anywhere
else — see Superscript and Subscript (§7.2.11). Equations inside the block stay in `$$ … $$` — see
Inline Equations (§7.2.6).

#### Why the fenced block

The fence gives the region a boundary, so a chunker keeps the diagram's labels together rather than
scattering them into surrounding prose — and a consumer that does not want diagrams can strip the
block wholesale.

##### ✅ **Sample** — an electrochemical cell with an equation in it

*(Source image bag-cell-voltage-diagram.png is available in the guide; this download is a text-only reference.)*

Two electrodes in a solution, `Δφ(…)` labels with arrows, boxed text (`The cell is
Pt/M′/S/M/Pt`, `ε can be measured`) and a full equation along the bottom edge. Every string
belongs to the figure. Six arrows point at the electrodes, but only five `Δφ(…)` labels are
legible: the sixth, at the right, is hidden behind the `ε can be measured` box, and only its
leading `Δ` shows — so only the `Δ` is transcribed. Expected boxes: the whole framed figure as one
Picture box.

<details>
<summary>Expected Markdown</summary>

````markdown
```description
## Cell Voltage and Electrode Potential
The diagram shows an electrochemical cell: electrodes M′ and M stand in a vessel whose lower part holds an ionic solution, a wire joins their tops through a PMI box, and six arrows point at the electrodes and contacts.
- **Pt**: contact on the wire at the top of each electrode, left and right.
- **PMI**: box on the wire between the two electrodes.
- **ε**: double-headed arrow between the two electrodes, below the PMI.
- **M′**: left electrode.
- **M**: right electrode.
- **Ionic solution**: the liquid in the lower part of the vessel.
- **φ(s)**: printed in the solution.
- **Δφ(Pt,S)**: arrow to the left Pt contact.
- **Δφ(S,Pt)**: arrow to the right Pt contact.
- **Δφ(Pt,M′)**: arrow to the top of electrode M′.
- **Δφ(M′,S)**: arrow to electrode M′ in the solution.
- **Δφ(Pt,M)**: arrow to the top of electrode M.
- **Δ**: arrow to electrode M at the solution surface; the rest of the label is hidden behind the "ε can be measured" box.
- **The cell is Pt/M′/S/M/Pt**: boxed statement, top right.
- **ε can be measured**: boxed statement, right, followed by $$\varepsilon = E(r) - E(l)$$
- Equation along the bottom edge: $$\varepsilon = [\Delta\varphi(Pt,M) + \Delta\varphi(M,S)] - [\Delta\varphi(M',S) + \Delta\varphi(Pt,M')]$$
```
````

</details>
